text: Our voyage beneath the waves enters its second phase. That initial stage concluded with the poignant event at the coral burial ground, an experience that etched itself firmly into my thoughts. In this manner, Captain Sorel’s existence was concluding within the heart of this vast ocean, reaching the final resting place he had arranged in one of its most profound depths. Within that location, no sea creature could disturb the eternal rest of the Meridian’s company, those companions bound together in their passing just as they were in their living years. “Nor any man, either,” had added the Captain. His unrelenting, bitter contempt for the world of men remained unchanged.
The hypothesis that contented Baptiste was no longer sufficient for me.

That respectable individual remained convinced that the Commander of the Meridian was among those obscure scholars who repay the world’s apathy with scorn. In his view, he was a misinterpreted mastermind who, weary of the world’s betrayals, had sought sanctuary in this unreachable environment, where he could pursue his impulses without restraint. To me, this clarifies merely a single facet of Captain Sorel’s personality. In truth, the enigma of that final night when we were held captive, the slumber, and the measure so aggressively executed by the Captain in tearing from my sight the lens I had lifted to scan the distance, the fatal injury of the man, caused by an inexplicable jolt of the Meridian, all directed me toward a different conclusion. No; Captain Sorel did not merely desire to avoid humanity. His imposing machine served not only his urge for independence, but possibly also the intent of some ghastly vengeance.

Right now, everything remains obscure to my understanding; I only perceive a faint glimmer of illumination within the surrounding gloom, and I am compelled to restrict my record to whatever the unfolding circumstances require.

On the 24th of January, 1868, at midday, the second officer arrived to measure the sun’s altitude. I climbed onto the platform, ignited a cigar, and observed the procedure. It appeared to me that the individual lacked an understanding of French; I repeatedly spoke aloud, which should have elicited some reflexive reaction from him had he grasped my words, yet he stayed silent and unmoved.

While he measured with the sextant, a seaman from the Meridian—the muscular fellow who had joined our initial underwater trip to the Island of Carrizo—approached to wipe the lantern lenses. I inspected the device’s components, whose power was magnified a hundred times by lenticular rings arranged like those in a lighthouse, casting their glow along a horizontal plane. The electric lamp was configured to yield its maximum illumination. In fact, it operated in vacuo, guaranteeing both stability and brightness. This vacuum saved the graphite points where the luminous arc formed—a vital saving for Captain Sorel, for whom replacements were difficult to obtain; given these circumstances, their deterioration was negligible. Once the Meridian was prepared to resume its submerged voyage, I descended to the cabin. The shutter was shut, and the heading set due west.

Our vessel was traversing the Indian Ocean, an immense watery expanse covering 1,200,000,000 acres, possessing a clarity so profound that gazing downward would induce vertigo. Typically, the Meridian remained submerged at depths ranging from fifty to one hundred fathoms. We continued in this fashion for several days. While others might have found the time tedious and repetitive, my own deep affection for the sea made it otherwise; the daily strolls upon the platform to breathe in the invigorating sea air, the view of the vibrant depths visible from the saloon windows, the library’s collection, and the drafting of my memoirs occupied my entire schedule, ensuring I felt neither boredom nor fatigue.

Over a period of several days, we observed a vast quantity of water-dwelling fowl, specifically gulls or sea-mews. A few were skillfully hunted and, once processed using a particular method, served as quite palatable wildfowl. Amidst the birds with expansive wingspans—which had been transported far from any shore and were settling on the swells to recover from the exhaustion of their journey—I spotted several splendid albatrosses, which produced harsh, jarring sounds resembling the call of a donkey, as well as creatures from the long-winged bird family.

Regarding the fish, they consistently inspired our wonder whenever we caught glimpses of their underwater existence by way of the unsealed shutters. I witnessed numerous varieties that I had previously lacked the opportunity to study.

My primary focus will be on ostracions native to the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, and the waters bordering tropical America. Much like the sea-hedgehog, the armadillo, the tortoise, and the Crustacea, these fish possess a protective breastplate composed of genuine bone rather than stone or chalk. This armor appears as a solid quadrangle in some species and a solid triangle in others. I observed triangular specimens measuring an inch and a half long, which offer a delicious flavour and healthy meat; their fins are yellow while their tails are brown, and I suggest they be introduced to fresh water, an environment to which various sea-fish adapt without difficulty. Furthermore, I would note the existence of quadrangular ostracions featuring four prominent tubercles upon their backs; some possess white spots across their lower bodies and can be domesticated similarly to birds; trigons equipped with spikes created by the extension of their bony shells, known as “seapigs” due to their peculiar grunting sounds; and dromedaries characterized by large, cone-shaped humps and leathery, extremely tough flesh.

I am currently drawing upon the journal entries belonging to Master Baptiste. “Specific fish belonging to the petrodon genus native to these waters, possessing red dorsal areas and white underbellies, identifiable by a trio of lengthwise filament lines; plus certain electrical varieties, measuring seven inches in length, adorned in the most vibrant hues. Furthermore, as examples of additional types, some ovoides, appearing like a dark brown egg, decorated with white stripes, and lacking tails; diodons, true sea-porcupines, equipped with quills, and able to inflate until they resemble pillows covered in needles; hippocampi, found in every sea; certain pegasi featuring extended snouts, whose pectoral fins, being greatly stretched and shaped like wings, permit them, if not to take flight, at least to dart through the air; pigeon spatulae, having tails encased in numerous shell rings; macrognathi possessing elongated jaws, a superior fish, nine inches long, and shining with highly pleasant colours; light-hued calliomores, with coarse heads; and numerous chaetodons, with lengthy, tube-like snouts, which slay insects by firing at them, as if from an air-gun, using a lone bead of water. These we might label the flycatchers of the oceans.”

Within the eighty-ninth category of fish, as categorized by Lacepede, which falls under the second inferior division of bony fish defined by bronchial membranes and opercules, I observed the scorpaena, a creature possessing a single dorsal fin and a head equipped with spines; these animals may or may not be armored with small shells, depending on their specific sub-class. The second sub-class provides examples of didactyles measuring fourteen to fifteen inches long, featuring yellow rays and heads that appear highly eccentric. Regarding the first sub-class, it presents various instances of that peculiar fish aptly named a ‘seafrog,’ which possesses a massive head that is occasionally riddled with apertures, sometimes distended by bumps, covered in tubercles, and armed with spikes; it features grotesque and uneven horns, while its tail and torso are encased in callosities; its venomous spine inflicts a perilous injury, and it is both repulsive and ghastly to behold.

Between January 21st and 23rd, the Meridian traveled at a speed of two hundred and fifty leagues every twenty-four hours, which equals five hundred and forty miles, or twenty-two miles per hour. We identified a vast array of fish species because they were drawn to the electric illumination and attempted to trail behind us; nevertheless, our velocity quickly outpaced most of them, although a few managed to remain within the waters of the Meridian for a short duration. On the morning of the 24th, at 12° 5′ S. lat. and 94° 33′ long., we sighted Keeling Island, a coral structure covered in stunning cocos that had previously been explored by Mr. Darwin and Captain Fitzroy. The Meridian traveled along the coastline of this uninhabited island for a brief span. Its nets hauled in an abundance of polypi and unusual molluscan shells. Several valuable specimens of the delphinulae variety increased the collection of Captain Sorel, to which I contributed an astraea punctifera, a type of parasitic polypus frequently discovered attached to a shell.
The horizon soon swallowed Keeling Island, and we steered our path north-west, heading toward the Indian Peninsula.

Our journey from Keeling Island proceeded with less speed and greater inconsistency, frequently leading us into profound abysses. On multiple occasions, they utilized the inclined planes, which consisted of specific internal levers positioned at an angle to the waterline. By these means, we traveled approximately two miles, yet we failed to attain the maximum depths of the Indian Sea, which soundings of seven thousand fathoms have yet to plumb. Regarding the temperature of the deeper layers, the thermometer consistently registered 4° above zero. I merely noted that, within the upper zones, the water remained perpetually colder at the higher levels than it was at the sea's surface.

The sea was completely empty on January 25th; the Meridian spent the entire day traveling upon the surface, its robust propeller striking the water and sending spray soaring upward. Under these conditions, who might have failed to mistake it for a massive whale? I passed three-quarters of the day on the deck. I observed the ocean. There was nothing to be seen at the edge of the horizon until roughly four o’clock, when a steamship traveling westward appeared on our opposite side. Its masts were briefly apparent, though it could not spot the Meridian, as our vessel sat too close to the water. I imagined this steamer was part of the P. O. Company fleet, which travels between Ceylon and Sydney, stopping at King George’s Point and Melbourne.
At five in the afternoon, prior to the brief dusk that connects darkness to light within equatorial regions, Baptiste and I were struck by a strange sight.
A cluster of argonauts drifted across the top of the water. We were able to tally hundreds of them. These were of the tubercle variety, a type unique to the Indian seas.

By utilizing their locomotive tubes to force out previously inhaled water, these elegant mollusks propelled themselves in reverse. Of their eight tentacles, two were flattened and unfurled like delicate sails, while the remaining six were lengthened and drifted upon the surface. I observed their fluted, spiral shells, which Cuvier accurately likens to a graceful skiff. A boat, in truth! It carries the animal that produces it, yet the creature does not remain attached to it.

The Meridian drifted for almost sixty minutes surrounded by this cluster of mollusks. I am uncertain what abrupt alarm seized them. Yet, as though following a command, each sail retracted, the limbs tucked away, the forms contracted, the shells inverted to shift their balance, and the entire armada vanished beneath the surface. No naval fleet ever executed a maneuver with greater synchronization.
The sun vanished abruptly, and the reeds, barely stirred by the wind, rested quietly beneath the hull of the Meridian.

On the 26th of January, the following day, we crossed the equator at the eighty-second meridian, arriving in the northern hemisphere. Throughout the daylight hours, a frightening school of sharks traveled alongside us; these horrific beasts proliferate in these waters, rendering them highly perilous. They were “cestracio philippi” sharks, possessing white bellies and brown backs, equipped with eleven tooth rows—eyed sharks—featuring a large black mark on their throats encircled by white, resembling an eye. Additionally, there were Isabella sharks, distinguished by rounded snouts and dark spots. These robust animals frequently threw their bodies against the saloon windows with enough force to leave us feeling quite unsafe. In those moments, Tom Harlan lost all self-control. He expressed a desire to ascend to the surface and spear the beasts, specifically certain smooth-hound sharks, which have mouths paved with mosaic-like teeth, and massive tiger-sharks measuring nearly six yards in length, the latter of which appeared to provoke him most intensely. Nevertheless, the Meridian increased its pace, effortlessly outdistancing the swiftest among them.

On the 27th of January, near the mouth of the expansive Bay of Bengal, we encountered a grim sight time and again: corpses drifting upon the water. These were the deceased from Indian villages, transported by the Ganges down to sea level, whom the vultures—the region’s sole morticians—had proven unable to consume. Yet, the sharks were quick to assist in their burial duties.

Around seven in the evening, the Meridian, partially submerged, navigated through a milky expanse. Initially, the sea appeared to have turned into milk. Could this be attributed to the moonlight? It could not; the moon, barely forty-eight hours into its cycle, remained concealed beneath the horizon amidst the sun’s glow. Although the heavens were illuminated by starlight, they looked dark when measured against the pale water.
Baptiste found the sight unbelievable and asked me what had brought about this peculiar occurrence. Fortunately, I possessed the means to provide him with an explanation.
“This is known as a milk sea,” I clarified. “A vast stretch of pale ripples frequently observed along the shores of Amboyna, as well as in these oceanic regions.”
“However, sir,” Baptiste remarked, “are you able to explain the reason for this phenomenon? as I assume the liquid has not actually transformed into milk.”

“No, my boy; and the pale hue that startles you is merely the result of countless infusoria, a type of glowing, tiny worm, transparent and jelly-like, no thicker than a strand of hair, and measuring no more than seven-thousandths of an inch. These creatures occasionally cling together for distances of several leagues,” said I.
“A number of leagues!” cried Baptiste.

“Indeed, my lad; and there is no reason to attempt calculating the quantity of these infusoria. It is impossible, because, unless I am wrong, vessels have sailed across these milky oceans for a distance exceeding forty miles,” said I.

Around midnight, the ocean abruptly returned to its customary hue; yet in our wake, stretching all the way to the edge of the horizon, the heavens mirrored the pale crests, appearing for a considerable duration to be saturated with the faint, flickering glow of an aurora borealis.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: At midday on the 28th of February, the Meridian surfaced at 9° 4′ N. lat., revealing land roughly eight miles to the west. I immediately observed a mountain chain reaching an elevation of approximately two thousand feet, characterized by highly irregular forms. After calculating our position, I realized we were approaching the island of Ceylon, the pearl dangling from the Indian Peninsula’s lobe.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: At this instant, Captain Sorel and his second arrived. The Captain cast a look at the chart. He then faced me and said:

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Ceylon is an island famous for its pearl-fisheries. Do you wish to see one of them, M. Delorme?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Of course, Captain.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “The matter is simple enough. Even so, while we might observe the fisheries, the fishermen themselves will be absent. The yearly export period has not commenced. Regardless, I shall direct us toward the Gulf of Manaar, reaching it by nightfall,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: The Captain spoke a few words to his second, and the man departed at once. Before long, the Meridian was back in her home environment, and the gauge indicated a depth of approximately thirty feet.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Well, sir,” Captain Sorel remarked, “you and your party are to go to the Bank of Manaar, and should a fisherman happen to be present, we will observe his labor.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “I concur, Captain!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Incidentally, M. Delorme, do you harbor any fear of sharks?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Sharks!” I cried out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: That query appeared to be quite difficult.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “So?” persisted Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “I acknowledge, Captain, that I have not grown well-acquainted with that species of fish as of yet.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “We have grown used to them,” Captain Sorel answered, “and eventually you will become so as well. Still, we will be carrying weapons, and while traveling we might manage to track down members of the tribe. It is intriguing. Therefore, until tomorrow, sir, and at an early hour.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: After speaking with an indifferent air, Captain Sorel exited the saloon. If you were asked to track a bear through the Swiss mountains, how would you respond?

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Agreed! we shall depart tomorrow to track the bear.” If someone requested that you pursue the lion across the Atlas plains, or the tiger within the jungles of India, how would you respond?

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Ha! ha! it appears that we are off to track the lion or the tiger!” Yet, when one is asked to pursue the shark within its own habitat, one might pause to consider the offer. Personally, I wiped my brow, which was covered in beads of frigid sweat. “We must ponder,” said I, “and not rush. Chasing otters through underwater woods, like our experience at the Island of Carrizo, is acceptable; but wandering the ocean floor, where an encounter with sharks is nearly inevitable, is a different matter entirely! I am aware that in some regions, most notably the Andaman Islands, the negroes do not falter to engage them, armed with a knife in one hand and a slipknot in the other; but I am also aware that those who challenge such beasts rarely survive. Still, I am no negro, and even if I were, I believe a moment of doubt here would be quite appropriate.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: Just then, the Canadian and Baptiste walked in, appearing entirely calm and perhaps even cheerful. They remained unaware of the fate that lay in store for them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Indeed, sir,” Tom Harlan remarked, “your Captain Sorel—may the devil claim him!—has recently presented us with a most agreeable proposal.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Oh!” I remarked, “are you aware?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “If it suits you, sir,” Baptiste broke in, “the captain of the Meridian has asked us to tour the grand Ceylon fisheries tomorrow, alongside you; he was gracious in his offer and acted as a true gentleman.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Did he offer any further remarks?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “There is nothing further, sir, other than the fact that he had previously mentioned this brief stroll to you,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Would you provide us with some information regarding the pearl fishery?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Regarding the actual act of fishing,” I inquired, “or the occurrences, which one?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Regarding the fishing,” the Canadian answered; “it is best to possess some knowledge of the area before we arrive there.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “All right; take a seat, my companions, and I shall instruct you,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: Tom and Baptiste took their places on a divan, and the initial inquiry from the Canadian was:

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “What is a pearl, sir?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “My worthy Tom,” I replied, “for the poet, a pearl represents a tear shed by the ocean; for the Orientals, it is a hardened droplet of dew; for women, it is an elongated gem, possessing a mother-of-pearl luster, worn upon their ears, necks, or fingers; for the chemist, it is a compound of carbonate and phosphate of lime, combined with a trace of gelatine; and finally, for the naturalist, it is merely a diseased secretion from the organ that generates mother-of-pearl within specific bivalves.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Mollusc phylum,” stated Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Exactly, my scholarly Baptiste; and, within this group of mollusks, the abalone, the giant clam, the top shell, in short, every variety that forms nacre, which is the blue, azure, purple, or colorless material coating the inside of their casings, has the potential to create pearls,” I remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Are there mussels as well?” the Canadian inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Indeed, mollusks from specific regions within Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Saxony, Bohemia, and France.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Excellent! I will remain vigilant from now on,” the Canadian answered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “However,” I went on, “the specific mollusc that produces the pearl is the pearl-oyster, the meleagrina margaritifera, that valuable pintadine. A pearl is merely a nacreous structure, laid down in a spherical shape, whether it is attached to the oyster’s shell or embedded within the animal’s tissues. It is fixed when on the shell; it is free when in the flesh; yet it consistently contains a tiny solid core, perhaps an infertile egg or a particle of sand, upon which the nacre accumulates over consecutive years in delicate, concentric strata.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Do you discover numerous pearls within a single oyster?” inquired Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Indeed, lad. Certain ones act as an ideal container. There is an oyster that has been spoken of, even if I permit myself some skepticism regarding it, which supposedly held at least one hundred and fifty sharks,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “One hundred and fifty sharks!” shouted Tom Harlan.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Did I mention sharks?” I stated quickly. “I intended to say a hundred and fifty pearls. Sharks would be illogical.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Of course not,” Baptiste replied; “but are you going to explain to us at this time how they obtain these pearls?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “They advance through different methods. Whenever they cling to the casing, those who fish for them frequently detach them using pliers; however, the standard procedure involves placing the oysters upon beds of the kelp that blankets the shoals. In this manner they perish under the sky; and following ten days they reach an advanced level of decay. Subsequently they are submerged within vast basins of ocean water; then they are pried apart and rinsed.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Do the costs of these pearls fluctuate based on their dimensions?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Beyond their dimensions,” I replied, “they are also distinguished by their form, their water—meaning their hue—and their brilliance: specifically, that vivid, variegated shimmer that renders them so visually captivating. The finest specimens are known as virgin pearls, or paragons. These develop in isolation within the mollusc’s flesh, appearing white, frequently opaque, and occasionally possessing the translucence of an opal; typically, they are spherical or egg-shaped. The spherical ones are fashioned into bracelets, while the egg-shaped ones become pendants, and because they are of greater value, they are retailed individually. Pearls attached to the oyster’s shell possess more uneven shapes and are traded by weight. Finally, grouped in a subordinate category are the diminutive pearls termed seed-pearls; these are traded by volume and are primarily utilized in needlework for ecclesiastical decorations.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “However,” Baptiste asked, “does this pearl-fishery involve danger?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Not at all,” I replied, with haste; “especially provided that specific measures are observed.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Is there any danger in a profession like this,” Tom Harlan asked, “beyond the possibility of gulping down a few swallows of ocean?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “In accordance with your words, Tom. Incidentally,” I remarked, attempting to adopt the indifferent manner of Captain Sorel, “do you harbor a fear of sharks, courageous Tom?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Me!” the Canadian answered; “a professional harpooner? My occupation is to treat them as trivial.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “However,” I remarked, “the matter does not involve angling for them using an iron-swivel, lifting them aboard the ship, severing their tails with a single stroke of a cleaver, gutting them, and casting their hearts into the ocean!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “In that case, the matter concerns——”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Exactly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Inside the liquid?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Inside the liquid.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Indeed, provided one has a proper harpoon! You see, sir, these sharks are poorly constructed creatures. They roll onto their stomachs to grab hold of you, and during that interval——”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: The manner in which Tom Harlan pronounced “seize” caused my blood to freeze.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “So, Baptiste, what is your opinion on sharks?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Me!” Baptiste stated. “I intend to be candid, sir.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “All the more reason,” I mused.

chapter_title: CHAPTER II A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN SOREL’S
text: “Should you intend to confront the sharks, sir, I fail to perceive a reason why your loyal servant ought not to encounter them alongside you,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: At four o’clock the following morning, the steward assigned to me by Captain Sorel roused me from sleep. I got up quickly, put on my clothes, and entered the saloon.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: I was being awaited by Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Are you prepared to begin?” asked he, “M. Delorme.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “I’m prepared.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Kindly accompany me, then.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “And my associates, Captain?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “They are aware and are standing by,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Shall we not don our diving suits?” I inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Not yet. I have kept the Meridian at a safe distance from this shoreline, and we remain a fair way off from the Manaar Bank; however, the vessel is prepared, and it shall transport us to the precise location for our departure, sparing us a lengthy trek. Our underwater gear is aboard, and we shall don it once we commence our trip beneath the surface,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Captain Sorel guided me toward the main stairs, providing access to the platform. Tom and Baptiste stood there, already thrilled by the prospect of the “pleasure party” currently being arranged. Five crewmen from the Meridian, holding their oars, stood ready in the boat secured to the flank of the vessel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Darkness persisted throughout the night. A blanket of clouds obscured the heavens, permitting only a handful of stars to remain visible. Gazing toward the direction of the shore, I perceived only a shadowy outline bordering three sides of the horizon, spanning from the south-west to the north-west. The Meridian, after sailing back along the western seaboard of Ceylon during the night, sat positioned to the west of the bay—or more accurately, the gulf—created by the mainland and the Island of Manaar. Beneath those murky depths lay the pintadine bank, a limitless pearl bed extending for a distance exceeding twenty miles.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Captain Sorel, Tom Harlan, Baptiste, and I positioned ourselves at the rear of the craft. The captain took hold of the tiller; his four associates rested against their oars, the mooring line was released, and we drifted away.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The vessel headed southward; the rowers maintained a leisurely pace. I observed that their pulls, powerful beneath the surface, occurred only at ten-second intervals, in accordance with the standard naval practice. As the boat glided forward through its own momentum, droplets of liquid hit the murky troughs of the swells sharply, resembling splashes of liquid lead. A small wave, expanding outward, caused the craft to sway gently, and a few samphire reeds brushed against its front.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A silence fell upon us. I wondered what Captain Sorel had on his mind. He might have been considering the shore that drew closer, which he felt was uncomfortably proximate, in opposition to the Canadian’s view, who deemed the distance excessive. Baptiste, meanwhile, was present solely out of inquisitiveness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: At approximately five-thirty, the initial hues upon the skyline rendered the northern coastal edge clearer. While level toward the east, the terrain ascended slightly in a southerly direction. A distance of five miles remained, though the haze above the ocean obscured the view. By six o’clock, full daylight arrived with the swiftness typical of the tropics, a zone devoid of both dusk and daybreak. Sunlight broke through the bank of clouds gathered along the eastern horizon, and the brilliant sun ascended quickly. I observed the shore clearly, noting a sparse collection of trees. Our vessel approached Manaar Island, navigating around its southern curve. Captain Sorel stood up from where he had been sitting and observed the water.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Upon his signal, the anchor was released, yet the chain barely moved, as the depth was scarcely over a yard, and this location was among the most elevated sections of the pintadines bank.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “We have arrived, M. Delorme,” stated Captain Sorel. “Do you observe that landlocked bay? Within one month, the many fishing vessels belonging to the exporters will gather here, and these are the depths their divers shall plunder with such audacity. Fortunately, this bay is ideally positioned for that specific type of fishing. It remains protected from the most intense gales; the ocean is never particularly turbulent in this location, rendering it advantageous for the tasks of the diver. We shall proceed to don our suits and commence our stroll.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Remaining silent, I started donning my thick maritime gear with the assistance of the crew as I kept my eyes on the waves I mistrusted. Captain Sorel and the others traveling with me were likewise getting dressed. No individuals from the Meridian were scheduled to join our upcoming trip.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Before long, we were encased up to our necks in india-rubber gear, with breathing equipment secured to our shoulders by straps. The Ruhmkorff apparatus was not required. Prior to enclosing my head within the copper helmet, I had posed a query to the Captain.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Those would be of no use,” he answered. “Our descent is not deep, and the sun’s beams shall provide sufficient illumination for our stroll. Furthermore, it would be unwise to transport the electric light through these currents; the intensity of its glow could draw some of the perilous creatures of the shoreline at a most inconvenient moment.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: When Captain Sorel uttered these remarks, I looked toward Tom Harlan and Baptiste. However, my pair of companions had previously enclosed their craniums within the steel helmet, rendering them unable to listen or respond.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: There was one final inquiry left to put to Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “What about our weapons?” I inquired; “and our firearms?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Weapons! Why? Don’t climbers confront the grizzly using only a knife, and isn’t cold steel more reliable than bullets? Take this sturdy blade; secure it at your waist, and we shall depart.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: I observed my associates; they carried weapons just as we did, and, furthermore, Tom Harlan was wielding a massive harpoon, which he had stowed in the vessel prior to our departure from the Meridian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Next, imitating the Captain, I permitted them to fit me with the weighty copper headpiece, and our oxygen tanks began functioning immediately. A moment later, we were set down, one by one, into roughly six feet of water on a level sandy bottom. Captain Sorel gestured with his hand, and we trailed him down a mild slope until we vanished beneath the surface.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Schools of monoptera fish, lacking any fins save for their tails, ascended past our feet as if they were flocks of snipe in a marsh. I identified the Javanese, a genuine serpent measuring two and a half feet in length, possessing a livid underside and sporting golden stripes along its flanks that would lead one to confuse it with a conger eel. Among the stromateus genus, characterized by flat, oval forms, I observed specimens of striking hue bearing dorsal fins shaped like scythes; this is a superior food fish, referred to as Karawade when pickled and dried. Following these were several tranquebars, members of the apsiphoroides genus, which feature bodies encased in a shell cuirass composed of eight longitudinal plates.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: As the sun climbed higher, it increasingly illuminated the vast expanse of water. The composition of the ground gradually shifted. A flawless path of boulders, draped in a layer of zoophytes and molluscs, replaced the fine sand. Within these groups, I observed certain placenae, characterized by their thin, uneven shells—a variety of ostracion native to the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. I also saw rounded, orange lucinae and rockfish measuring three and a half feet in length, which surged beneath the swells as if they were hands prepared to grasp. Furthermore, there were faintly glowing panopyres and, finally, oculines resembling grand fans, which constituted some of the most opulent plant life found in these waters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Surrounded by these organic growths, beneath the shelters of the hydrophytes, lay strata of awkward articulates, most notably certain raninae, possessing carapaces shaped like a mildly curved triangle; alongside several grotesque-appearing parthenopes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Around seven o’clock, we finally arrived to examine the oyster-beds where millions of pearl-oysters are propagated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Captain Sorel gestured toward the vast pile of oysters; I realized that this supply was limitless, as the generative force of Nature exceeds the human impulse to destroy. Tom Harlan, following his own nature, quickly gathered the best examples into a net he kept at his side. However, we were unable to linger. We were required to trail the Captain, who appeared to navigate by routes familiar only to him. The terrain was noticeably ascending, and at times, when I raised my arm, it reached past the ocean’s surface. Afterward, the elevation of the shelf would dip unpredictably. Frequently, we skirted tall crags shaped like pyramids. Within their shadowed crevices, massive crustaceans, balanced on long legs like instruments of war, observed us with unblinking gazes, while diverse species of annelids slithered beneath our boots.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Just then, a vast cavern appeared in front of us, hollowed out within a scenic pile of stones and layered with the dense weave of underwater vegetation. Initially, the space struck me as quite dim. The sun’s beams appeared to fade by degrees, until their faint clarity turned into mere submerged illumination. Captain Sorel walked inside; we went after him. My vision quickly grew used to this comparative gloom. I was able to make out the arches rising whimsically from stone supports, resting wide on their rock foundations, similar to the massive pillars of Tuscan design. For what reason had our mysterious leader brought us to the floor of this underwater vault? I would learn shortly. Following a walk down a somewhat steep slope, we stepped onto the base of a sort of round hollow. There Captain Sorel halted, and pointed with his hand toward a thing I had not yet noticed. It was an oyster of massive proportions, a colossal tridacne, a vessel that might have held an entire basin of baptismal water, a shell with a width exceeding two and a half yards, and therefore bigger than the one decorating the Meridian’s lounge. I walked toward this remarkable shellfish. It was attached by its threads to a granite slab, and there, alone, it grew in the tranquil depths of the cave. I calculated the mass of this tridacne to be 600 lbs. An oyster of this size would hold 30 lbs. of flesh; and one would require the appetite of a Gargantua to consume several dozen of them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Captain Sorel clearly knew of this bivalve’s presence and appeared to have a specific reason for checking the current condition of this tridacne. Because the shells were slightly parted, the Captain approached and inserted his dagger to keep them from snapping shut; he then used his hand to lift the fringed-edge membrane that served as the animal’s mantle. Tucked within the folded layers, I spotted a detached pearl as large as a coco-nut. Its spherical form, flawless transparency, and exquisite shine rendered it a gem of priceless worth. Overcome by my own inquisitiveness, I reached out to grasp, heft, and feel it; however, the Captain halted me, signaled his denial, and swiftly pulled out his dagger, causing the two shells to snap together. I then grasped the purpose of Captain Sorel. By keeping this pearl concealed inside the mantle of the tridacne, he was permitting it to develop gradually. With every passing year, the mollusc’s secretions would deposit additional concentric layers. I calculated its worth to be no less than £500,000.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Captain Sorel came to an abrupt halt following ten minutes. I assumed he had paused before heading back. Instead, he signaled for us to duck down near him within a wide crevice in the stone, while his finger indicated a specific section of the fluid expanse, which I observed with focus.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A dark shape emerged roughly five yards away, then dropped toward the seabed. The unsettling thought of sharks crossed my mind, yet I was wrong; and for another time, it was not a sea beast that concerned us.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A human being, a breathing person, an Indian, a fisherman, a wretched soul who, I imagine, arrived to gather prior to the reaping, was there. I observed the underside of his canoe moored several feet over his cranium. He plunged and ascended repeatedly. A rock shaped like a sugar loaf, gripped between his feet and attached to his vessel by a cord, assisted his swift descent. This constituted his entire equipment. Upon arriving at the floor, approximately five yards down, he knelt and stuffed his sack with oysters collected haphazardly. He then rose, discharged the contents, hoisted his rock, and commenced the process again, a cycle that endured for thirty seconds.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: We remained unseen by the diver. Our concealment was provided by the rock’s shadow. In what way could this unfortunate Indian imagine that humans, creatures identical to him, were positioned beneath the surface observing his actions and missing nothing of his harvest? He ascended and descended in this fashion repeatedly. He retrieved no more than ten per dive, as he had to detach them from the ledge where they were fastened by their powerful byssus. How many of the oysters he endangered his existence to collect proved to be devoid of pearls! I observed him with care; his movements were methodical; and for thirty minutes, no peril seemed to loom over him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: I had started to grow used to watching this fascinating fishing, when all at once, while the Indian remained on the seafloor, I observed him display a sign of panic, stand up, and leap toward the ocean’s surface.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: His fear was clear to me. Directly over the doomed diver, a massive silhouette emerged. A shark of immense proportions moved at an angle, its gaze burning and its mouth agape. Paralyzed by terror, I could not stir.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The ravenous beast darted at the Indian, who flung his body sideways to dodge the shark’s fins; yet the tail escaped him, hitting his torso and leveling him to the earth.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The event endured for only a brief moment: the shark circled back and, rolling onto its spine, readied itself to bisect the Indian, at which point I observed Captain Sorel spring up, and then, clutching a dagger, march directly toward the beast, prepared to engage it in a head-on struggle. Just as the shark was about to sever the unfortunate fisherman, it spotted its fresh opponent and, flipping around, headed directly for him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: I retain a clear memory of where Captain Sorel stood. Maintaining his composure, he braced for the shark with impressive calm; then, as it lunged toward him, he dodged to the side with remarkable speed, escaping the impact and plunging his blade far into its flank. Yet the struggle had not concluded. A ferocious battle followed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A horrific battle commenced.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: It appeared as though the shark had roared, if such a description is permissible. Crimson fluid poured in great streams from the injury. The ocean turned a deep shade of red, and beyond that clouded substance, I was unable to perceive anything else. I saw nothing further until the instant when, with the speed of a bolt of lightning, I spotted the resolute Captain clinging to a fin of the beast, battling it as if in a close-quarters fight, and striking repeated hits against his adversary, though he remained incapable of landing a final strike.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The water was churned into such a violent state by the shark’s thrashing that the resulting motion put me at risk of being tipped over.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Though I longed to hasten to the Captain’s aid, I remained rooted where I stood by terror, unable to move.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: My gaze caught the weary eye; I observed the various stages of the struggle. The Captain tumbled to the ground, toppled by the vast weight pressing down on him. The shark’s mouth gaped, resembling a set of industrial shears, and the Captain’s fate would have been sealed; however, with the speed of an idea, Tom Harlan dashed toward the shark, harpoon gripped in his hand, and pierced it with the pointed weapon.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A volume of blood saturated the swells. They swayed beneath the shark’s motions, as it thrashed them with an unutterable violence. Tom Harlan had struck true. It was the creature’s final gasp. Pierced through the heart, it writhed in horrific spasms, the impact of which knocked Baptiste over.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: However, Tom Harlan had freed the Captain, who rose uninjured, walked directly toward the Indian, swiftly severed the rope binding him to his stone, lifted him into his embrace, and, with a forceful kick of his heel, ascended to the surface.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: A few seconds later, the three of us trailed behind, rescued through a miracle, and arrived at the fisherman’s boat.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The primary concern for Captain Sorel was bringing the luckless individual back to consciousness. I doubted his ability to achieve this. My hope remained, as the duration of the wretched being’s submersion was brief; nevertheless, the impact delivered by the shark’s tail could well have proven fatal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: To my delight, the intense rubbing performed by the Captain and Baptiste gradually brought him back to awareness. His eyes fluttered open. Imagine his shock, or perhaps his dread, upon finding four massive copper heads hovering above him! Furthermore, what could have been running through his mind as Captain Sorel pulled a pouch of pearls from his clothing and pressed it into his palm? This generous gift from the man of the waters was received by the destitute Cingalese with a shaking hand. His bewildered gaze revealed he had no idea which supernatural entities had granted him both his wealth and his survival.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Upon a gesture from the Captain, we returned to the shore, and, retracing the path we had previously walked, arrived in roughly thirty minutes at the anchor securing the Meridian’s canoe to the ground.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Upon boarding, the crew assisted us in removing our cumbersome copper helmets.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The initial utterance from Captain Sorel was directed toward the Canadian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “I am grateful, Master Harlan,” he stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “I did it for vengeance, Captain,” answered Tom Harlan. “That was a debt I had to settle with you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: The Captain’s lips curled into a hideous grin, and that was the extent of it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “Toward the Meridian,” he stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Our vessel skimmed across the surface of the swells. A few moments later, we encountered the lifeless carcass of the shark drifting in the water. From the dark pigment at the tips of its appendages, I identified the fearsome melanopteron native to the Indian Seas, belonging to the shark species that bears such a fitting name. It measured in excess of twenty-five feet in length, with a massive maw that accounted for one-third of its total frame. The creature was fully mature, a fact evidenced by the six tiers of teeth arranged in an isosceles triangle within its top jaw.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: As I pondered that motionless heap, twelve of those ravenous creatures emerged surrounding our vessel; and, ignoring our presence, they lunged at the corpse, battling each other for the fragments.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: By eight-thirty, I had returned to the Meridian. Once there, I contemplated the events that had occurred during our trip to the Manaar Bank.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: I am forced to arrive at two deductions from this—the first concerning the singular bravery of Captain Sorel, the second regarding his loyalty toward a person, a member of that species from which he escaped under the ocean. Regardless of his claims, this peculiar individual had not managed to fully extinguish his own heart.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: Upon sharing this remark with him, he replied in a voice that held a touch of emotion:

chapter_title: CHAPTER III A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
text: “That Indian, sir, belongs to a subjugated nation; and I remain, and will continue to be, until my final moment, one of their number!” said I.

On the 29th of January, the island of Ceylon vanished beneath the skyline, and the Meridian, traveling at twenty miles per hour, glided through the complex network of channels dividing the Maldives from the Laccadives. It passed by the Island of Kiltan, a coral-based territory found by Vasco da Gama in 1499 and one of the nineteen primary islands forming the Laccadive Archipelago, positioned between 10° and 14° 30′ N. lat., and 69° 50′ 72″ E. long.
Our journey from the Japanese Seas had reached a distance of 16,220 miles, which is equivalent to 7,500 (French) leagues.

On the following day, the 30th of January, the Meridian ascended to the ocean’s surface, yet no terrain appeared. The vessel steered N.N.E. toward the Sea of Oman, situated amidst Arabia and the Indian Peninsula, a body of water acting as the Persian Gulf’s gateway. It was clearly a cul-de-sac offering no route for departure. What was the destination Captain Sorel had in mind for us? I had no answer. The Canadian, however, remained unsatisfied, approaching me that day to inquire about our trajectory.
“Our destination is wherever the Captain chooses to steer us, Master Tom.”

“His imagination is insufficient to carry us a great distance,” the Canadian remarked. “The Persian Gulf possesses no exit; consequently, should we enter, our departure will follow shortly thereafter.”

“All right, we shall emerge once more, Master Harlan; and should the Meridian desire to see the Red Sea following our time in the Persian Gulf, the Straits of Bab-el-mandeb are available to provide us passage,” I said.

“It is unnecessary for me to inform you, sir,” said Tom Harlan, “that the Red Sea is just as inaccessible as the Gulf, given that the Isthmus of Suez remains uncut; and, even if it were, a vessel of such enigmatic nature as ours would not venture into a waterway obstructed by sluices. Furthermore, the Red Sea does not provide the route for our return to Europe.”
“However, I didn't state that our return to Europe was happening.”
“What do you imagine, therefore?”

“I imagine that, having seen the strange shores of Egypt and Arabia, the Meridian shall head back down the Indian Ocean, maybe traversing the Mozambique Channel, or possibly past the Mascarenhas, in order to reach the Cape of Good Hope,” said I.
“And after we reach the Cape of Good Hope?” inquired the Canadian, stressing the words in a strange manner.

“We are going to enter that Atlantic that remains unknown to us. Oh, Tom, my friend, you are becoming weary of this underwater expedition; you have had your fill of the constantly changing display of oceanic marvels. As for me, I will regret the conclusion of a trip that so few people are granted the chance to experience,” said I.

Until the 3rd of February, for a duration of four days, the Meridian traversed the Sea of Oman, alternating between different velocities and levels of submersion. Its movements appeared erratic, as though it were undecided regarding its path, yet we remained south of the Tropic of Cancer throughout.

As we departed these waters, we caught a brief glimpse of Muscat, a primary urban center within the nation of Oman. I was struck by its peculiar appearance, set against dark stone cliffs that highlighted the stark white of its dwellings and strongholds. I observed the curved tops of the houses of worship, the graceful tips of the towers, and the lush, green gardens. Yet it was merely a fleeting sight! Before long, the Meridian vanished beneath the swells of that region of the ocean.

Our vessel navigated the Mahrah and Hadramaut shores of Arabia for a six-mile stretch, where the rolling mountain range was now and then broken by the sight of some antique wreckage. On the 5th of February, we finally arrived at the Gulf of Aden, a flawless conduit leading into the Bab-el-mandeb strait, serving as the passage for Indian currents to flow into the Red Sea.

On the 6th of February, the Meridian drifted into view of Aden, situated on a headland connected to the continent by a slender isthmus, a sort of unreachable Gibraltar, whose defenses the English reconstructed following their 1839 occupation. I observed the octagonal minarets belonging to this settlement, a location that once served as the most affluent trading depot along the shoreline.
It was my firm belief that Captain Sorel, having reached this juncture, would retreat once more; however, I was wrong, as he did nothing of the sort, which greatly astonished me.
On the 7th of February, the following day, we sailed into the Straits of Bab-el-mandeb, a title that signifies The Gate of Tears in the language of the Arabs.

Its length is merely thirty-two miles, while its width reaches twenty. Given the Meridian’s top velocity, the transit took barely sixty minutes. I observed zero, failing to spot even the Island of Perim, where the British Government established fortifications to secure Aden. So many French or English vessels traveled the route from Suez to Bombay, Calcutta to Melbourne, and Bourbon to the Mauritius, churning up this confined strait, that the Meridian dared not reveal its presence. Consequently, it stayed cautiously submerged. By midday, we finally entered the Red Sea.

I had no desire to fathom the whim that led Captain Sorel to steer into the gulf. Yet, I fully endorsed the Meridian making its way inside. Its velocity was reduced; at times it remained atop the waves, while at others it submerged to evade a ship, allowing me to study both the surface and the depths of this strange sea.

On the 8th of February, beginning at the earliest light, Mocha appeared, currently a devastated settlement, with ramparts ready to collapse from a single blast, though it still protects scattered green date-palms; formerly a significant metropolis, housing six marketplaces, and twenty-six mosques, and whose fortifications, guarded by fourteen strongholds, created a perimeter measuring two miles around.

Next, the Meridian neared the African coastline, a region where the ocean floor dropped to deeper levels. In that location, amidst waters of crystalline clarity, the open shutters granted us a view of exquisite thickets of radiant coral and massive stone formations draped in a magnificent coat of emerald algae and seaweed. What a vision beyond words, and what a diversity of vistas and terrains across those sandy shoals and volcanic islets bordering the Libyan shore! Yet, it was along the eastern seaboard, which the Meridian reached shortly after, that these plants were seen in their full splendor. This was the Tehama coast, where such a collection of zoophytes not only thrived below the waterline, but also created striking patterns that stretched roughly sixty feet above the surface, appearing more whimsical yet lacking the vivid hues of those sustained by the life-giving force of the sea.
How delightful those moments were that I spent by the saloon window! What novel examples of underwater plant and animal life I observed in the glow of our electric lantern!

On February 9th, the Meridian drifted across the widest section of the Red Sea, an expanse measuring ninety miles in diameter that lies between the western shore of Souakin and the eastern shore of Komfidah.

At midday, following the recording of our coordinates, Captain Sorel stepped onto the deck where I chanced to be standing, and I resolved that I would not permit him to depart before questioning him about his hidden intentions. Upon noticing me, he drew near and kindly presented me with a cigar.

“Is this Red Sea to your liking, sir? Have you taken enough time to examine the marvels hidden beneath its surface, the marine life, the zoophytes, the sponge beds, and the coral groves? Did you manage to see the settlements along its shores?”
“I confirm, Captain Sorel,” I answered; “furthermore, the Meridian possesses excellent equipment for this type of research. Oh! what a brilliant vessel it is!”
“Indeed, sir, it is both clever and indestructible. It is not afraid of the Red Sea’s fearsome storms, nor its tides, nor its shoals,” said I.
“Of course,” I replied, “this ocean is cited as among the most treacherous, and during the era of the ancients, unless I am in error, its standing was loathsome.”

“Abominable, M. Delorme. Ancient Greek and Roman chroniclers write of it with disdain, and according to Strabo, it is quite perilous throughout the rainy period and when the Etesian winds blow. The Arab scholar Edrisi describes it as the Gulf of Colzoum, noting that many ships were lost there upon the shoals and that sailors avoided navigating it after dark. He claims it is a body of water prone to terrifying storms, filled with barren islands, and ‘which offers nothing good either on its surface or in its depths.’”
“It is evident,” I answered, “that such chroniclers were never passengers upon the Meridian.”

“Precisely,” the Captain answered with a smile; “and regarding that matter, people today possess no greater sophistication than those of antiquity. It took numerous eras to discover the force of steam. Perhaps in a century’s time, we shall witness another Meridian? Advancement moves at a sluggish pace, M. Delorme.”
“It is a fact,” I replied; “your vessel is ahead of its age by a hundred years, maybe an epoch. How tragic that the mystery behind this creation must perish alongside its creator!”
Captain Sorel remained silent. Following a pause of several minutes, he went on:
“You were discussing the views held by chroniclers of antiquity regarding the perilous sailing conditions of the Red Sea.”
“That is the case,” I remarked; “yet, was their apprehension not blown out of proportion?”

“Both yes and no, M. Delorme,” answered Captain Sorel, appearing to possess an intimate knowledge of the Red Sea. “What poses no threat to a contemporary craft, properly equipped, sturdily constructed, and capable of steering its own path by means of reliable steam, presented every kind of danger to the vessels of antiquity. Imagine those early sailors braving the waters in boats crafted from boards fastened with palm-fiber ropes, soaked in seal blubber, and coated in pulverized resin! Lacking any tools to determine their position, they navigated by intuition through currents they barely understood. Given such circumstances, disasters were, and inevitably had to be, frequent. Yet today, steamships traveling between Suez and the South Seas need not dread the rage of this gulf, despite opposing trade-winds. Neither the captain nor the passengers ready themselves for departure by presenting appeasing offerings; nor, upon arriving home, do they adorn themselves with garlands and golden bands to express gratitude to the deities at the local temple.”

“I am in accord with your view,” I remarked; “furthermore, it appears that steam has extinguished every trace of thankfulness within the souls of mariners. Nevertheless, Captain, given that you have evidently conducted a particular study of this body of water, are you able to explain how it acquired its title?”
“There are a number of theories regarding this matter, M. Delorme. Do you care to hear what a fourteenth-century chronicler had to say?”
“With pleasure.”
“This imaginative author claims that it was named following the Israelites’ crossing, at the time Pharaoh was lost in the waters that shut together upon the command of Moses.”
“That is a poet’s reasoning, Captain Sorel,” I answered; “yet it does not satisfy me. I am requesting your own perspective.”

“There it is, M. Delorme. In my view, we are to interpret this designation of the Red Sea as a rendering of the Hebrew term ‘Edom’; and the reason the people of antiquity bestowed that title was the unique hue of its waves.”
“However, until now, I have observed only clear swells devoid of any distinct hue.”

“It is quite probable; however, as we proceed toward the base of the abyss, you shall observe this unique phenomenon. I recall witnessing the Bay of Tor looking completely crimson, resembling a blood-filled ocean,” I said.
“Do you credit the existence of a tiny seaweed for this hue?” I asked.
“Indeed.”
“Is it not true, Captain Sorel, that this is not your initial crossing of the Red Sea while commanding the Meridian?”
“Negative, sir.”

“Since you mentioned the crossing of the Israelites and the disaster that befell the Egyptians some time back, I am curious if you have encountered any underwater evidence of this major historical event?” I asked.
“Negative, sir; and there is a valid cause for it.”
“What’s that?”

“The location where Moses and his followers crossed is currently so obstructed by sand that the camels are only just able to wet their legs in it. You can easily grasp that there would be insufficient water for my Meridian.”
“And the location?” I inquired.

“This location lies slightly north of the Isthmus of Suez, within the inlet that once formed a vast estuary during the era when the Red Sea reached the Salt Lakes. Regardless of whether that crossing was a miracle, the Israelites still traversed it to arrive at the Promised Land, and the forces of Pharaoh were destroyed at that exact point; and I believe that digging into the center of the sand would uncover a great quantity of weaponry and tools dating back to Egypt.”

“It is clear,” I answered; “and for the benefit of those who study antiquity, we must trust that such digging occurs eventually, once fresh settlements arise upon the isthmus, following the building of the Suez Canal; a waterway, nonetheless, quite pointless for a ship such as the Meridian.”

“Quite possibly; yet it serves the entire globe,” stated Captain Sorel. “The people of antiquity grasped the benefit of connecting the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for their trade: however, they avoided excavating a straight waterway, opting instead to utilize the Nile as a link. It is highly probable that the channel joining the Red Sea to the Nile was initiated by Sesostris, provided tradition holds true. It is an established fact that in 615 before Jesus Christ, Necos commenced the construction of a canal to feed the Nile’s waters across the Egyptian plains, facing Arabia. Navigating this passage required four days, and its breadth allowed two triremes to pass side by side. Darius, son of Hystaspes, continued the project, which was likely completed by Ptolemy II. Strabo observed it in use: yet the drop from its starting point, close to Bubastes, down to the Red Sea was so minimal that it could only be traversed for a few months annually. This waterway met all trade requirements until the era of Antonius, at which time it was deserted and filled with sand. Reopened by the command of the Caliph Omar, it was permanently ruined in 761 or 762 by Caliph Al-Mansor, who sought to block the delivery of supplies to Mohammed-ben-Abdallah, who had rebelled against his rule. Throughout the campaign in Egypt, your General Bonaparte unearthed remnants of these excavations in the Desert of Suez; and, caught off guard by the rising water, he almost lost his life before reaching Hadjaroth, at the exact site where Moses had pitched his tents three millennia prior.”

“So, Captain, the very thing the ancients feared to attempt—this connection of the two oceans that shall reduce the journey from Cadiz to India—M. Lesseps has managed to accomplish; and in a short time, he will have transformed Africa into a vast island.”

“Indeed, M. Delorme; you are justified in feeling pride regarding your fellow countryman. A person of this stature confers greater glory upon a land than even the most eminent commanders. He commenced his path, much like a multitude of others, amid repulsion and rejection; yet he has emerged victorious, possessing as he does the brilliance of determination. Furthermore, it is a melancholy reflection that an achievement of such magnitude, which truly should have served as a global endeavor and possessed the capacity to define an entire era, was brought to fruition solely through the vigor of a single individual. All glory belongs to M. Lesseps!”
“Indeed! glory to the distinguished citizen,” I answered, taken aback by the tone Captain Sorel had utilized a moment ago.

“I am sorry,” he went on, “that I am unable to convey you via the Suez Canal; however, you shall have a view of the extended pier at Port Said the day after tomorrow, at which time we will have reached the Mediterranean.”
“The Mediterranean!” I cried out.
“Indeed, sir; is that a surprise to you?”
“It is the thought that we will arrive the day after to-morrow that amazes me,” I said.
“Really?”
“Indeed, Captain, even if I should have grown used to finding nothing astonishing by now, given the duration of my stay upon your vessel.”
“However, what is the reason for this astonishment?”
“Indeed! the Meridian must maintain a terrifying pace if she is to reach the Mediterranean by the day after tomorrow, after having circled Africa and rounded the Cape of Good Hope!”
“Sir, who informed you that she was going to sail around Africa and navigate past the Cape of Good Hope?”
“So, providing the Meridian does not travel across solid ground, and moves over the isthmus——”
“Or underneath it, M. Delorme.”
“Underneath it?”
“Certainly,” answered Captain Sorel in a low voice. “A great while back, Nature fashioned beneath this strip of earth what humanity has constructed upon its exterior today.”
“How is this! does such a route truly exist?”
“Indeed; an underground corridor, to which I have given the title of the Arabian Tunnel. It carries us under Suez and emerges within the Gulf of Pelusium,” said I.
“However, is this neck of land made entirely of shifting sands?”
“Down to a specific point. However, at a depth of fifty-five yards, a firm stratum of stone exists.”
“Have you happened upon this corridor accidentally?” I inquired, my astonishment growing steadily.

“Luck and logic, sir; and logic to a greater degree than luck. This channel is not merely present, but I have utilized it on multiple occasions. Had that not been the case, I would never have risked entering the impassable Red Sea today. I observed that the Red Sea and the Mediterranean contained a specific group of fish that were entirely the same. Being certain of this, I questioned whether it was possible that no connection existed between these two bodies of water. If one did exist, a subterranean current would have to flow from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, simply due to the variance in their levels. I captured many fish near Suez. I threaded a copper ring through their tails and released them back into the water. Several months afterward, along the Syrian coast, I recovered some of those fish adorned with the ring. Consequently, the link between the two was confirmed. I then searched for it using my Meridian; I located it, traveled through it, and before long, sir, you also will have traversed my Arabian tunnel!”

During that identical night, at 21° 30′ N. lat., the Meridian drifted atop the ocean waves, drawing near to the coast of Arabia. I observed Djeddah, the primary trading hub for India, Turkey, Syria, and Egypt. I could discern its structures with sufficient clarity, along with the ships moored at the docks and those forced by their depth to remain in the roadstead. The sun, hanging quite near the horizon, shone directly upon the town's dwellings, highlighting their pale color. Beyond the town, a collection of huts constructed from reeds and wood marked the area where the Bedouins resided. Before long, the darkness of night obscured Djeddah from sight, and the Meridian submerged into water that glowed with a faint luminescence.

On the 10th of February, the following day, we observed a number of vessels moving against the wind. The Meridian submerged once more to travel beneath the surface; however, at midday, after her position was calculated and the ocean appeared empty, she ascended back to the waterline.
With Tom and Baptiste in my company, I took a seat upon the platform. The eastern shoreline appeared as a shape dimly stamped against a humid mist.
As we rested our weight against the gunwales of the pinnace, discussing various topics, Tom Harlan gestured toward a particular location on the water and said:
“Is there anything visible to you, sir?”
“I do not have your vision, Tom, you realize,” I answered.
“Observe closely,” Tom remarked, “over there, off the starboard side, level with the lamp! Can you not perceive a shape that appears to be shifting?”
“Of course,” I replied, following a careful observation; “there appears to be a lengthy dark form upon the surface of the sea.”
It was not long before the dark shape sat less than a mile away from our position. To my eyes, it resembled a massive bank of sand left behind in the middle of the ocean. It was a colossal dugong!

Tom Harlan gazed with anticipation. A greedy gleam ignited in his eyes as he beheld the creature. His arm appeared poised to strike it with a harpoon. An observer might have assumed he was bracing for the instant to plunge into the ocean and battle it within its own domain.
Just then, Captain Sorel emerged onto the deck. Upon observing the dugong and grasping the Canadian’s stance, he spoke to him, saying:
“Would your hand not be scorched, Master Harlan, provided you were gripping a harpoon at this moment?”
“Exactly, sir.”
“And you wouldn't feel any regret returning, just for a single day, to your work as a fisherman and including this whale among the others you have previously slaughtered?”
“I ought not to, sir.”
“You are welcome to attempt it,” I said.
“I am grateful, sir,” Tom Harlan stated, his gaze burning.
“However,” the Captain went on, “I suggest that you do not fail to hit the beast, for your own benefit.”
“Does the dugong pose a threat when provoked?” I inquired, ignoring the Canadian’s gesture of indifference.

“Indeed,” the Captain answered; “at times the creature retaliates against those attacking it and capsizes their vessel. Yet Master Harlan need not dread such a peril. His vision is quick, his hand steady.”

Just then, seven members of the ship’s company, silent and motionless as always, climbed onto the deck. A harpoon and a rope, like the gear used for whaling, were held by one of them. The pinnace was hoisted off the bridge, wrenched from its mounting, and lowered into the water. The coxswain grabbed the tiller, and six rowers settled into their places. I, along with Tom and Baptiste, moved to the stern of the vessel.
“Are you not accompanying us, Captain?” I inquired.
“I do not, sir; however, I hope you have good sport.”
Propelled by the six oarsmen, the vessel departed and surged swiftly in the direction of the dugong, which was drifting at a distance of approximately two miles from the Meridian.

When we reached a position a few cables-length from the cetacean, our pace diminished, and the oars submerged silently into the still sea. Tom Harlan, clutching a harpoon, remained at the front of the vessel. Typically, the harpoon employed to pierce a whale connects to an extensive rope that unspools quickly while the injured animal pulls it along. In this instance, however, the line measured no more than ten fathoms, and its end fastened to a compact cask intended to indicate the path the dugong followed beneath the surface by bobbing on the waves.

I remained upright, observing the Canadian’s opponent with great attention. This halicore, otherwise known as a dugong, bears a strong likeness to the manatee; its elongated frame ended in a tail of significant length, while its side fins possessed flawless digits. The distinction between it and the manatee lay in its upper jaw, which featured a pair of sharp, extended teeth that grew into diverging tusks on either side.

The dugong that Tom Harlan was getting ready to strike was of immense size; it measured over seven yards in length. Remaining motionless, it appeared to be slumbering upon the swells, a situation that simplified its seizure.

The craft drew to a distance of six yards from the creature. The oars lay still upon the rowlocks. I stood up halfway. Tom Harlan, leaning his torso slightly rearward, flourished the harpoon with his practiced grip.
A hissing sound erupted all at once, and the dugong vanished. Even though the harpoon had been cast with significant power, it seemed to have merely hit the surface of the water.
“Confound it!” the Canadian shouted in a rage; “I failed to hit it!”
“No,” I replied; “the beast is injured—see the blood; however, your implement did not pierce his flesh.”
“My harpoon! my harpoon!” shouted Tom Harlan.
The crew continued to pull at their oars, and the coxswain steered toward the drifting cask. Having recovered the harpoon, we gave chase to the creature.
Every so often, it rose to the top to inhale. Despite its injury, the creature showed no signs of fatigue, surging forward at a tremendous speed.

Driven by powerful limbs, the vessel sped along its course. On multiple occasions, it drew near by a distance of only a few yards, and the Canadian prepared to deliver a blow, yet the dugong escaped with an abrupt dive, rendering it out of range.

Consider the intensity that fueled the restless Tom Harlan! He shouted the most powerful curses in the English language at the miserable beast. As for me, I felt nothing but annoyance watching the dugong evade every one of our strikes.

For an hour, we chased it relentlessly, and I started to believe that seizing it would be a challenge, until the creature, driven by a stubborn desire for retribution that it would soon regret, wheeled around toward the pinnace and launched its own attack against us.
The Canadian noticed this movement.
“Watch yourself!” he shouted.
The coxswain uttered a few remarks in his peculiar language, surely cautioning the crew to remain vigilant.

Approaching to within twenty feet of our vessel, the dugong halted and inhaled the atmosphere sharply through its expansive nostrils, which were situated on the top of its snout rather than at the tip. Following this, the creature launched itself upward and lunged toward us.

Unable to dodge the impact, the pinnace tilted precariously and took on a minimum of two tons of water that required bailing; however, because of the coxswain, we took the blow on our flank rather than head-on, preventing us from capsizing entirely. As Tom Harlan gripped the bow and struck the massive beast repeatedly with his harpoon, the animal sank its teeth into the gunwale, hoisting the entire craft from the sea just as a lion handles a roebuck. We were thrown atop each other, and I am uncertain how the struggle might have concluded had the Canadian, still furious at the creature, not pierced its heart.

I listened as its fangs rasped against the metal plating, then the dugong vanished, dragging the harpoon along. Before long, the cask floated back to the top, and not much later, the creature’s carcass appeared, belly facing upward. Our craft reached the beast, secured it with a line, and headed directly toward the Meridian.
To lift the dugong onto the deck, gear of immense power was necessary. The creature had a weight of 10,000 lbs.

On 11th February, the following day, the Meridian’s pantry gained a supply of finer game. A flock of sea-swallows alighted upon the Meridian. This bird belonged to the Sterna nilotica variety, native to Egypt; it possesses a black beak, a pointed grey head, white-spotted eyes, a greyish back, wings, and tail, a white throat and belly, and red claws. Additionally, they captured about twelve Nile ducks, a flavorful wild bird featuring a white throat and a white upper head marked with black spots.

At approximately five in the evening, we observed the Cape of Ras-Mohammed toward the north. The Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Acabah enclose this cape, which constitutes the furthest point of Arabia Petraea.
