The Meridian entered the Straits of Jubal, the passage opening toward the Gulf of Suez. I clearly observed a lofty peak rising up between the twin gulfs of Ras-Mohammed. That was Mount Horeb, the Sinai summit where Moses beheld God face to face.

At six o’clock, the Meridian, alternating between floating and submerging, traveled a ways from Tor, which lay at the bay’s terminus, where the sea appeared stained a reddish hue, a detail Captain Sorel had previously noted. Darkness subsequently arrived amid a profound stillness, occasionally interrupted by the shrieks of pelicans and various nocturnal birds, the sound of surf crashing against the coastline, rubbing against the stones, or the rhythmic gasping of a distant steamer churning the Gulf with its clamorous paddle wheels.

Between the hours of eight and nine, the Meridian stayed submerged several fathoms deep. Based on my own reckoning, our position had to be in close proximity to Suez. Via the saloon’s viewport, I observed the rocky seabed illuminated vividly by the glow of our electric lamp. It appeared that we were steadily putting the Straits further into the distance.

When the clock struck nine-fifteen, the ship had ascended to the water’s surface, and I climbed onto the deck. Driven by a restless desire to traverse Captain Sorel’s tunnel, I found it impossible to remain still, choosing instead to step out and inhale the cool evening atmosphere.
Before long, a faint glow appeared within the darkness, partially obscured by the mist, radiating from a location approximately one mile away.
“A floating lighthouse!” remarked an individual beside me.
The Captain came into my view as I pivoted.
“That is the Suez beacon drifting,” he went on. “We shall reach the mouth of the passage shortly.”
“Is the entry not simple?”

“No, sir; that is why I make a habit of entering the steersman’s cage to personally guide our path. And now, M. Delorme, if you would descend, the Meridian is about to submerge, and it shall not reappear above the water until we have traversed the Arabian Tunnel.”

Captain Sorel guided me in the direction of the main stairs; upon reaching the midpoint, he unlatched a door, crossed the upper deck, and arrived inside the pilot’s cage, which, as one might recall, stood at the edge of the platform. This cabin was six feet square, bearing a strong resemblance to those used by pilots on Mississippi or Hudson steamboats. A vertically mounted wheel operated in the center, connected to the tiller-rope that extended to the rear of the Meridian. Four ports equipped with lenticular lenses, set into a groove within the cabin wall, provided the helmsman with a view in every direction.

The interior of this cabin was dim, yet my vision adjusted to the gloom before long, and I noticed the pilot, a robust individual, with his palms positioned upon the wheel’s spokes. Beyond, the ocean seemed brightly illuminated by the lantern, casting its beams from the cabin’s rear toward the opposite end of the deck.
“At this moment,” Captain Sorel stated, “we shall attempt to complete our crossing.”

The pilot’s cabin was linked to the engine compartment by electrical cables, allowing the Captain to relay both velocity and heading to his Meridian at the same time. Upon his pressing a steel button, the rotation of the propeller slowed immediately.

I gazed quietly upon the towering, vertical barrier we were currently passing, the solid foundation of a vast shoreline of sand. For an hour, we trailed alongside it, maintaining a distance of merely a few yards.
Captain Sorel kept his gaze fixed upon the knob, which hung within its pair of concentric circles inside the cabin. With a mere motion, the pilot adjusted the Meridian’s trajectory at every moment.
Stationed by the port-scuttle, I observed impressive foundations of coral, zoophytes, seaweed, and fucus, their massive claws swaying as they reached out from the crevices in the stone.

At ten-fifteen, the Captain personally assumed control of the steering. Ahead of us appeared a vast, dark, and cavernous gallery. The Meridian entered it fearlessly. An odd rumbling noise echoed about the hull. These were the currents of the Red Sea, which the tunnel’s downward slope forced forcefully in the direction of the Mediterranean. Carried along by the rushing stream, the Meridian moved with the speed of a projectile, notwithstanding the mechanical attempts to slow it down by churning the water with a reversed screw.

Against the sides of the cramped corridor, I observed only luminous beams, linear streaks, and grooves of flame, etched by the immense velocity beneath the intense electric illumination. My pulse quickened.
At ten thirty-five, Captain Sorel abandoned the wheel and, facing me, said:
“The Mediterranean!”
The Meridian had traversed the Isthmus of Suez in under twenty minutes, swept forward by the rushing current.

On the 12th of February, when the sun began to break the following morning, the Meridian ascended to the water's surface. I hurried toward the deck. A faint silhouette of Pelusium appeared three miles to the south. We had been transported from one sea to the next by a rushing current. Tom and Baptiste arrived to meet me near seven o’clock.
“And the Mediterranean?” the Canadian asked, his voice carrying a hint of cheer, “Well, Sir Naturalist.”
“My friend Tom, we are drifting upon the top of it.”
“What!” Baptiste exclaimed, “this exact evening.”
“Indeed, tonight; within moments we shall have crossed this uncrossable isthmus,” I said.
“I find that hard to credit,” the Canadian answered.

“You are mistaken, Master Harlan,” I persisted; “this flat shoreline curving toward the south is the coast of Egypt. And you, Tom, possessing such keen vision, can observe the Port Said jetty extending out into the water.”
The Canadian observed with care.

“You are surely correct, sir, and your Captain is a top-tier individual. We find ourselves in the Mediterranean. Excellent! Now, I ask that you discuss our private matter, yet in a way that ensures no one overhears us,” said I.

Understanding the Canadian’s intent, I decided it was preferable to permit him to speak, since that was his desire; consequently, the three of us moved to sit in the vicinity of the lantern, a spot where the propeller spray reached us less frequently.
“Tom, we are listening now; what is it you have to say to us?”

“My message for you is quite straightforward. We find ourselves in Europe; and prior to Captain Sorel’s whims pulling us down to the depths of the Polar Seas again, or guiding us toward Oceania, I request to depart from the Meridian.”
It was not my intention to restrict the freedom of those traveling with me, yet I possessed absolutely no inclination to depart from Captain Sorel.

Owing to him and his equipment, I drew closer to finishing my underwater research with every passing day; I was drafting my manuscript on the deep sea while situated within that very environment. Would I ever encounter another chance to witness the marvels of the ocean? Certainly not! I found it impossible to entertain the notion of leaving the Meridian until the full sequence of my inquiry had reached its conclusion.
“Tell me honestly, friend Tom, do you find life on this vessel wearisome? Do you regret that fate has placed us under the command of Captain Sorel?”
For a few instants, the Canadian offered no reply. Folding his arms across his chest, he said:

“To be honest, I feel no remorse regarding this voyage beneath the ocean. I will be pleased to have completed it; however, now that the task is finished, it is time to conclude our involvement. That is my perspective.”
“The conclusion is approaching, Tom.”
“Where and when?”
“I am uncertain of the location—I cannot name the time; or, perhaps, I imagine it shall conclude once these waters possess no further lessons for us.”
“What is it you expect, then?” the Canadian inquired.
“It is possible that situations could arise half a year from today, just as they might at this moment, from which we possess the ability and the duty to gain.”
“And where are we going to find ourselves half a year from now, if you would be so kind, Sir Naturalist?” asked Tom Harlan.

“Maybe in China; you are aware that the Meridian travels quickly. It moves across the ocean like a swallow in the sky, or like a train on the ground. It has no dread of busy waters; who is to claim that it might not reach the shores of France, England, or America, where escaping could be tried just as effectively as in this place.”

“M. Delorme,” the Canadian answered, “the basis of your reasoning is flawed. You discuss what is to come, saying, ‘We shall be there! we shall be here!’ I focus on the current moment, stating, ‘We are here, and we must profit by it.’”
The reasoning provided by Tom Harlan weighed heavily upon me, and I perceived that I had been defeated in that arena. I was uncertain as to what line of persuasion might currently serve my interests.
“Sir,” Tom went on, “let us imagine a scenario that cannot be: if Captain Sorel were to present you with your freedom today; would you take it?”
“I am unsure,” I replied.
“And if,” he continued, “the proposal presented to you today were never offered again, would you take it?”

“My reply is this, Friend Tom. Your logic stands in opposition to mine. We cannot depend upon the benevolence of Captain Sorel. Basic caution prevents him from granting our freedom. Conversely, caution dictates that we take advantage of the earliest chance to depart the Meridian.”
“That is a wise observation, M. Delorme.”

“There is but a single point to note—merely one. This event demands gravity, and our initial endeavor is required to be triumphant; should it miscarry, we will be denied a second chance, and Captain Sorel will not offer us his pardon.”

“That is all correct,” the Canadian answered. “However, your point is just as valid for every effort to escape, regardless of whether it happens in two years or two days. Nevertheless, the dilemma remains: whenever a positive chance arises, we have to take it.”
“Agreed! And now, will you explain to me, Tom, what you imply by a favourable opportunity?” said I.
“That is what, during a pitch-black night, shall place the Meridian a brief span away from a European shore,” I said.
“Are you planning to attempt to rescue yourself through swimming?” I asked.
“Indeed, provided we were in close proximity to the shore, and assuming the vessel remained buoyant then. Not in the event that the shore was distant, and the boat had submerged.”
“In that event?”

“In that event, I ought to attempt to take command of the pinnace. I am familiar with its operation. We need to enter, and after the bolts are pulled back, we will emerge at the water’s surface, while the pilot, stationed in the bows, remains unaware of our escape,” said I.
“Keep an eye out for the chance, Tom; however, bear in mind that a single snag shall be our undoing.”
“I shall remember, sir.”
“And would you care to hear my opinion regarding your project now, Tom?”
“Of course, M. Delorme.”
“It is my belief—I am not claiming to wish for it—that this advantageous chance shall not occur again.”
“For what reason?”

“Since Captain Sorel is unable to conceal from his own mind that we have not abandoned every expectation of recovering our freedom, he shall remain vigilant, especially while we are upon the seas and within view of the European shores.”
“We shall see,” Tom Harlan answered, his head moving in a firm shake.

“And at this point, Tom Harlan,” I continued, “we shall cease. Not one more syllable regarding this matter. When the time arrives that you are prepared, approach us with the news, and we shall accompany you. I place my complete trust in you.”

So concluded a dialogue that, before long, brought about such serious consequences. I ought to mention that events appeared to validate my predictions, much to the Canadian’s misery. Was Captain Sorel suspicious of us in these busy waters? or was his only goal to remain concealed from the many ships, of every nationality, traversing the Mediterranean? I had no way of knowing; yet we remained submerged more frequently and stayed at a distance from the shore. Or, whenever the Meridian did surface, there was nothing visible except for the pilot’s cage; and occasionally it descended to significant depths, since, in the area between the Grecian Archipelago and Asia Minor, we were unable to reach the seabed at a distance of over a thousand fathoms.
The only way I understood our proximity to the Island of Carpathos, a member of the Sporades, was through Captain Sorel quoting these verses from Virgil:
“In the depths of the Neptunian abyss dwells a prophet, the azure Proteus,”
while he indicated a location on the planisphere.

This was truly the archaic dwelling of Proteus, the aged herdsman of Neptune’s herds, currently the Island of Scarpanto, positioned amidst Rhodes and Crete. Through the saloon’s glass panes, I observed only the granite foundation.

On the 14th of February, the following day, I determined to dedicate a portion of my time to the examination of the marine life within the Archipelago; however, for some unknown cause, the shutters stayed tightly fastened. By observing our path along the Meridian, I discovered our trajectory was directed toward Candia, the historic island of Crete. When I first boarded the Evangeline, the entirety of that land was in open revolt against the tyranny of the Turks. Yet, I possessed no knowledge regarding the success of the rebels since that period, and Captain Sorel, cut off from any connection to the shore, was unable to provide me with information.

I did not mention this occurrence later that evening while I was by myself with him in the saloon. Furthermore, he appeared to be withdrawn and lost in thought. Then, breaking from his usual habits, he requested that both panels be slid back, and, moving between them, he watched the volume of water with care. I had no idea why; therefore, for my part, I spent my hours observing the sea life drifting past my view.

A diver emerged from the center of the sea, a pouch made of leather fastened to his waist. This was no corpse left to the currents; rather, it was a man alive, pulling himself through the water with powerful strokes and vanishing now and then to inhale air above the waves.
Facing Captain Sorel, I cried out in a troubled tone:
“A castaway! It is imperative that he be rescued regardless of the cost!”
“A shipwrecked sailor! A man!” I shouted.
The Captain offered no reply to my words, instead approaching to rest his weight upon the panel.
The individual had drawn near, and, pressing his visage against the pane, he observed us.
I was astonished when Captain Sorel gestured toward him. Responding with a wave, the diver climbed straight to the water’s surface and vanished from sight.

“There is no need for unease,” remarked Captain Sorel. “This is Nicholas of Cape Matapan, who goes by the name Pesca. He possesses great renown throughout the Cyclades. A courageous diver! The sea is his true home, and he spends more time submerged than on solid ground, traveling constantly between islands, reaching as far as Crete.”
“Are you acquainted with him, Captain?”
“For what reason, M. Delorme?”

With that remark, Captain Sorel walked over to an item of furniture positioned by the saloon’s left side. Beside that piece, I noticed an iron-strapped chest, featuring a copper plaque upon its lid that displayed the Meridian emblem and its motto.
Just then, the Captain, unaware that I was standing there, unlocked the chest, a kind of iron safe, containing a large number of gold bars.
These were gold bars. Where did this valuable substance originate, accounting for such a vast fortune? From what source did the Captain acquire this gold? and what were his intentions for it?

Not a single syllable escaped my lips. I watched. Captain Sorel gathered the ingots individually, placing them in an orderly fashion within the chest until it was completely full. I calculated the total mass to be upwards of 4,000 lbs. of gold, which equates to a value of almost £200,000.
The lid of the chest was locked tight, and the Captain inscribed a destination upon it, utilizing symbols that appeared to be from Modern Greece.

Following this, Captain Sorel pushed a button connected to the crew’s living area by a wire. A quartet of men arrived and, struggling somewhat, shoved the trunk out of the cabin. Afterward, I listened as they used pulleys to haul it up the metal stairs.
Captain Sorel pivoted toward me at that exact instant.
“And you were mentioning, sir?” he remarked.
“I wasn’t speaking, Captain.”
“In that case, sir, if you permit it, I shall bid you good night.”
He then pivoted and exited the saloon.

Deeply disturbed, as you might imagine, I went back to my quarters. My attempts to rest were fruitless; I hunted for the connection between the vision of the diver and the trunk packed with gold. Before long, the Meridian’s rolling and heaving motions signaled to me that the vessel was departing the deep and heading toward the surface.

Footsteps sounded on the platform, and I realized they were detaching the pinnace and setting it onto the water. The vessel collided with the hull of the Meridian for a single moment, after which every sound vanished.

Following a two-hour interval, that identical clamor and the recurring bustle began once more; the vessel was lifted onto the deck, settled back into its cradle, and the Meridian submerged beneath the water again.
Thus, these millions were conveyed to their destination. To which location on the landmass? With whom was Captain Sorel corresponding?

Following the arrival of the next morning, I recounted to the Canadian and Baptiste the occurrences from the previous night, which had stimulated my interest to an extreme level. My associates were just as astonished as I was.
“However, to what location does he transport his millions?” inquired Tom Harlan.

No reply could be made to that. Following my morning meal, I went back to the saloon and began my tasks. I spent the time until five o’clock in the afternoon organizing my records. Just then—(should I ascribe it to some odd quirk)—a sensation of intense warmth forced me to remove my jacket. This was odd, as we were in low latitudes; furthermore, the Meridian, while underwater, should not have been subject to variations in temperature. I checked the manometer; it indicated a depth of sixty feet, a level that the heat of the atmosphere could not reach.
My labor persisted, yet the heat climbed to a degree that became unbearable.
“Is it possible that there is a fire on the ship?” I wondered.
As I was exiting the saloon, Captain Sorel walked in; he went over to the thermometer, checked it, and, facing me, said:
“Forty-two degrees.”
“I have observed it, Captain,” I answered, “and should the temperature rise any further, it will become intolerable.”
“It will not grow any warmer, sir, provided we do not desire it,” I said.
“So, you are able to diminish it however you like?”
“No; however, I am able to move a greater distance away from the heater that generates it.”
“We are heading out, then!”
“Of course; we are drifting within a stream of scalding liquid.”
“Could it be!” I cried out.
“Observe.”

The shutters slid back, revealing an ocean that had turned completely white in every direction. Amidst the surging waves, which churned like liquid inside a heated copper vessel, plumes of brimstone vapor spiraled upward. I pressed my palm against one of the glass sections, yet the intensity of the warmth forced me to pull it away instantly.
“At what location are we?” I inquired.
“In the vicinity of the Island of Santorin, sir,” the Captain answered. “I desired to provide you with a view of the strange phenomenon of an underwater volcanic outburst.”
“I believed,” I remarked, “that the creation of these fresh islands had ceased.”

“In the volcanic regions of the ocean, nothing truly concludes,” Captain Sorel answered; “the world is constantly being shaped by fires beneath the earth. Back in the nineteenth year of our era, as noted by Cassiodorus and Pliny, a fresh island known as Theia (the divine) surfaced exactly where these small islands have lately taken shape. They subsequently vanished beneath the water, only to reappear in the year 69, before sinking once more. From that period until our own, this Plutonian activity had ceased. However, on the 3rd of February, 1866, a novel island, which was titled George Island, rose from the heart of the sulfurous mist close to Nea Kamenni, and it submerged again on the 6th of that same month. A week later, on the 13th of February, the Island of Aphroessa emerged, creating a channel ten yards wide between itself and Nea Kamenni. I happened to be in these waters when the event took place, allowing me to witness every distinct stage. The Island of Aphroessa, circular in shape, was 300 feet across and 30 feet tall. It consisted of dark, glassy lava combined with pieces of felspar. More recently, on the 10th of March, a tinier island named Reka became visible near Nea Kamenni, and since that time, these three have merged to create a single, unified island.”
“And the waterway where we currently find ourselves?” I inquired.
“It is right here,” Captain Sorel answered, as he displayed a chart of the Archipelago to me. “Observe, I have indicated the locations of the recent islands.”

I went back to the pane. The Meridian had ceased its motion, and the temperature grew intolerable. The ocean, previously white, had turned red because of iron salts. Although the vessel was airtight, a stifling scent of sulphur permeated the lounge, and the vivid electric light was completely blotted out by glowing crimson fire. I was drenched in sweat, I was gasping for air, I was roasting.
“It is impossible for us to stay in this scalding liquid any longer,” I remarked to the Captain.
“It would not be wise,” answered the stoic Captain Sorel.

A command was issued; the Meridian veered away, departing the inferno it lacked the resilience to withstand. Fifteen minutes later, we were inhaling clean atmosphere above the water. It then occurred to me that had Tom Harlan selected this region of the ocean for our escape, we would have surely perished within this burning expanse.

On the 16th of February, the following day, we departed from the basin that is estimated to be approximately 1,500 fathoms deep between Alexandria and Rhodes, and the Meridian, traveling a ways from Cerigo, exited the Grecian Archipelago once we had rounded Cape Matapan.

text: Between the night of February 16th and 17th, we arrived in the second Mediterranean basin, where the maximum measurement of the floor reached 1,450 fathoms. Propelled by the rotation of its screw, the Meridian descended along the sloping gradients to entrench itself within the deepest reaches of the ocean.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII THE MEDITERRANEAN IN FORTY-EIGHT HOURS
text: At approximately three in the morning on the 18th of February, our position was at the mouth of the Straits of Gibraltar. Two currents were once thought to be present: a surface flow, identified long ago, that carries oceanic water into the Mediterranean basin; and a deeper opposing current, whose presence has now been logically established. In truth, the Mediterranean’s total water volume, constantly increased by Atlantic swells and inflowing rivers, would elevate the sea’s level annually, as evaporation alone cannot maintain a balance. Since this does not occur, we are forced to acknowledge an under-current that discharges the Mediterranean’s excess water into the Atlantic basin by way of the Straits of Gibraltar. This is a reality, and it was this opposing flow that the Meridian utilized. It moved swiftly through the constricted passage. For a brief moment, I saw the lovely remains of the temple of Hercules, interred in the earth as Pliny described, along with the small island upon which it rests; shortly thereafter, we were drifting upon the Atlantic.

The Atlantic! an enormous expanse of liquid, possessing a surface area of twenty-five million square miles, stretching nine thousand miles in length, and maintaining an average width of two thousand seven hundred—a sea whose winding, parallel coastlines enclose a colossal perimeter, fed by the globe’s greatest rivers, the St. Lawrence, the Mississippi, the Amazon, the Plata, the Orinoco, the Niger, the Senegal, the Elbe, the Loire, and the Rhine, all of which transport currents from the most cultured, as well as the most primitive, lands! Splendid watery domain, constantly furrowed by ships of all countries, protected by the banners of every nation, and ending at those two fearsome locations so feared by sailors, Cape Horn and the Cape of Tempests.

Cutting through the waves with its pointed prow, the Meridian had finished a journey of almost ten thousand leagues in three and a half months, a span exceeding the earth's entire circumference. What was our destination, and what lay ahead for us? Having departed the Straits of Gibraltar, the Meridian had traveled a vast distance. We were back on the surface of the sea, and our routine strolls upon the deck were once again possible.

I climbed aboard immediately, with Tom Harlan and Baptiste beside me. Roughly twelve miles away, the south-western tip of the Spanish peninsula, Cape St. Vincent, was visible as a faint outline. A powerful gale from the south raged. Because the ocean was surging and choppy, the Meridian swayed with great force. Maintaining one’s balance on the deck was nearly unmanageable, as the massive swells crashed across it constantly. Consequently, we went below once we had breathed in a few gulps of open air.

I went back to my quarters, while Baptiste headed for his own; however, the Canadian trailed behind me, appearing deep in thought. Because our journey through the Mediterranean had been so swift, he had been unable to carry out his plan, and his frustration was evident. Once I had closed the door to my room, he took a seat and gazed at me without speaking.
“I comprehend you, Friend Tom,” I remarked, “yet you must not blame yourself. It would have been madness to try to depart the Meridian given the situation.”
Tom Harlan remained silent; the way his mouth was tightly shut and his forehead furrowed revealed how completely this obsession had seized his thoughts.

“We shall observe,” I persisted; “there is no reason for us to lose hope just yet. Our path takes us back along the Portuguese shoreline; France and England lie nearby, offering us simple sanctuary. Had the Meridian steered toward the south upon exiting the Straits of Gibraltar, or had it conveyed us into areas devoid of landmasses, I would certainly join in your apprehension. However, it is evident that Captain Sorel avoids shunning populated waters, and I believe that within a few days, you will be able to proceed with confidence.”
Tom Harlan continued to stare directly at me; eventually, his set mouth opened, and he remarked, “It is for to-night.”
I pulled myself upright in an instant. It is true that I was scarcely ready for this message. I attempted to reply to the Canadian, yet my speech failed me.

“We decided to hold out for a chance,” Tom Harlan went on, “and that chance is here. Tonight, we will be positioned just a short distance from the Spanish shore. The sky is overcast. The breeze is strong. I have your promise, M. Delorme, and I am counting on you.”
The Canadian drew near to me while I remained quiet.

“At nine o’clock this evening,” he stated. “I have alerted Baptiste. By then, Captain Sorel shall be locked inside his quarters, likely sleeping. The crew and the engineers will be unable to observe us. Baptiste and I are going to reach the main stairs, while you, M. Delorme, stay in the library, a mere two paces away, and await my cue. The sail, the mast, and the oars are stored in the canoe. I have managed to secure a supply of food as well. I obtained an English wrench to remove the bolts securing it to the hull of the Meridian. Everything is prepared for tonight.”
“The ocean is rough.”

“I grant that,” the Canadian answered; “yet we are required to take the chance. Freedom is deserving of the cost; furthermore, the vessel is sturdy, and traveling a few miles when assisted by a favorable breeze is not a significant task. Perhaps by tomorrow we might be a hundred leagues distant? Provided conditions are in our favor, we will have reached a piece of terra firma by ten or eleven o’clock, whether we survive or not. However, farewell until this evening.”

Following these remarks, the Canadian departed, rendering me nearly speechless. I had supposed that, once the opening was lost, I would possess a moment to ponder and deliberate on the subject. My stubborn associate had allowed me no such interval; and, in the end, what might I have uttered to him? Tom Harlan was entirely correct. There was nearly an occasion to leverage. Might I withdraw my promise, and assume the burden of jeopardizing the destiny of my associates? By to-morrow Captain Sorel could convey us a great distance from any shore.
Just then, a fairly audible hiss signaled to me that the tanks were taking on water, and the Meridian was descending beneath the Atlantic’s surface.
I spent a melancholy day, torn between the urge to reclaim my freedom to act and the prospect of deserting the marvelous Meridian, leaving my underwater research unfinished.

How agonizing the time I endured in that state! At moments I envisioned my associates and myself arriving securely, while at others I harbored a desire, contrary to my better judgment, that an unexpected event might hinder the execution of Tom Harlan’s plan.

On two occasions, I visited the saloon. My intention was to check the compass. I wanted to determine whether the course of the Meridian was moving us closer to or further away from the shore. However, it was not to be; the Meridian remained within the waters of Portugal.
It is necessary for me to assume my role and get ready to depart. My belongings were light; I carried only my notes.

Regarding Captain Sorel, I pondered his potential reaction to our flight; the complications or harm it could bring upon him, and his likely response should our actions be revealed or miscarry. I had no reason to find fault with him; rather, his generosity was unparalleled. My departure could not be labeled as ungrateful. We were under no sworn obligation to him. He depended on the nature of our situation, rather than any promise from us, to ensure our permanent stay.

Not once had I laid eyes on the Captain following our excursion to the Island of Santorin. Might fortune lead me into his company prior to our leaving? I both desired and dreaded such an encounter. I strained to detect his footsteps within the chamber adjacent to my own. Not a noise came to me. A restless discomfort consumed me. This period of anticipation felt endless. Each hour tolled with such lethargy that it could not match my eagerness.

As was customary, my evening meal was brought to my quarters. I consumed only a small portion, for my mind was elsewhere. At seven o’clock, I vacated the table. Two hours—a duration I tracked precisely—remained until I was scheduled to meet Tom Harlan. My nervousness intensified. My heart hammered against my ribs. I found it impossible to sit still. I paced back and forth, seeking to soothe my restless state through incessant motion. While the prospect of our daring mission failing was the least of my worries, the possibility that our scheme might be unearthed prior to our departure from the Meridian, or that I might be hauled before Captain Sorel to face his annoyance or—more distressingly—his sorrow over my abandonment, caused my heart to race.

My desire was to behold the saloon one final occasion. I walked down the steps and reached the museum, a location where I had spent a great number of productive and pleasant periods. I gazed upon every one of its valuables, every one of its prizes, similar to an individual on the night before a permanent banishment, who was departing with no intention of coming back.

I was about to depart from these marvels of Nature and these triumphs of craftsmanship, which had been the sole focus of my existence for so many days, never to return! I wished to gaze one final time through the saloon’s portholes at the Atlantic depths; however, the shutters were sealed tight, and a barrier of steel cut me off from that sea I had not yet investigated.

As I walked by the saloon, I approached the entrance positioned at the corner that led to the Captain’s room. To my immense astonishment, this door stood slightly open. I recoiled instinctively. Should Captain Sorel be inside his quarters, he might spot me. Yet, detecting no noise, I edged closer. The chamber was empty. I nudged the door wider and stepped inside. It maintained the identical ascetic, monastic quality of appearance.

The clock chimed eight all at once. I was roused from my slumber by the initial strike of the hammer against the bell. A shudder took hold of me, as though an unseen gaze had peered into my deepest reflections, and I rushed out of the chamber.
I caught sight of the compass. We remained on a northerly heading. The log showed a steady pace, and the manometer recorded a depth near sixty feet.

Back in my quarters, I dressed in heavy gear—sea boots, an otterskin cap, and a massive byssus coat, furred with sealskin; I stood prepared and expectant. Only the shuddering of the propeller disturbed the profound stillness that held the vessel. I hearkened with care. Might some booming shout abruptly reveal that Tom Harlan had been caught in his intended escape. An agonizing fear gripped me, and I struggled unsuccessfully to recover my usual composure.

I pressed my ear against the door of the Captain at a time just before nine. There was silence. After leaving my quarters, I went back to the saloon, which was empty and partially shrouded in darkness.

I unlatched the entryway connecting to the library. Identical inadequate illumination, identical isolation. I positioned myself by the portal accessing the main staircase, and there stood awaiting the sign from Tom Harlan.

Just then, the vibration of the propeller noticeably lessened, before ceasing altogether. The only sound breaking the quiet was the thumping of my heart. All at once, a minor jolt occurred; I realized the Meridian had come to a halt on the seafloor. My anxiety grew. The Canadian’s sign failed to arrive. I wanted to go find Tom Harlan and plead with him to delay his plan. I sensed that we were not traveling as we normally did.
Just then, the entrance to the spacious lounge swung wide, and Captain Sorel stepped into view. Upon noticing me, he spoke immediately in a pleasant manner:
“Oh, sir! I have been searching for you. Are you aware of the history of Spain?”

Though a person might possess an intimate knowledge of their nation’s past, in the state I occupied then, suffering from a restless spirit and a completely muddled brain, I would have been unable to utter a single syllable concerning it.
“Well,” Captain Sorel went on, “you listened to what I asked! Are you familiar with the past of Spain?”
“In a minor way,” I replied.

“So, here we find scholars forced to study,” the Captain remarked. “Approach, take a seat, and I shall recount a strange incident from this chronicle. Sir, pay close attention,” he added; “this narrative will intrigue you in one particular regard, as it shall resolve a query you have surely been unable to answer.”
“I am listening, Captain,” I replied, unaware of my interlocutor’s objective and wondering whether this occurrence related to our planned departure.

“If you do not mind, sir, we shall return to the year 1702. You are certainly aware that your monarch, Louis XIV, believing that a sovereign’s decree sufficed to subject the Pyrenees to his rule, forced the Spaniards to accept his grandson, the Duke of Anjou. This royal, who governed with varying degrees of incompetence as Philip V, faced significant foreign opposition. In fact, the year prior, the monarchies of England, Austria, and Holland formed a pact at the Hague, aiming to remove the Spanish crown from Philip V and bestow it upon an archduke whom they had already begun to style Charles III.”

“Spain must defy this alliance; yet the nation lacked nearly all necessary troops and mariners. Still, funds would be sufficient, assuming their galleons, carrying precious metals from America, successfully reached their harbors. Near the conclusion of 1702, they anticipated a valuable shipment protected by France with a naval force of twenty-three ships, led by Admiral Chateau-Renaud, as the coalition’s vessels were already scouring the Atlantic. This fleet was intended for Cadiz, but the Admiral, learning that an English squadron was patrolling that area, decided to steer toward a port in France.

“The Spanish commanders of the convoy objected to this decision.” They requested transport to a Spanish harbor, and, failing Cadiz, they asked for Vigo Bay, located on Spain’s northwest coast, which remained unblocked.
“Admiral Chateau-Renaud possessed the impulsiveness to follow this command, and the galleons sailed into Vigo Bay.

“Regrettably, it created an accessible path that was impossible to protect by any means. They were consequently required to speed up the offloading of the galleons prior to the joint fleet appearing; and they would have had sufficient time if a wretched matter of competition had not unexpectedly emerged,” I said.
“Are you tracking the sequence of occurrences?” inquired Captain Sorel.
“In every way,” I replied, unaware of the conclusion intended by this lecture on history.

“I shall proceed. This is how it occurred. The traders of Cadiz held a monopoly granting them the authority to accept every shipment arriving from the West Indies. Consequently, unloading those bars at the harbor of Vigo meant stripping them of their entitlements. They lodged a protest in Madrid and secured an agreement from the feeble-willed Philip that the fleet, while keeping its freight on board, was to stay held in the bay of Vigo until the foe had departed.”

“However, during the process of reaching this conclusion, on October 22nd, 1702, the English fleet reached Vigo Bay, at which point Admiral Chateau-Renaud, notwithstanding his disadvantage in numbers, engaged with courage. Yet, realizing the wealth was destined to be captured by the opposition, he set fire to and sank each galleon, causing them to descend to the seabed along with their vast fortunes.”
Captain Sorel halted. I confess that I was unable to perceive at that moment the reason this narrative ought to concern me.
“So?” I inquired.
“Indeed, M. Delorme,” answered Captain Sorel, “we have arrived at Vigo Bay; and it is up to you to determine if you shall uncover its secrets.”

The Captain stood up and instructed me to accompany him. My strength had returned during the interval. I complied. Although the saloon remained in shadow, the ocean surface shimmered beyond the clear glass. I gazed out.

The waters for a distance of half a mile encircling the Meridian appeared to be illuminated by electricity. The floor of sand was luminous and pristine. A portion of the crew of the ship, clad in diving-suits, were occupied with the removal of decayed casks and vacant crates from among the charred remains of shipwrecks. Gold and silver bars, along with showers of jewels and piastres, spilled out from these containers. The sand was piled high with such items. Carrying their valuable plunder, the divers journeyed back to the Meridian, deposited their haul, and departed once more to that bottomless source of silver and gold.

At last, I grasped the truth. This location served as the site for the conflict on the 22nd of October, 1702. It was upon this precise ground that the vessels carrying cargo for the Spanish Government went down. It was here that Captain Sorel arrived, following his own desires, to gather the millions that he loaded onto the Meridian. America had surrendered her valuable ores for him, and him exclusively. He stood as the sole inheritor, with no one to divide the wealth, of those riches ripped away from the Incas and the defeated subjects of Ferdinand Cortez.
“Are you aware, sir,” he inquired with a smile, “that the ocean held these treasures?”
“I was aware,” I replied, “that the sum of two millions is the value they place upon the currency kept suspended within these depths.”

“Undoubtedly; yet the cost of retrieving these funds would exceed the gain. Conversely, I merely need to collect what humanity has abandoned—not solely in Vigo Bay, but across a thousand additional harbors where vessels have foundered, all of which are charted on my underwater map. Do you grasp the origin of my immense wealth at last?”
“I grasp your meaning, Captain. However, permit me to inform you that by investigating Vigo Bay, you have merely anticipated a competing organization,” I said.
“And what one?”

“A group that has been granted the right by the Spanish Government to hunt for those sunken galleons. The investors are driven by the temptation of a massive reward, as they estimate the worth of these wealthy wrecks at five hundred millions.”
“They numbered five hundred million,” Captain Sorel replied, “yet that is not the case at present.”

“Precisely,” I replied; “and notifying those shareholders might be considered a charitable deed. Yet, is there any certainty it would be welcomed? The thing gamblers generally lament most is not the squandering of their capital, but the vanishing of their naive expectations. Ultimately, I feel less sympathy for them than for the countless destitute people who could have benefited from such wealth if it were properly allocated, whereas in their hands, it shall remain perpetually unproductive.”
No sooner had I voiced this remorse than I sensed it surely caused Captain Sorel pain.

“Barren!” he cried out, animatedly. “Do you imagine, sir, that these riches vanish simply because I acquire them? Is it for my own sake, as you suppose, that I go to the effort of amassing these fortunes? Who suggested to you that I do not put them to proper use? Do you believe I am unaware that there are suffering souls and downtrodden peoples on this planet, wretched beings to comfort, and victims to vindicate? Do you fail to comprehend?”

Captain Sorel paused after these final remarks, possibly feeling remorse for having revealed so much. Yet I had surmised that, regardless of the reason that compelled him to pursue autonomy beneath the ocean, he remained human, his spirit still pulsed with empathy for the tribulations of mankind, and his vast benevolence extended to both persecuted peoples and solitary souls. I grasped then the intended recipients of those millions dispatched by Captain Sorel while the Meridian navigated the seas near Crete.
On the following morning, February 19th, the Canadian walked into my quarters. I had anticipated this arrival. He appeared quite dejected.
“So, sir?” he asked.
“It seems, Tom, that luck turned away from us yesterday.”
“Indeed; that Captain is required to halt precisely at the moment we planned to depart his ship.”
“Indeed, Tom, he possessed affairs at his financial institution,” I said.
“The bankers of his!”
“Or instead his financial institution; by that I signify the sea, in which his wealth is more secure than within the vaults of the State.”

I subsequently recounted the previous night’s occurrences to the Canadian, with the intention of persuading him to reconsider deserting the Captain; however, my narrative merely prompted Tom to voice a vigorous lament that he had missed the chance to stroll across the Vigo battlefield by himself.
“Nevertheless,” he remarked, “everything has not concluded. It is merely a missed harpoon strike. We shall prevail another time; and this evening, should it be required——”
“Toward which point is the Meridian headed?” I inquired.
“I am uncertain,” answered Tom.
“We will observe the headland at midday,” I said.

Baptiste was rejoined by the Canadian. Once I had finished dressing, I made my way to the saloon. The readings on the compass offered no comfort. The Meridian was steering a course of S.S.W. We were moving away from Europe.

I felt a certain restlessness as I lingered until the ship’s position was marked upon the map. Near eleven-thirty, the tanks were drained, and our craft ascended to the top of the water. I hurried to the deck. Tom Harlan had arrived there before me. There was no longer any ground visible. Only a vast expanse of ocean remained. A few ships appeared in the distance, surely vessels bound for San Roque to find helpful breezes for rounding the Cape of Good Hope. The sky was overcast. A storm was brewing. Tom ranted, attempting to gaze through the hazy skyline. He persisted in the belief that past the mist lay the terrain he desired so deeply.
The sun appeared briefly at midday. Taking advantage of the illumination, the second measured its altitude. Following this, as the waves grew rougher, we went down, and the hatch was shut.

Sixty minutes later, after I examined the map, I noted that the Meridian’s location was indicated at 16° 17′ long. and 33° 22′ lat., situated 150 leagues away from the closest shore. Escape was impossible, and I invite you to picture the fury of the Canadian once I relayed our circumstances to him.
Personally, I did not feel much regret. A weight that had burdened me had been lifted, allowing me to resume my habitual tasks with a measure of serenity.
Around eleven that evening, Captain Sorel paid me a highly unforeseen call. He inquired with great politeness whether I was exhausted following my shift the night before. I replied, “No.”
“In that case, M. Delorme, I suggest an interesting trip.”
“Suggest, Captain?”
“Up until now, you have only explored the ocean floor during the day, beneath the sun’s radiance. Would you be interested in viewing them under the cover of night?”
“With pleasure.”
“I caution you, the journey will be exhausting. We have a long distance to travel on foot, and a mountain to ascend. The paths are poorly maintained,” I warned.
“Your words, Captain, merely increase my interest; I am prepared to accompany you.”
“We shall don our diving-suits now, sir,” I said.

Upon reaching the robing-room, I observed that neither my associates nor any members of the ship’s crew were intended to accompany us on this outing. Captain Sorel had not suggested that I bring along either Tom or Baptiste.
Shortly thereafter, we donned our diving-suits; they secured the air-filled reservoirs to our backs, though no electric lamps had been readied. I pointed this out to the Captain.
“These won’t be of any use,” he answered.

I believed my ears had deceived me, yet I was unable to restate my remark, as the Captain had already withdrawn his head into its steel housing. I completed my equipment. I sensed an iron-tipped rod being placed in my grasp, and some moments afterward, following the customary procedure, we stepped onto the Atlantic floor at a depth of 150 fathoms. It was nearly midnight. The ocean was intensely black, but Captain Sorel indicated a crimson glow far off, a kind of massive beacon radiating intensely roughly two miles from the Meridian. I could not explain the nature of this flame, what sustained it, or the reason and method by which it illuminated the fluid expanse. Regardless, it did provide a path for us, albeit indistinctly, but I rapidly grew used to the strange gloom, and I grasped, in such a situation, why the Ruhmkorff apparatus was unnecessary.

While we moved forward, a pattering sound reached me from overhead. Because the clamor intensified, occasionally creating an unbroken downpour, the reason became clear to me before long. It was a torrential rain, dimpling the tops of the swells. My mind immediately struck upon the notion that I would be soaked! By the water! surrounded by the water! I was unable to suppress a laugh at the strange concept. Yet, truly, inside the heavy diving-dress, the fluid medium is not perceived, and one merely feels as though they are in an environment slightly more compressed than the air on land. Nothing else.

Thirty minutes of trekking later, the ground turned rocky. A faint, glowing luminescence emanated from medusae, tiny crustaceans, and pennatules. I observed fragments of rock blanketed by countless zoophytes and thick clusters of seaweed. My footing frequently gave way on this viscous layer of vegetation, and I surely would have tumbled repeatedly had I not possessed my metal-shod staff. Looking back, the Meridian’s pale beacon remained visible, though its light was fading in the far distance.

Yet the pink glow that directed our path grew stronger, illuminating the skyline. I was utterly bewildered by the existence of this underwater blaze. Could I be approaching a geological occurrence not yet documented by the world’s scholars? Or—a notion that flickered through my mind—might human agency be responsible for this burning? Had someone stoked this fire? Was I destined to encounter, in these abyssal reaches, associates and comrades of Captain Sorel whom he intended to call upon, and who shared his peculiar way of life? Would I discover a complete settlement of outcasts below, who, exhausted by terrestrial hardships, had pursued and secured liberty within the oceanic depths? Such irrational and absurd conjectures haunted me. In this state of agitation, stimulated by the constant parade of marvels unfolding in my view, it would not have astonished me to encounter one of the submerged cities envisioned by Captain Sorel upon the seafloor.

The path ahead became increasingly illuminated. Beams of pale radiance emanated from the peak of a mountain roughly 800 feet tall. However, the sight before me was merely a mirror image, sharpened by the transparency of the liquid. A blaze situated on the far side of the mountain served as the origin for this mysterious glow.

Navigating the rocky labyrinth that creased the Atlantic floor, Captain Sorel moved forward resolutely. This dismal path was familiar to him. He had surely traversed it many times, making it impossible for him to go astray. My trust in him remained firm as I trailed behind. He appeared to be a spirit of the ocean; watching his figure silhouetted in dark relief against the glowing skyline as he led the way, I found myself filled with admiration for his frame.
At one o’clock in the morning, we reached the initial inclines of the mountain; however, reaching them required us to traverse the arduous trails of an expansive thicket.

Indeed; a grove of lifeless timber, devoid of foliage and moisture, wood turned to stone by the water’s influence and occasionally surpassed in height by immense pines. It resembled a coal mine remaining upright, anchored by its roots to the fractured earth, with limbs resembling delicate silhouettes of black paper that stood out sharply against the liquid canopy. Imagine a woodland in the Hartz clinging to the mountain slopes, yet a woodland submerged. The trails were blocked by kelp and seaweed, amidst which a multitude of crustaceans crawled. I proceeded, scaling the stones, stepping over fallen logs, snapping the sea bind-weed that stretched from tree to tree; and startling the fish, which darted from bough to bough. Continuing forward, I experienced no weariness. I trailed my guide, who remained tireless. What a sight! In what way might I describe it? how depict the appearance of those forests and crags within this element—their bases somber and rugged, their summits stained with crimson hues by the illumination that the water’s reflective capacity magnified? We ascended crags that plummeted immediately afterward with massive leaps and the muffled rumbling of a landslide. To the left and right stretched lengthy, shadowed passages, where vision vanished. Here, expansive clearings emerged that appeared to have been shaped by human effort; and I occasionally wondered if some denizen of these underwater domains might not abruptly reveal themselves to me.

Yet Captain Sorel continued his ascent. I was unable to remain in the rear. With courage, I pursued him. My walking stick provided excellent support. Any misstep upon the slender paths inclined toward the edges of the chasms would have posed a peril; nevertheless, I strode with confidence, experiencing no dizziness. At one moment, I leaped across a fissure, the profundity of which might have caused me to pause were it situated amidst terrestrial glaciers; at another, I braved the wobbling log of a tree cast from one precipice to the next, ignoring the space beneath my soles, my gaze occupied entirely by the untamed vistas of this territory.

In that place, massive stones, resting upon their evenly-trimmed foundations, appeared to challenge every principle of balance. Between their rocky joints, vegetation burst forth, resembling a stream forced by intense pressure, and supported further growths that in turn sustained them. Towering natural formations and vast, vertical cliffs, shaped like a “curtain,” tilted at a pitch that the rules of gravity would have forbidden anywhere on Earth.

Following our departure from the Meridian by two hours, we had traversed the tree line, and the mountain’s peak towered a hundred feet overhead, throwing a shadow across the radiant glow of the facing hillside. Strange, fossilized bushes sprawled in erratic patterns. Beneath our feet, fish startled like birds in the tall grass. The immense boulders were split by solid fissures, profound caverns, and bottomless pits, from the depths of which the movements of terrifying beasts were audible. My blood ran cold at the sight of massive antennae obstructing my path or a ghastly claw snapping shut with a clatter within the gloom of a hollow. Countless glowing points sparkled intensely throughout the dark. These were the eyes of colossal crustaceans huddled in their dens; gargantuan lobsters standing like sentries, shifting their pincers with a metallic snap; mammoth crabs aimed like cannons upon their mounts; and hideous octopuses, their tentacles entwined like a writhing nest of snakes.

We had reached the initial landing, a location where further unexpected sights confronted me. In front of us were scattered scenic remains, revealing human craftsmanship rather than divine intervention. Great mounds of rock sat there, within which the indistinct and ghostly outlines of fortresses and shrines could be discerned, draped in a multitude of flowering zoophytes, and covered by a dense botanical cloak of seaweed and fucus in place of ivy. Yet, what segment of the earth had been engulfed by such disasters? Who had positioned those boulders and stones in the manner of ancient dolmens? Where did I stand? To what destination had the imagination of Captain Sorel brought me?

I had a strong desire to inquire of him; since I could not, I halted him—I gripped his arm. Yet, gesturing toward the peak of the mountain while he moved his head from side to side, he appeared to say:
“Follow, follow me; ascend further!”
I trailed behind, and after several minutes I reached the summit, where a ten-yard radius provided a view over the entire rocky formation.

I gazed back down the slope we had recently ascended. The peak stood no higher than seven or eight hundred feet over the flatlands; yet, on its reverse face, it loomed twice as tall above the abyssal waters of this Atlantic region. My vision swept across a vast area illuminated by intense flashes of lightning. The mountain was, in truth, a volcano.

Fifty feet over the summit, surrounded by a shower of rocks and scoriae, a massive crater spewed forth gushes of lava that tumbled in a fiery waterfall into the heart of the fluid body. Positioned in this way, the volcano illuminated the bottom plain like a giant torch, reaching even to the furthest edges of the horizon. I said that the submarine crater ejected lava, yet no flames. Flames necessitate atmospheric oxygen to sustain them and are unable to form beneath the water; however, lava flows, possessing the foundations of their own incandescence, are capable of reaching a white heat, struggling intensely against the liquid element, and transforming it into steam upon contact.
Swift flows carrying all those gases in mixture and cascades of molten rock glided toward the base of the peak similar to a Vesuvius outburst upon another Terra del Greco.

Right there before me, demolished and in ruins, sat a city—its temple structures collapsed, its roofless dwellings exposed to the heavens, its pillars toppled onto the earth, though one could yet identify the sturdy nature of Tuscan design. Beyond that, fragments of a colossal aqueduct; nearby, the elevated foundation of an Acropolis, featuring the drifting silhouette of a Parthenon; elsewhere, remnants of a wharf, suggesting a harbor of old had once reached the edge of the sea, vanishing along with its warships and trading ships. Further still, extended rows of submerged barricades and wide, empty avenues—a flawless Pompeii preserved under the waves. This was the spectacle that Captain Sorel revealed to my sight!

At what location was I? At what location was I? I have to be aware regardless of the price. I attempted to utter a word, yet Captain Sorel halted me with a motion, and, retrieving a fragment of chalk-stone, moved toward a boulder of black basalt, and sketched the single word:
ATLANTIS

How brilliant an illumination flashed across my thoughts! Atlantis! The Atlantis described by Plato, that landmass rejected by Origen and Humbolt, who categorized its vanishing as mere folklore. I beheld it presently, providing undeniable evidence of its destruction. This submerged territory lay past Europe, Asia, and Lybia, past the columns of Hercules, the home of that mighty civilization, the Atlantides, who fought the earliest conflicts against the ancient Greeks.

Guided by the most peculiar fate, I found myself stepping across the peaks of this landmass, my fingers brushing against remnants from a thousand generations past that dated back to the geological eras. I traversed the exact ground where those who lived alongside the first human once roamed.

As I endeavored to commit every feature of this magnificent scenery to memory, Captain Sorel stood still, appearing frozen in silent rapture while resting against a stone covered in moss. Did he ponder the lineages vanished so long ago? Was he questioning them regarding the mystery of man’s fate? Had this peculiar individual journeyed here to immerse himself in memories of history and relive that bygone existence—he who rejected the present one? How much would I have sacrificed to perceive his reflections, to partake in them, to grasp them! For an hour, we stayed at that spot, observing the expansive lowlands beneath the glow of the lava, which occasionally shone with marvelous brilliance. Swift vibrations traveled across the mountain, triggered by subterranean churning, and profound sounds, clearly carried through the fluid environment, resonated with imposing majesty. Just then, the moon emerged through the volume of waters, casting its wan beams upon the submerged landmass. It was merely a flicker, yet what a profound impression it made! The Captain stood up, took one final glance at the vast expanse, and then instructed me to accompany him.

Our descent down the mountain was swift, and after we had cleared the mineral forest, the lantern of the Meridian became visible to me, glowing like a star. The Captain moved directly toward it, and we boarded the vessel just as the initial beams of daylight turned the ocean surface white.

On the following day, February 20th, I rose at a late hour; my exhaustion from the night before had kept me slumbering until eleven. I got ready in a rush and hurried to discover the path the Meridian was following. According to the readings, it remained headed south, traveling at a velocity of twenty miles per hour at a submerged level of fifty fathoms.

The varieties of fish in this location were not significantly distinct from the ones previously observed. Massive rays existed, measuring five yards in length and possessing immense muscular power, a trait that allowed them to propel themselves over the surface of the sea; various types of sharks were present; including one that reached fifteen feet, featuring pointed triangular teeth, and whose clear body made it nearly impossible to see beneath the waves.

Within the bony fish, Baptiste observed several measuring approximately three yards in length, featuring a sharp blade upon their upper jaw; additionally, there were vividly hued beings, identified during the era of Aristotle as the sea-dragon, which pose a hazard to seize due to the spines located along their dorsal side.

Around four, the ground, usually made of dense mire blended with fossilized timber, gradually altered, turning rockier and appearing scattered with conglomerate and basalt fragments, along with a dusting of lava. I surmised that a range of mountains was replacing the extensive flats; consequently, following several rotations of the Meridian, I observed the southern skyline obstructed by a towering barrier that appeared to seal every passage. Its peak clearly rose above the sea’s surface. It had to be a landmass, or perhaps an isle—one of the Canaries, or the Cape Verde Islands. Since the coordinates had not yet been recorded, possibly on purpose, I remained unaware of our precise location. Regardless, such a rampart appeared to me to define the boundaries of that Atlantis, of which we had actually traversed merely the tiniest fraction.

I would have stayed by the window for a far greater duration, taking in the splendor of the heavens and the water, had the shutters not shut. Just then, the Meridian reached the edge of this sheer, vertical cliff. I had no way of knowing what its next action would be. I went back to my quarters; the vessel was stationary. I reclined, fully expecting to rouse myself following a sleep of several hours; yet it was eight o’clock the following morning when I walked into the saloon. I observed the manometer. It indicated that the Meridian was resting upon the sea’s surface. Furthermore, I detected footsteps upon the deck. I approached the panel. It was unsealed; however, rather than the bright light I had anticipated, I found myself enveloped in absolute blackness. Where had we arrived? Had I miscalculated? Was it yet dark? No; not a single star glimmered, and night does not possess such total obscurity.
Near a mountain, the Meridian was drifting.
My thoughts were in a state of confusion, at the moment a voice close by remarked:
“Are you there, Professor?”
“Oh! Captain,” I replied, “at what location are we?”
“Below ground, sir.”
“Below the surface!” I cried out. “With the Meridian yet hovering?”
“It stays buoyant at all times.”
“However, I fail to comprehend.”
“Stay for a short while, we shall ignite our lantern, and, should you prefer bright surroundings, you will be pleased.”

I remained on the deck, waiting. The blackness was so absolute that Captain Sorel was invisible to me; however, when I gazed toward the zenith directly overhead, I perceived a hesitant glimmer, a sort of dusk occupying a round aperture. At that moment, the lantern ignited, and its brilliance banished the dim illumination. I shut my blinded eyes for a second, then reopened them. The Meridian sat motionless, drifting beside a mountain that served as a type of wharf. Consequently, the lake holding it was a body of water confined by a ring of barriers, spanning two miles across and six miles around. Its elevation (as indicated by the manometer) had to match the external level, since a connection between the lake and the ocean was inevitable. The towering walls, tilting inward from their foundation, merged into a domed ceiling resembling a vast inverted funnel, reaching a height of roughly five or six hundred yards. At the peak sat a round opening, through which I had spotted the faint glow, clearly sunlight.
“At what location are we?” I inquired.

“Deep within a dead volcano, whose center was flooded by the ocean following a massive terrestrial upheaval. During your slumber, Professor, the Meridian entered this basin via a subterranean passage that begins roughly ten yards under the sea’s level. This serves as its sanctuary, a secure, convenient, and enigmatic haven, protected against every tempest. Point out to me, should you be able, along the shores of any of your landmasses or isles, a harbor capable of offering such absolute safety from all gales.”

“Of course,” I answered, “you remain secure in this location, Captain Sorel. What individual might possibly attain this place within the center of a volcano? However, was there not a gap I observed at the peak?”
“Indeed; that opening, once brimming with molten rock, steam, and fire, now serves as a gateway for the vital atmosphere we inhale.”
“However, what exactly is this mountain of fire?”
“It is part of the many isles scattered across this sea—a mere sandbar to ships—but a vast grotto to us. I happened upon it by luck, and fortune favored me greatly.”
“However, what purpose does this sanctuary serve, Captain? The Meridian desires no harbor.”

“No, sir; however, it requires electricity for propulsion, and the resources to generate that electricity—sodium to power the cells, coal to produce the sodium, and a coal-mine to provide the coal. Right here, the ocean conceals complete forests buried throughout geological eras, which have since become mineralised and turned into coal; to me, they represent a limitless supply.”
“So, Captain, your crew is engaged in the profession of mining in this location?”

“Precisely. These excavations reach beneath the ocean just as the collieries of Newcastle do. Clad in diving-suits, wielding shovels and pickaxes, my crew retrieves the coal that I have no need to request from terrestrial pits. As I incinerate this fuel to produce sodium, the fumes venting from the mountain’s summit create the illusion of a functioning volcano.”
“Will we be observing your associates as they perform their tasks?”

“No; at the very least not now, since I am eager to proceed with our underwater journey around the globe. Therefore, I will satisfy myself by utilizing the sodium supply I currently hold. We have a single day for replenishment, and then our trip resumes. Consequently, M. Delorme, you should seize the opportunity today if you desire to explore the grotto and circle the lagoon.”

I expressed my gratitude to the Captain before setting out to locate my associates, as they remained inside their quarters. I requested that they accompany me, though I withheld our destination. They climbed onto the platform. Baptiste, a man whom nothing could surprise, acted as if it were entirely ordinary to rouse beneath a mountain following a slumber under the sea. Conversely, Tom Harlan focused solely on discovering if the grotto possessed an outlet. Following our ten o’clock meal, we descended onto the mountain.
“We have arrived, back on solid ground,” said Baptiste.
“This is not what I term land,” the Canadian remarked. “Furthermore, we are not situated upon it, but rather underneath it.”

A sandy beach stretched between the mountain faces and the lake, reaching a maximum width of five hundred feet. Walking the entire perimeter of the lake was simple on this terrain. However, the foundation of the towering barriers consisted of rocky earth, where volcanic boulders and massive pumice fragments were piled in scenic mounds. Every one of these loose pieces, coated in enamel and smoothed by underground heat, glittered brilliantly under the glow of our electric lantern. As we walked, mica dust from the ground kicked up, drifting like a swarm of sparks. The floor began to incline noticeably, and we quickly reached extended, winding gradients or slanted paths that gradually led us upward; nevertheless, we had to tread cautiously across these loose aggregates, which lacked any binding agent, as our feet slid on the slick crystal, felspar, and quartz.
I indicated to my associates that the igneous origins of this vast hollow were corroborated in every direction.

“Imagine for yourselves,” said I, “how this crater appeared while brimming with molten lava, and when the surface of that glowing fluid ascended to the mountain’s opening, just as if it were liquefying atop a heated stove.”
“It is clear in my mind,” said Baptiste. “However, sir, would you explain the reason the Great Architect halted all work, and why the lake’s still water has taken the place of the furnace?”

“In all likelihood, Baptiste, the reason is that a subterranean tremor created the exact gap that allowed the Meridian to enter. Subsequently, the Atlantic’s currents surged into the mountain’s core. A violent clash between the two forces surely occurred, a battle that concluded with Neptune’s triumph. Yet, countless eras have passed since that time, and the sunken volcanic crater is currently a tranquil cavern.”
“I agree,” answered Tom Harlan; “I acknowledge your account, sir; however, for the sake of our safety, I am sorry that the aperture you mention was not constructed higher than the ocean surface.”
“However, comrade Tom,” Baptiste remarked, “had the route not been submerged, the Meridian would have been unable to traverse it.”

Our ascent persisted. The staircase grew increasingly vertical and constricted. Profound pits, which we were forced to traverse, severed the path periodically; we were compelled to bypass inclined mounds. We crept on our knees and dragged ourselves forward. Yet the agility of Baptiste and the vigor of the Canadian overcame every hindrance. At an elevation of roughly 31 feet, the composition of the terrain altered, though it remained no easier to navigate. The conglomerate and trachyte gave way to black basalt, the former scattered in porous strata, the latter arranged in orderly prisms, positioned like a colonnade propping up the base of the vast dome, a magnificent example of geological construction. Winding amidst the basaltic slabs were elongated flows of lava, chilled long ago and coated in bituminous streaks; in certain areas, expansive mats of sulphur were strewn. A more intense radiance filtered down through the summit crater, casting a dim glow across these volcanic hollows eternally entombed within the heart of this dead mountain. However, our climb was abruptly halted at an altitude of approximately two hundred and fifty feet by insurmountable barriers. A solid stone arch spanned above us, and our vertical progress shifted into a horizontal circuit. At this final transition, flora commenced a struggle against the stone. A few bushes, and even some trees, sprouted from cracks in the rock face. I identified certain euphorbias, exuding their acrid sap; heliotropes, failing entirely to live up to their designation, hung their flower heads in sorrow, their vibrancy and scent largely faded. Scattered about, a few chrysanthemums emerged shyly at the base of an aloe characterized by elongated, pallid foliage. Nevertheless, amidst the lava channels, I spotted some small violets that retained a faint fragrance, and I confess I inhaled them with pleasure. “Perfume is the soul of the flower, and sea-flowers have no soul.”
Upon reaching the base of several robust dragon-trees, whose powerful roots had displaced the stones, Tom Harlan cried out:
“Oh! gentleman, a swarm! a swarm!”
“A hive!” I answered, gesturing with disbelief.
“Indeed, a hive,” the Canadian reiterated, “with bees buzzing about it.”

I drew near, forced to credit my own sight. There, at an opening drilled into one of the dragon-trees, existed some thousands of those clever insects, found throughout all the Canaries, and whose output is held in such high regard. It followed that the Canadian desired to collect the honey, and I found it difficult to contest his intent. A heap of withered leaves, combined with sulphur, he ignited using a spark from his flint, and he commenced smoking the bees out. The buzzing gradually died away, and the hive finally provided several pounds of the most delicious honey, which Tom Harlan packed into his haversack.
“Once I have combined this honey with the artocarpus paste,” he remarked, “I will be in a position to provide you with a delicious cake.”
“It shall be gingerbread,” stated Baptiste, “upon my word.”
“Forget about the gingerbread,” I stated; “we should proceed with our engaging stroll.”

The lake revealed its entire expanse at each bend of the trail we traveled. Our lantern illuminated the tranquil water, which lacked any sign of waves or ripples. The Meridian stayed entirely still. Upon the mountain and the platform, the ship’s crew moved like dark silhouettes etched sharply into the glowing air. We were circling the peak of the primary rock strata that supported the ceiling. I realized then that bees were not the sole creatures inhabiting the volcano's interior. Predatory birds circled in the darkness or retreated from nests atop the crags. There were white-breasted sparrow hawks and kestrels, while various plump bustards scurried down the inclines on long legs. I let the reader picture the Canadian’s desire upon seeing such delicious prey, and whether he lamented lacking a firearm. Yet he attempted to substitute stones for lead, and following various failed tries, he managed to injure a superb bird. It is the truth to say he endangered his life twenty times to retrieve it; however, he succeeded, and the animal was placed alongside the honey-cakes in his bag. We were forced to move down toward the bank, as the ridge had become impassable. The crater yawned above us like a well’s opening. From this spot, the sky was visible, and clouds, broken apart by the west wind, left behind misty traces even on the mountain’s peak—a certain sign they were not very high, as the volcano rose no more than eight hundred feet over the ocean. Thirty minutes following the Canadian’s final feat, we arrived back at the interior shore. The flora here consisted of vast mats of marine crystal, a small umbelliferous plant excellent for pickling, also known as sea-fennel or pierce-stone. Baptiste collected several armfuls. Regarding the fauna, it numbered in the thousands of various crustaceans, including crabs, lobsters, chameleon shrimps, and spider-crabs, alongside numerous limpets and rockfish. Forty-five minutes later, our winding journey concluded and we were back on board. The crew had just completed loading the sodium, and the Meridian was ready to depart immediately. However, Captain Sorel issued no command. Was he hoping to wait for nightfall to exit the submarine passage in secret? Perhaps. Regardless, the following day, the Meridian departed its port and navigated away from all land a few yards under the Atlantic waves.

On that date, the Meridian traversed a unique section of the Atlantic Ocean. It is impossible for anyone to be unaware that a warm water current exists, which is called the Gulf Stream. Following our departure from the Gulf of Florida, we steered toward Spitzbergen. Yet, prior to reaching the Gulf of Mexico, near 45° N. lat., the current splits into two branches; the main one heads toward the shores of Ireland and Norway, whereas the other turns southward near the latitude of the Azores. It then brushes the African coast, follows a stretched oval path, and heads back to the Antilles. This secondary branch—more of a ring than a branch—encircles with its warm currents that area of the chilly, still, stationary ocean known as the Sargasso Sea, which acts as a true lake within the vast Atlantic. It requires at least three years for the massive current to complete a circuit around it. The Meridian was currently exploring this very territory, a flawless pasture, a dense mat of seaweed, fucus, and tropical berries, so dense and tightly packed that a ship’s bow could barely force a path through. Captain Sorel, desiring to avoid fouling his propeller in this vegetation, maintained a position several yards below the ocean surface. The term Sargasso originates from the Spanish “sargazzo,” meaning kelp. This kelp, or berry-plant, constitutes the primary material of this vast accumulation. And this explains why these plants congregate within the calm basin of the Atlantic. The sole reason that can be offered, he says, appears to me to stem from a principle familiar to everyone. If you put bits of cork or another buoyant object into a bowl and stir the water in a circular motion, the drifting pieces will gather together in the middle of the liquid’s surface, which is the area with the least turbulence. In the event we are observing, the Atlantic acts as the bowl, the Gulf Stream as the circular flow, and the Sargasso Sea as the middle spot where the floating objects collect.

My view aligns with that of Maury, and I had the opportunity to examine the occurrence from its center, a location seldom reached by ships. Suspended overhead were various materials, piled amidst those tan-colored weeds; timber fragments ripped from the Rocky Mountains or the Andes, carried along by the Mississippi or the Amazon; countless ruins, remnants of hulls, or ship bases, with side-planks crushed, and so heavily coated in barnacles and shells that they were unable to surface once more. Eventually, time will validate the additional theory of Maury, that these materials gathered over eras shall undergo petrification through the influence of the sea and subsequently create boundless coal-deposits—a valuable stockpile arranged by a provident Nature for the era when humanity has depleted the mines of the landmasses.

Surrounded by this tangled thicket of vegetation and marine flora, I observed several delightful pink halcyons and actiniae, dragging their elongated tentacles behind them, along with medusae in shades of green, red, and blue.

We spent the entire 22nd of February within the Sargasso Sea, a region where fish that favor aquatic vegetation discover plentiful sustenance. By the following day, the sea had resumed its usual appearance. For the nineteen days that followed, spanning from the 23rd of February until the 12th of March, the Meridian remained centered in the Atlantic, maintaining a steady pace of one hundred leagues every twenty-four hours. It was clear that Captain Sorel meant to carry out his underwater agenda, and I supposed he planned to head back toward the Australian waters of the Pacific once he had rounded Cape Horn. Tom Harlan had reason to be afraid. Within these vast stretches of ocean, lacking any islands, we were unable to try escaping the vessel. Furthermore, we possessed no way to resist the desires of Captain Sorel. We had no choice but to comply; yet I preferred to believe that what we could not achieve through strength or strategy might be reached through convincing him. Once this journey concluded, might he not agree to grant us our freedom, provided we swore never to disclose his presence?—a vow of honor we would have strictly observed. However, we needed to approach that sensitive matter with the Captain. Yet, was I at liberty to demand such freedom? Had he not stated quite clearly from the start that the mystery of his life required our permanent confinement aboard the Meridian? And would my four months of silence not seem to him like a quiet agreement to our circumstances? Moreover, would revisiting the topic not stir up doubts that could prove damaging to our plans, should a promising chance to act on them arise later?
