Throughout the nineteen days previously noted, our journey remained entirely uneventful. I rarely encountered the Captain, as he remained occupied. Within the library, I frequently discovered his volumes lying open, particularly those concerning natural history. My own research regarding submarine depths, which he had studied, contained numerous marginal annotations that frequently challenged my systems and theories; yet, the Captain was satisfied merely to refine my writing in this manner, as he seldom spoke to me about it. Occasionally, I listened to the mournful sounds of his organ, though this occurred only after dark, during the profound darkness, while the Meridian drifted across the empty sea. For a portion of our trip, we traveled across the surface of the water for entire days. The ocean appeared deserted. A small number of sailing ships, bound for India, were heading toward the Cape of Good Hope. On one occasion, we were pursued by the small craft of a whaler, which surely mistook us for a massive and valuable whale; however, Captain Sorel chose not to let those honest men waste their effort and time, so he concluded the pursuit by submerging. Our travel persisted until March 13th; on that date, the Meridian was engaged in measuring depths, a task that fascinated me. By then, we had traversed approximately 13,000 leagues since leaving the open Pacific. Our coordinates were 45° 37′ S. lat. and 37° 53′ W. long. These were the same waters where Captain Denham of the Herald had measured 7,000 fathoms without reaching the seabed. In that same location, Lieutenant Parker, of the American frigate Congress, had also failed to reach the bottom at 15,140 fathoms. Captain Sorel planned to reach the ocean floor by using a sufficiently extended diagonal path, achieved by setting lateral planes at an angle of 45° relative to the water-line of the Meridian. The screw was then engaged at its highest velocity, its four blades striking the water with immense power. Driven by this intense force, the frame of the Meridian trembled like a vibrating string and descended steadily beneath the surface.

At a depth of 7,000 fathoms, I observed dark peaks emerging from the center of the sea; yet these crests could have pertained to towering ranges such as the Himalayas or Mont Blanc, or perhaps even loftier ones, and the profoundness of the chasm stayed immeasurable. The Meridian continued its descent, notwithstanding the immense force. I perceived the steel plating vibrating at the bolt connections; its girders warped, its bulkheads creaked; the saloon’s portholes appeared to bow beneath the weight of the ocean. And this sturdy frame would surely have succumbed, if, as its Captain had said, it had not possessed the capacity for endurance akin to a single mass. We reached a profundity of 16,000 yards (four leagues), and the hull of the Meridian sustained a force of 1,600 atmospheres, which is to say, 3,200 lbs. for every square two-fifths of an inch of its exterior.

“What a position to find ourselves in!” I cried out. “To traverse these profound territories where no human foot has ever stepped! Observe, Captain, observe these splendid stones, these vacant caverns, these ultimate basins of the earth, where existence is no longer sustainable! What unfamiliar wonders are present! For what reason must we be denied the ability to keep a record of them?”
“Do you desire to take back something beyond just the memory?” asked Captain Sorel.
“How are you defining that statement?”
“It is my intention to state that capturing a photographic image of this underwater territory is a simple task,” I said.

Before I could voice my astonishment regarding this fresh suggestion, an objective was carried into the saloon at the summons of Captain Sorel. Across the broad aperture of the panel, the fluid substance glowed with electricity, spread so evenly that our artificial illumination lacked any trace of shadow or variation. The Meridian stayed still, the power of its propeller dampened by the tilting of its planes; the apparatus was braced against the floor of the underwater location, and within moments, we had secured an ideal negative.
However, now that the procedure had concluded, Captain Sorel remarked, “Let us go up; we must not abuse our position, nor expose the Meridian too long to such great pressure.”
“Ascend once more!” I shouted.
“Grip tightly.”

Before I could grasp the reason for the Captain’s warning, the force of the movement cast me onto the rug. Upon the Captain’s command, the screw was stowed and its vanes positioned upright; the Meridian vaulted skyward akin to a balloon, ascending with breathtaking speed while slicing through the body of water with a resonant churning. I could see nothing; within four minutes, the vessel had traversed the four leagues between it and the sea, and, having breached the surface like a flying-fish, it plummeted, causing the swells to splash to a vast altitude.

Throughout the nights of March 13th and 14th, the Meridian maintained its southward heading. I imagined that upon reaching the latitude of Cape Horn, he would steer toward the west to navigate the Pacific waters and finish the circumnavigation. Instead, he persisted in his journey toward the Antarctic. What was his destination? The pole? It was insane! I started to believe that the Captain’s recklessness validated the apprehensions of Tom Harlan. For a while, the Canadian had ceased discussing his escape plans with me; he had grown withdrawn, nearly mute. It was evident that this prolonged confinement was burdening him, and I sensed a fury smoldering inside him. Whenever he encountered the Captain, his gaze ignited with stifled wrath; I worried that his inherent aggression might drive him to a desperate act. On that day, March 14th, he and Baptiste arrived at my cabin. I asked why they had come.
“I have a straightforward inquiry for you, sir,” the Canadian answered.
“Talk, Tom.”
“Do you suppose there are many men aboard the Meridian?” I asked.
“My friend, I am unable to say.”
“It is my opinion that operating it does not call for a numerous staff,” I said.
“Ten men, at the most, should be sufficient, given the current circumstances,” I said.
“So, what reason is there for additional ones?”

“For what reason?” I asked, my gaze locked on Tom Harlan, whose intentions were transparent. “The reason is,” I continued, “that if my deductions are accurate, and if I have properly grasped the nature of the Captain’s life, the Meridian is more than a mere ship: it serves as a sanctuary for individuals who, much like its leader, have severed all worldly connections.”
“It might be,” Baptiste remarked; “yet, regardless, the Meridian is limited to a specific capacity of crew. Would you be able, sir, to calculate the highest amount they could hold?”
“In what manner, Baptiste?”

“Through my computations; considering the dimensions of the craft, which are known to you, sir, and therefore the volume of atmosphere held within, while also accounting for the amount consumed by each individual per respiration, and weighing these figures against the reality that the Meridian must ascend to the surface once every twenty-four hours.”
Before Baptiste could conclude his statement, I grasped the point he was making.
“I grasp your meaning,” I replied; “nonetheless, while that arithmetic is straightforward, it can only yield a highly imprecise outcome.”
“Forget it,” Tom Harlan stated pressingly.

“This is the situation,” I stated. “Every individual uses up the oxygen within twenty gallons of air during a single hour; consequently, in twenty-four hours, they use the amount found in 480 gallons. It is necessary, then, for us to calculate the number of times 480 gallons of air fits into the Meridian.”
“Exactly,” remarked Baptiste.

“Alternatively,” I went on, “given that the Meridian measures 1,500 tons, and since each ton accommodates 200 gallons, there are 300,000 gallons of air inside, which, when partitioned by 480, results in a figure of 625. This implies, to be precise, that the atmosphere within the Meridian would be adequate for 625 individuals for a duration of twenty-four hours.”
“Six hundred and twenty-five!” Tom reiterated.
“However, keep in mind that the entirety of our group, comprising the sailors, officers, and passengers, would fail to reach even a tenth of that total.”
“There are yet an excessive amount for three men,” Baptiste muttered.
Shaking his head, the Canadian drew a hand over his brow and exited the chamber, offering no reply.

“May I offer a single remark, sir?” Baptiste asked. “Tom is suffering from a deep desire for all the things beyond his reach. He constantly dwells on his former days; he mourns for every pleasure we are denied. His mind is occupied with memories of the past. We have to be sympathetic toward him. What purpose does he serve in this place? None; he lacks your education, sir, and does not share our appreciation for the wonders of the ocean. He would gamble with his life just to visit a pub in his homeland again.”

The Canadian, used to a life of freedom and movement, surely found the boredom aboard the ship unbearable. Occasions that might stir him to display any energy were infrequent; yet, that day, something occurred that brought back the vivid times of the harpooner. Near eleven o'clock in the morning, while the Meridian was on the ocean's surface, it met a pod of whales—a meeting that did not surprise me, as I was aware that these animals, pursued until they were killed, had sought safety in northern regions.

Upon the platform we sat, while the ocean remained calm. During October, those regions provided us with several beautiful days of autumn. The Canadian—there was no possibility of error—pointed toward a whale visible on the eastern skyline. By observing closely, it was possible to discern its dark spine surfacing and submerging amidst the swells at a distance of five miles from the Meridian.

“Ah!” exclaimed Tom Harlan, “if I were serving on a whaling vessel, this encounter would bring me joy. It is a massive specimen. Observe the power with which its blow-holes eject jets of vapor and air! Blast it, for what reason am I confined to these metal decks?”
“Tell me, Tom,” I remarked, “you haven’t abandoned your former notions regarding fishing, have you?”
“Is it possible for a whale-fisher to lose memory of his former profession, sir? Can the sensations stirred by such a pursuit ever grow wearisome to him?”
“Tom, have you never cast a line in these waters?”
“Under no circumstances, sir; solely in the northern regions, and equally within Behring as in Davis Straits,” I replied.

“In that case, the southern whale remains a mystery to you. You have only pursued the Greenland whale until now, and that species would never venture into the heated equatorial currents. By nature, whales remain within specific oceans that they do not abandon. Should one of these animals travel from Behring to Davis Straits, it could only occur because a route exists between those two seas, whether along the American or the Asiatic coast.”
“In that event, since I have not once cast a line in these waters, I am unfamiliar with the species of whale that inhabits them!” said I.
“Tom, I have informed you.”
“A more significant motive for becoming familiar with them,” remarked Baptiste.
“Observe! observe!” the Canadian cried, “they are drawing near: they irritate me; they are aware that I am unable to reach them!”
Tom struck his feet against the ground. His fingers shook while he gripped a phantom harpoon.
“Do these cetaceans reach the same size as the ones found in northern waters?” he inquired.
“Almost, Tom.”

“For I have witnessed massive whales, sir, whales that reach a hundred feet in length. I have even heard reports that the ones found at Hullamoch and Umgallick, in the Aleutian Islands, occasionally grow to be a hundred and fifty feet long,” said I.
“That strikes me as an overstatement. These beings are merely balaeaopterons, equipped with dorsal fins; and, similar to the cachalots, they are typically far tinier than the Greenland whale.”
“Ah!” cried the Canadian, his gaze fixed steadily upon the sea, “they are approaching; they occupy the identical waters as the Meridian.”
Afterwards, he resumed the discussion and said:

“You described the cachalot as a diminutive beast. I have been told of massive specimens. They are sentient cetacea. Rumor holds that certain ones cloak their bodies in kelp and fucus, leading them to be mistaken for landmasses. Travelers pitch tents on their backs, establish homes, and kindle fires——” said I.
“And construct dwellings,” said Baptiste.
“Indeed, comedian,” Tom Harlan remarked. “And eventually the beast will dive, dragging everyone aboard down to the ocean floor.”
“It is akin to the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor,” I answered, with a laugh.
“Ah!” Tom Harlan cried out abruptly, “it is not a single whale; there are ten—there are twenty—it is an entire pod! And I am helpless to act! my hands and feet are bound!”
“However, friend Tom,” Baptiste remarked, “for what reason do you refrain from requesting Captain Sorel’s authorization to pursue them?”
Baptiste had yet to complete his statement before Tom Harlan descended via the hatch in search of the Captain. Shortly thereafter, the pair emerged onto the platform in unison.
The Meridian was about a mile away when Captain Sorel observed the pod of cetacea frolicking in the waves.
“Those are whales from the south,” he remarked; “there vanishes the wealth of an entire whaling fleet.”
“Is it possible, sir,” the Canadian inquired, “for me to pursue them, if just to recall my former profession as a harpooner?”
“And to what purpose?” replied Captain Sorel; “merely to annihilate! The whale-oil aboard is of no concern to us.”
“However, sir,” the Canadian persisted, “you permitted us to pursue the dugong while in the Red Sea.”

“Next, I had to obtain new provisions for my ship’s company. In this instance, it would be slaughter purely for the sake of slaughter. I am aware that such a right is claimed by humanity, yet I do not condone this homicidal hobby. By exterminating the southern whale (a harmless beast, much like the Greenland whale), you merchants are committing a blameworthy deed, Master Harlan. You have already emptied Baffin’s Bay and are currently wiping out a species of beneficial creatures. Let these pitiable cetacea be. They possess an abundance of natural predators—cachalots, swordfish, and sawfish—without the need for your interference.”

The Captain had spoken truly. Someday, the cruel and thoughtless avarice of these anglers shall result in the extinction of the final whale within the sea. With a whistle of “Yankee-doodle” escaping his teeth, Tom Harlan shoved his hands deep into his pockets and pivoted away from our group. Captain Sorel, however, kept his gaze fixed upon the pod of cetacea and spoke to me, saying:

“I was correct to claim that whales possessed sufficient natural adversaries, even excluding humanity. These creatures shall soon be quite busy. Do you observe, M. Delorme, those shifting dark specks approximately eight miles downwind?”
“I agree, Captain,” I answered.

“Those are cachalots—dreadful beasts, which I have encountered in groups numbering two or three hundred. Regarding them, they are vicious, troublesome animals; it would be proper to wipe them out,” said I.
At those final remarks, the Canadian pivoted with speed.
“It remains the right moment, for the sake of the whales,” he remarked to the Captain.
“Exposing yourself is pointless, Professor. The Meridian shall scatter them. I expect it carries a steel spur equal to the harpoon of Master Harlan,” I said.
The Canadian did not exert himself sufficiently to lift his shoulders. To strike cetaceans with the impact of a spur! Who had encountered such an idea before?

“Hold on, M. Delorme,” Captain Sorel remarked. “We are going to reveal a sight you have not witnessed previously. We possess zero mercy for these savage beasts. They consist entirely of teeth and maw.”

Jaws and fangs! No individual might provide a superior characterization of the macrocephalous cachalot, which occasionally exceeds seventy-five feet in length. Its massive cranium comprises one-third of its total frame. Better equipped than the whale, whose top jaw possesses solely whalebone, it is equipped with twenty-five substantial tusks, roughly eight inches in length, cylindrical and tapering to a point, each with a weight of two pounds. Within the upper region of this vast head, inside expansive chambers partitioned by cartilages, one discovers between six and eight hundred pounds of that valuable substance known as spermaceti. The cachalot is an unpleasant beast, resembling a tadpole more than a fish, per the account of Fredol. It is misshapen, the entirety of its left side being (if one might express it), a “failure,” and possessing the capacity to see solely with its right eye. Nevertheless, the dangerous group was approaching our position. They had spotted the whales and were getting ready to assault them. One could anticipate in advance that the cachalots would emerge triumphant, not merely because they were superiorly structured for combat than their harmless opponents, but also because they possessed the ability to stay submerged for longer durations without surfacing. There was barely sufficient time to proceed to the aid of the whales. The Meridian submerged. Baptiste, Tom Harlan, and I assumed our positions before the saloon window, and Captain Sorel accompanied the pilot into his enclosure to operate his device as an instrument of annihilation. Before long I perceived the vibrations of the propeller accelerate, and our velocity grew. The conflict between the cachalots and the whales had already commenced by the time the Meridian reached the scene. They did not initially display any alarm at the appearance of this novel monster entering the fray. Yet they soon were forced to defend against its strikes. What a fight! The Meridian was merely a powerful harpoon, wielded by the hand of its Captain. It threw itself against the corporeal bulk, traversing from one side to the other, leaving in its wake two shuddering halves of the creature. It remained unaffected by the powerful impacts of their tails upon its flanks, nor the collision which it generated itself, to a much greater degree. One cachalot dispatched, it charged the next, maneuvering on the spot so as not to fail to strike its target, advancing and retreating, responding to its rudder, submerging when the cetacean descended into the profound depths, ascending with it when it returned to the top, hitting it head-on or laterally, slicing or rending in every orientation and at any velocity, impaling it with its fearsome spike. What slaughter! What a clamor upon the crests of the swells! What piercing whistling, and what snorting unique to these furious beasts! In the center of these waters, usually so tranquil, their tails generated absolute surges. For sixty minutes this total destruction persisted, from which the cachalots could not flee. On several occasions ten or twelve gathered together attempted to overwhelm the Meridian with their mass. From the glass we observed their vast maws, lined with tusks, and their menacing eyes. Tom Harlan could not restrain his emotions; he menaced and cursed at them. We could sense them adhering to our craft like hounds harassing a wild boar in a thicket. Yet the Meridian, engaging its screw, transported them here and there, or to the higher strata of the sea, indifferent to their immense bulk, nor the intense pressure upon the ship. Eventually the cluster of cachalots dispersed, the swells grew still, and I perceived that we were ascending to the top. The hatchway parted, and we rushed onto the deck. The ocean was strewn with mangled remains. A powerful detonation could not have fractured and shredded this fleshy mass with greater force. We were drifting amongst colossal carcasses, azure on the dorsal side and pale underneath, marked with massive swellings. Several panicked cachalots were fleeing toward the skyline. The waters were stained crimson for several leagues, and the Meridian drifted in a pool of gore: Captain Sorel came to us.
“So, Master Harlan?” he asked.
“Indeed, sir,” the Canadian answered, his initial excitement having dampened somewhat; “it is a ghastly sight, to be sure. However, I am no slaughterer. I am a hunter, and I label this a slaughter.”
“This is a slaughter of playful beings,” the Captain answered; “and the Meridian is no meat cleaver.”
“I prefer my harpoon,” the Canadian remarked.
“To each his own,” the Captain replied, his gaze locked upon Tom Harlan.

I worried he might perform a violent deed, resulting in tragic outcomes. However, his fury shifted upon viewing a whale that the Meridian had recently reached. The animal had failed to fully evade the cachalot’s fangs. I identified the southern whale by its level, completely black head. In terms of anatomy, it differs from the North Cape whale and the white whale due to its seven cervical vertebrae, and it possesses a pair of ribs beyond those of its relatives. The ill-fated marine mammal rested on its flank, pierced by bite marks and entirely lifeless. Clinging to its mangled fin was a calf it had been unable to protect from the slaughter. Water surged in and out of its agape maw, creating a sound like surf crashing against the coast. Captain Sorel navigated near the animal’s remains. A pair of his crew climbed onto its flank, and I observed, with some astonishment, that they were extracting all the milk held within its breasts, amounting to roughly two or three tons. The Captain presented me with a vessel of the still-warm milk. I could not hide my distaste for the liquid; yet he insisted it was superb and identical to cow’s milk. I sampled it and agreed with his assessment. It provided a beneficial supply for us, as it could be processed into salt butter or cheese to provide a pleasant change from our standard diet. From that point on, I observed with anxiety that Tom Harlan’s hostility toward Captain Sorel grew, and I determined to keep a sharp eye on the Canadian’s movements.

The Meridian maintained a steady southward path, traveling along the fiftieth meridian at a rapid pace. Was it his intention to arrive at the pole? I doubted this, as every prior endeavor to attain that location had ended in failure. Furthermore, the season was quite late, given that the 13th of March in the Antarctic corresponds to the 13th of September in the north, marking the start of the equinoctial period. On March 14th, I observed ice drifting at 55° latitude; these were simply light-colored fragments between twenty and twenty-five feet in length, creating shoals where the waves broke. The Meridian stayed atop the water. Tom Harlan, having worked in the Arctic Seas, recognized these icebergs, whereas Baptiste and I were witnessing them for the first time. A brilliant white strip extended across the sky near the southern horizon. Whalers from England refer to this as the “ice blink.” Regardless of how dense the cloud cover becomes, it remains perceptible, signaling the existence of an ice pack or field. Consequently, more substantial chunks quickly emerged, their luster shifting with the whims of the mist. Certain of these structures displayed emerald streaks, appearing as though lengthy, curving marks had been drawn using copper sulfate; others looked like massive amethysts illuminated from within. A few cast daylight across countless crystal surfaces. Others, tinted with bright limestone-like hues, looked like a complete marble city. As we drew closer to the south, these drifting isles grew both more frequent and more significant.

Every passage had vanished by 60° lat. Nevertheless, after a diligent search, Captain Sorel quickly located a slender gap, into which he steered courageously, fully aware that it would seal shut in his wake. Consequently, steered by such skillful hands, the Meridian navigated the entirety of the ice with an accuracy that thoroughly delighted Baptiste; whether icebergs or peaks, ice-fields or level expanses that appeared boundless, drift-ice or floating ice-packs, or fractured plains—termed palchs when round and streams when composed of elongated strips. The air was frigid; the thermometer, left in the open, registered 2 deg. or 3° below zero, yet we remained bundled in furs taken from the sea-bear and seal. Inside the Meridian, kept at a steady heat by its electric equipment, the most severe frost was held at bay. Furthermore, we only needed to descend a few yards under the surface to encounter a milder climate. Two months prior, we would have experienced constant sunlight in these zones; however, we had already endured three or four hours of darkness, and soon these circumpolar areas would face six months of night. On the 15th of March, we reached the latitude of New Shetland and South Orkney. The Captain informed me that “formerly numerous tribes of seals inhabited them; but that English and American whalers, in their rage for destruction, massacred both old and young; thus, where there was once life and animation, they had left silence and death.”

At roughly eight in the morning on March 16th, the Meridian crossed the Antarctic polar circle while tracking the fifty-fifth meridian. Glacial ice encompassed us, sealing off the horizon. Nevertheless, Captain Sorel navigated from one passage to the next, continuing his ascent. I am unable to convey how amazed I was by the splendor of these unfamiliar territories. The ice assumed the most remarkable shapes. In one place, the clusters resembled an Eastern metropolis, complete with countless minarets and mosques; in another, it looked like a ruined city cast down by some natural upheaval. The entire scene shifted continuously due to the sun’s slanted light, or vanished into ash-colored mist during snowstorms. Sounds of crashing and collapsing echoed everywhere as massive icebergs toppled, shifting the scenery like a diorama. Frequently, when I saw no way out, I felt certain we were trapped; yet, guided by intuition at the smallest sign, Captain Sorel would find a fresh route. He was never wrong when spotting the slender veins of blue water running through the ice-fields; I felt certain he had traveled these Antarctic waters previously. On March 16th, though, the ice-fields completely obstructed our path. It was not yet the icebergs themselves, but rather expansive plains fused by the frost. Still, this barrier did not deter Captain Sorel: he drove the ship into it with terrifying force. The Meridian pierced the fragile structure like a wedge, shattering it with alarming snaps. It acted as an ancient battering ram propelled by boundless energy. Ice was flung high into the sky, raining down upon us. Through its own momentum, our vessel carved a channel; occasionally, carried by its own speed, it would mount the ice-field, pulverizing it under its mass, or at other times it would plunge underneath, cleaving the ice with a mere pitching motion and creating wide fissures. Fierce winds battered us during this period, joined by dense fogs that prevented us from seeing from one side of the deck to the other. The gale gusted sharply from every direction, and the snow accumulated in such solid mounds that we were forced to clear it with pickaxes. The temperature remained at 5 deg. below zero; every exterior surface of the Meridian was encased in ice. A ship with rigging would have been trapped in the obstructed channels. Only a vessel lacking sails, powered by electricity and requiring no coal, could withstand such extreme latitudes. Finally, on March 18th, following numerous futile attempts, the Meridian was firmly stuck. It was no longer a matter of currents, drift ice, or ice-fields, but an endless, stationary wall composed of mountains fused into one.
“A glacier!” the Canadian remarked to me.

I understood that for Tom Harlan, just as for every navigator who had gone before us, this barrier was unavoidable. As the sun showed itself briefly at midday, Captain Sorel made a measurement as precise as he could, which placed our coordinates at 51° 30′ long. and 67° 39′ of S. lat. We had pushed one degree further into these Antarctic waters. Not a single patch of open water remained visible. Beneath the bow of the Meridian extended a sprawling flatland, cluttered with jumbled masses. Scattered about were jagged peaks and thin spires reaching 200 feet upward; beyond them, a precipitous coastline, appearing as if shaped by a blade and covered in shades of grey; massive ice sheets, catching faint sunlight, partially submerged in mist. A grim quiet dominated this bleak landscape, interrupted only by the occasional flutter of petrel and puffin wings. All was solidified—the very sounds were trapped in ice. The Meridian was forced to halt its daring journey within these frozen expanses. Despite our struggles, and despite the heavy equipment utilized to shatter the ice, the Meridian stayed stuck. Usually, when movement forward is blocked, we retain the option of retreating; yet here, going back was as unfeasible as going forward, since every channel had sealed up behind us; and during the brief period we sat still, we risked being completely trapped, which in fact occurred around two o’clock in the afternoon, with new ice hardening against the hull with incredible speed. I had to concede that Captain Sorel had been more than reckless. I was standing on the deck at that time. The Captain had been studying our predicament for a while when he said to me:
“What is your opinion of this, sir?”
“It is my belief that we have been trapped, Captain.”
The Meridian was obstructed.
“So, M. Delorme, do you truly believe the Meridian is incapable of breaking free?”
“The season is already too far advanced for you to count on the ice breaking, Captain; it will be difficult.”

“Oh! sir,” remarked Captain Sorel, with an ironical inflection, “you remain unchanged. You perceive only hindrances and impediments. I maintain that the Meridian is capable of not just freeing itself, but of advancing even further.”
“Moving deeper into the South?” I inquired, my gaze fixed upon the Captain.
“Indeed, sir; the pole is where it will be sent.”
“To the pole!” I cried out, failing to hold back a sign of disbelief.

“Yes,” the Captain answered, with detachment, “toward the Antarctic pole—to that mysterious location where all the world’s meridians originate. You are aware of my ability to manipulate the Meridian as I wish!”

I was aware of that. I understood that this man possessed a boldness bordering on recklessness. Yet, to overcome the barriers surrounding the South Pole, making it even more unreachable than the North, a location that the most daring explorers had failed to attain—was this not an insane undertaking, a project only a lunatic could imagine? It occurred to me then to inquire of Captain Sorel whether he had ever found that pole which no person had ever set foot upon?

“No, sir,” he answered; “yet we shall find it in company. I will not be defeated where others have been. I have not previously steered my Meridian this deep into the southern waters; nevertheless, I say again, it is going further still.”

“I find your words quite credible, Captain,” I remarked with a touch of irony. “I believe you! We shall proceed! Nothing stands in our way! We will shatter this iceberg! We will detonate it; and, should it prove stubborn, we will grant the Meridian wings so that it might soar above it!”
“Across it, sir!” Captain Sorel remarked in a low voice; “no, not across it, but beneath it!”

“Beneath it!” I cried out, as a quick realization regarding the Captain’s plans dawned on me. I grasped the truth; the extraordinary capabilities of the Meridian would be utilized for this godlike undertaking.

“It appears we are starting to reach a mutual understanding, sir,” the Captain remarked, wearing a partial smile. “You are starting to perceive the potential—or rather, the triumph—of this endeavor. What would be unachievable for a standard ship is simple for the Meridian. Should a landmass exist in front of the pole, it must halt at that landmass; however, if the pole is instead surrounded by unobstructed water, it shall travel all the way to the pole.”

“Of course,” I replied, swayed by the Captain’s logic; “while the ocean’s top may be frozen solid, the depths remain liquid due to the divine principle that sets the greatest density of seawater one degree above the freezing mark; and, unless I am wrong, the ratio of the iceberg’s visible mass to its submerged portion is one to four.”

“Almost, sir; because for every single foot of glacier visible over the waves, there exist three submerged. Provided these frozen peaks do not exceed 300 feet in height, they reach no further than 900 feet down. And what significance do 900 feet hold for the Meridian?”
“There is nothing, sir.”
“It might also pursue the constant temperature of the ocean at deeper levels, and there withstand the thirty or forty degrees of surface chill without risk,” I said.
“Precisely, sir—precisely,” I answered, growing lively.
“The sole complication,” Captain Sorel went on, “is that of enduring multiple days lacking a fresh supply of air.”
“Is that all? The Meridian possesses immense storage tanks; we are able to replenish them, and they shall provide us with every bit of oxygen we require.”
“A clever idea, M. Delorme,” the Captain answered with a smile. “However, so that you do not charge me with recklessness, I shall present my concerns to you first.”
“Do you have any others to produce?”
“Just a single one. It is feasible, provided the ocean is present at the South Pole, that it might be concealed; and, as a result, we will be incapable of reaching the top.”
“Excellent, sir! but have you overlooked the fact that the Meridian possesses a formidable spur, and might we not direct it at an angle toward these ice floes, causing them to part under the impact.”
“Oh! sir, your mind is brimming with notions this day.”

“Furthermore, Captain,” I remarked, with fervor, “what prevents us from discovering an ice-free sea at the South Pole, just as we might at the North? The frigid poles of our planet are not aligned, whether in the southern or northern zones; and, so long as no evidence refutes it, we are entitled to imagine that either a landmass or a body of water exists, devoid of ice, at both of these locations on the earth.”

“I am of the same opinion, M. Delorme,” Captain Sorel answered. “I merely desire you to note that, having raised numerous protests against my plan, you are currently overwhelming me with reasons supporting it!”

The arrangements for this bold endeavor commenced. Meridian’s robust pumps forced air into the tanks, holding it under intense pressure. Near four o’clock, Captain Sorel declared the platform panels would be sealed. I cast a final glance at the enormous iceberg we intended to traverse. The sky was bright, the air quite clean, and the chill extreme at 12° below zero; however, because the breeze had died away, the cold felt less severe. Approximately ten individuals climbed the flanks of the Meridian, carrying picks to shatter the ice surrounding the craft, which was liberated shortly thereafter. The task was finished rapidly, as the new ice remained quite fragile. We all retreated inside. The standard tanks were flooded with the newly-freed water, and the Meridian began its descent. I had joined Baptiste in the saloon; via the unlatched port, we observed the deep layers of the Southern Ocean. The thermometer climbed, and the compass needle shifted across the face. At roughly 900 feet, just as Captain Sorel had anticipated, we drifted under the rolling underside of the ice mass. Yet the Meridian continued downward—it reached a depth of four hundred fathoms. The water temperature at the surface had been twelve degrees, and it was now merely ten; we had achieved an increase of two. There is no need to mention that the Meridian’s internal warmth was elevated by its heating system to a far greater level; every maneuver was executed with remarkable accuracy.
“We are going to go by it, if it is agreeable to you, sir,” said Baptiste.
“It is my belief that we will,” I stated, my voice carrying a note of resolute certainty.

Across these wide waters, the Meridian steered a path straight toward the pole, never deviating from the fifty-second meridian. Between 67° 30′ and 90 deg., there were twenty-two and a half degrees of latitude left to cover, which equals roughly five hundred leagues. The Meridian maintained an average velocity of twenty-six miles per hour, matching the pace of a fast locomotive. Provided this rate continued, we would arrive at the pole in forty hours.

The strangeness of our circumstances held us by the window for a portion of the night. Although the electric lantern illuminated the sea, it remained empty; no fish lingered within these confined waters, as they merely utilized the space as a route from the Antarctic Ocean to the open polar sea. We were traveling at a high velocity, a fact made evident by the vibrations of the elongated steel hull. At approximately two o’clock in the morning, I sought a few hours of rest, as did Baptiste. While traversing the waist, I did not encounter Captain Sorel, whom I assumed to be situated within the pilot’s cage. On the following morning, the 19th of March, I returned to my station in the saloon. The electric log indicated that the Meridian had reduced its velocity. The vessel was ascending toward the surface, though it was cautiously purging its reservoirs at a very gradual rate. My heart hammered against my ribs. Were we about to surface and return to the open polar atmosphere? No! A jolt signaled that the Meridian had collided with the base of the iceberg, which, based on the muffled noise, remained quite substantial. We had indeed “struck,” to employ a nautical term, though in a reverse manner, at a depth of a thousand feet. This implied three thousand feet of ice existed above us, with one thousand feet protruding above the waterline. The iceberg was therefore taller than it appeared at its edges, which was not a particularly comforting realization. Throughout the day, the Meridian made several more attempts, each time impacting the barrier that functioned like a ceiling overhead. On occasion, it encountered only 900 yards, with a mere 200 yards extending above the surface. This was double the height it had been when the Meridian first submerged. I meticulously recorded the varying depths, thereby creating a submarine profile of the formation as it unfolded beneath the waves. No shift in our status occurred that night. Ice remained between four and five hundred yards thick! It was clearly thinning, yet what a massive depth separated us from the ocean’s surface! It was eight o’clock. Following the standard routine aboard the Meridian, the air should have been refreshed four hours prior; however, I felt little distress, even though Captain Sorel had not yet drawn upon his oxygen reserves. My rest was troubled that night, as I was alternately gripped by hope and dread; I stood up multiple times. The Meridian continued its tentative navigation. Around three in the morning, I observed that the underside of the iceberg was only fifty feet deep. A mere one hundred and fifty feet now remained between us and the surface of the water. The iceberg was gradually transforming into an ice-field, the mountain becoming a plain. I kept my gaze fixed on the manometer. We continued to ascend diagonally toward the surface, which shimmered under the electric beams. The iceberg extended into elongated slopes both above and below; it grew thinner with every passing mile. Finally, at six in the morning on that unforgettable day, the 19th of March, the saloon door swung open, and Captain Sorel entered.
“The ocean is unobstructed!” was his only remark.

I hurried onto the deck. Indeed! the unobstructed ocean, containing only a handful of drifting ice fragments and shifting icebergs—an expansive reach of water; a realm filled with avian life above, and countless fish beneath those waves, which shifted in hue from deep azure to brownish green, depending on the seafloor. The temperature gauge indicated 3° C. over freezing. It felt relatively like spring, confined as we remained behind this iceberg, the elongated shape of which was faintly visible on the northern skyline.
“Have we reached the pole?” I inquired of the Captain, my heart pounding.
“I am uncertain,” he answered. “When it is noon, I shall determine our position.”
“Will the sun reveal its face through this mist?” I asked, gazing up at the gray heavens.
“It shall suffice, regardless of how slight the appearance may be,” the Captain answered.

A lone isle stood one hundred and four yards high roughly ten miles to the south. We steered toward it with caution, fearing the waters could be littered with shoals. We arrived there sixty minutes later, and after two more hours, we had circled the entire perimeter. Its circumference was four or five miles. A thin channel divided it from a vast expanse of territory—possibly a continent, as its boundaries remained hidden from our view. The presence of this terrain appeared to lend support to the hypothesis of Maury. The clever American noted that the ocean between the sixtieth parallel and the South Pole is filled with massive drifting ice, a phenomenon absent in the North Atlantic. He deduced from this that the Antarctic Circle must contain large landmasses, since icebergs require coasts to develop rather than open water. Based on these estimates, the ice belt encircling the southern pole creates a giant cap measuring at least 2,500 miles around. However, the Meridian halted about three cable-lengths from a beach topped by a magnificent formation of rocks to avoid grounding. We lowered the boat, which carried the Captain, myself, Baptiste, and two crewmen equipped with instruments. It was ten o’clock in the morning. I had not spotted Tom Harlan. The Canadian surely preferred not to acknowledge the existence of the South Pole. A few oar strokes carried us to the beach, where we landed. I restrained Baptiste just as he was about to leap onto the shore.
“To you belongs the honour of first setting foot on this land,” I remarked to Captain Sorel, “Sir.”
“Indeed, sir,” the Captain replied, “and the reason I feel no reluctance to set foot upon this South Pole is that, until now, no person has ever marked it with their presence.”

With these words, he leaped nimbly onto the beach. His pulse quickened from the intensity of his feelings. He ascended a boulder that slanted toward a small headland, where, standing silent and still with his arms folded and an expectant gaze, he appeared to claim these southern territories as his own. Once five minutes of this rapture had elapsed, he faced us.
“Whenever you choose, sir.”

I disembarked, with Baptiste behind me, while the pair of men remained in the vessel. For a considerable distance, the ground consisted of a red sandy rock, resembling pulverized brick, volcanic dross, lava flows, and pumice. Its volcanic source was unmistakable. In certain areas, thin wisps of vapor released a sulfurous odor, which demonstrated that the subterranean fires retained their full eruptive force, although, after ascending a steep slope, I observed no volcano within a range of many miles. It is known that in those Antarctic territories, James Ross discovered two active craters, the Erebus and Terror, situated on the 167th meridian at latitude 77° 32′. The plant life of this barren land appeared quite limited to me. A few lichens covered the dark stones; some tiny organisms, basic diatoms, a type of cell encased between two quartz valves; and long violet and crimson seaweed, held up by small floating bladders, which the surf deposited on the beach. These formed the sparse botanical life of this area. The coastline was covered in shellfish, small mussels, and limpets. I also spotted countless northern clios, measuring one-and-a-quarter inches in length, of which a whale might consume an entire universe in one gulp; as well as various flawless sea-butterflies, which brought life to the water near the edge of the coast.

Coral shrubs emerged upon the deep seabed, a variety that James Ross noted inhabits Antarctic waters at depths exceeding 1,000 yards. Small starfish and kingfishers dotted the ground thereafter. Yet, the atmosphere teemed with the greatest density of life. Countless birds of every sort beat their wings and soared, their calls overwhelming our ears; additional birds swarmed the stones, observing our movement without trepidation and brushing against our feet with ease. Penguins were present, possessing grace in the sea but appearing clumsy and cumbersome on land; they produced grating sounds, gathered in a vast group that remained restrained in movement while being boisterous in noise. Albatrosses glided overhead, their wingspans measuring no less than four yards and a half, rightfully known as the vultures of the ocean; there were also massive petrels and damiers, a species of small duck with black and white undersides; finally, a wide array of petrels appeared, some pale with brown-edged wings, others blue and unique to the Antarctic seas, and so laden with oil, as I told Baptiste, that the people of the Ferroe Islands needed only to insert a wick to use them as lamps.
“Just a bit further,” Baptiste remarked, “and they would make flawless lamps! Beyond that, we shouldn't anticipate that Nature had already provided them with wicks!”

Roughly five hundred yards ahead, the ground was covered in ruffs’ nests, a nesting area from which numerous birds were emerging. Captain Sorel ordered the hunting of several hundred. These creatures, roughly the dimensions of geese, emitted sounds resembling donkey brays; their plumage was slate-grey dorsally and white ventrally, featuring a yellow band encircling their necks. They made no attempt to flee, permitting themselves to be struck down with stones. Still, the mist remained, and by eleven o'clock the sun had failed to appear. I felt anxious due to its disappearance. Lacking it, I could perform no measurements. How, therefore, were we to determine if we had arrived at the pole? Upon returning to Captain Sorel, I observed him resting against a boulder, gazing quietly at the heavens. He appeared irritated and restless. Yet, what alternative existed? This bold and formidable individual could not dictate the movements of the sun as he controlled the ocean. Midday passed without the solar disc revealing itself for even a moment. We remained unable to discern its location through the veil of mist; shortly thereafter, the fog transitioned into snowfall.
“Until tomorrow,” the Captain stated calmly, and we went back to the Meridian through those weather irregularities.

Snowstorms raged until the following morning. Staying out on the platform was out of the question. Inside the saloon, where I recorded the events of this trip to the polar continent, the shrieks of albatrosses and petrels playing within the fierce gale reached my ears. The Meridian did not stay still, instead hugging the shoreline and pushing ten miles further south within the dim glow of the sun as it grazed the horizon’s rim. By the next day, March 20th, the snowfall stopped. The temperature dropped slightly, with the thermometer reading 2° below zero. As the mist lifted, I felt optimistic that we could conduct our observations that day. Since Captain Sorel had not yet emerged, the boat ferried Baptiste and me to the shore. The ground retained its volcanic character; basalt, scoriae, and lava remnants were visible everywhere, though the crater that had expelled them remained hidden from my view. Just as in the lower regions, this continent teemed with countless birds. However, they now shared their domain with vast groups of sea-mammals that observed us with gentle eyes. Various species of seals were present, some lying on the ground, others resting on ice floes, and many moving between the land and the sea. Having never encountered humans before, they did not retreat when we drew near; I estimated that there were enough supplies there to sustain hundreds of ships.
“Will you provide the titles of these beings?” asked Baptiste.
“Those are morses and seals.”

The time had reached eight o'clock in the morning. We had four hours left until the sun could be viewed to our benefit. I guided our path to a wide inlet carved into the precipitous granite coastline. At that location, I can confirm that the land and frost were hidden from view by the multitude of marine mammals swarming upon them, and I instinctively looked for the ancient Proteus, the legendary herdsman who guarded these vast herds of Neptune. Seals were the most numerous, organized into separate clusters, with the father guarding his brood, the mother nursing her young, some of whom were already robust enough to wander a short distance. When they desired to relocate, they moved in small leaps, achieved by tensing their frames and assisted quite clumsily by their rudimentary fins, which, similar to their relatives the lamantin, constitute a complete forearm. I must note that, within the water—their natural domain—the spinal column of these animals is supple; possessing sleek, dense hides and webbed appendages, they are excellent swimmers. While resting upon the ground, they assume highly elegant postures. Consequently, the ancients, noting their gentle and meaningful gazes, which rival the most exquisite look a woman might offer, their bright, sensuous eyes, their delightful poses, and the grace of their behavior, transformed them, the males into tritons and the females into mermaids. I pointed out to Baptiste the significant growth of the brain lobes in these fascinating cetaceans. Excluding humans, no mammal possesses such a volume of cerebral tissue; they are also able to acquire a level of training, are readily tamed, and I concur with other naturalists that, if trained correctly, they would prove highly useful as fishing-dogs. Most of them were slumbering upon the stones or the sand. Among these seals, strictly defined as lacking external ears (a trait distinguishing them from the otter, which has visible ears), I observed various types of seals roughly three yards in length, featuring white fur, bulldog-like faces, and equipped with teeth in each jaw, four incisors above and four below, along with two large canine teeth shaped like a fleur-de-lis. Moving among them were sea-elephants, a type of seal possessing brief, pliable trunks. The largest of this breed were twenty feet in circumference and ten and a half yards long; yet, they did not stir as we drew near.
“Are these beings not a threat?” inquired Baptiste.
“No; not unless you provoke them. Because their fury is fearsome when they are forced to protect their offspring, it is quite frequent for them to shatter the fishing-boats into fragments,” I said.
“They are entirely correct,” stated Baptiste.
“I am not claiming they aren't.”

After traveling another two miles, we encountered the headland that protects the bay against winds from the south. Past that point, we listened to intense roars similar to those made by a herd of grazing animals.
“Excellent!” Baptiste remarked; “a symphony of oxen!”
“No; a musical performance by walruses.”
“The battle is underway!”
“Either they are playing or they are fighting.”

We commenced our ascent of the dark-hued crags, encountering unexpected trips and traversing boulders rendered slick by frost. On multiple occasions, I tumbled, bruising my lower back. Baptiste, possessing greater caution or perhaps better balance, remained upright and assisted me, remarking:
“If you would be so kind as to lengthen your stride, sir, you might maintain your balance more effectively,” I said.

Upon reaching the high crest of the headland, I beheld an expansive snowy expanse teeming with morses. They were frolicking with one another, and the sounds we perceived were roars of delight, rather than fury.

I had the opportunity to study these strange creatures at my own pace as I walked by, since they remained stationary. Their hides were coarse and heavy, colored a yellowish shade that leaned toward red, and their fur was sparse and brief. A few measured four yards and a quarter in length. Being less fearful and more placid than their northern relatives, they failed to station guards about the perimeter of their gathering. Once I had inspected this colony of morses, I considered heading back. It was eleven o’clock, and I desired to witness the procedure should Captain Sorel determine the circumstances were right for taking measurements. We walked along a thin trail that traced the top of the precipitous coast. By half-past eleven, we arrived at our point of arrival. The vessel had been pulled ashore, conveying the Captain. I observed him positioned upon a basalt slab, his tools nearby, his gaze locked on the northern skyline, where the sun was tracing an elongated arc. I positioned myself next to him and remained silent. Midday came, and, just as previously, the sun remained hidden. It was a stroke of bad luck. The measurements remained incomplete. Should we fail to finish them tomorrow, we would have to abandon the prospect of obtaining any. We were, in fact, precisely at the 20th of March. The following day, the 21st, would mark the equinox; the sun would vanish beneath the horizon for a duration of six months, signaling the start of the extended polar night. From the time of the September equinox, it had risen above the northern horizon, climbing in widening coils until the 21st of December. At that time, the summer solstice for the northern territories, it had started its descent; and tomorrow was destined to cast its final light upon them. I shared my concerns and findings with Captain Sorel.

“You are correct, M. Delorme,” he remarked; “should I fail to measure the sun’s altitude tomorrow, I will be unable to do so for another half-year. Yet, since it is by fortune that I find myself in these waters on March 21st, determining my position will be simple, provided we can observe the sun at noon.”
“For what reason, Captain?”
“For at that time the sun’s sphere traced arcs of such great length that calculating its precise elevation over the skyline becomes arduous, and one might commit serious mistakes using tools.”
“Then what are you going to do?”

“My chronometer is all I require,” Captain Sorel answered. “Should the sun’s disc, once refraction is accounted for, be bisected by the northern horizon on the 21st of March, it will prove my position at the South Pole.”
“Exactly,” I replied. “However, this assertion lacks mathematical accuracy, since the equinox does not have to commence at midday.”
“It is highly probable, sir; however, the mistake shall not exceed a hundred yards, and we require no further distance. Until tomorrow, then!” said he.

Captain Sorel came back onto the vessel. Baptiste and I stayed behind to examine the coastline, watching and researching until five o’clock. Afterward, I retired to my sleeping quarters, though not before requesting, in the manner of the Indian, the blessing of the glowing sphere. On the following day, the 21st of March, at five in the morning, I climbed to the platform. Captain Sorel was already there.
“The conditions are improving slightly,” he remarked. “I feel somewhat optimistic. Once we have finished our morning meal, we shall head to the coast to select a location for our watch.”

With that matter resolved, I looked for Tom Harlan. My intention was to have him accompany me. However, the stubborn Canadian declined, and I observed his silence and irritability increasing as time passed. Ultimately, I did not regret his stubbornness given the situation. Truly, there were an excessive number of seals on the beach, and we should not place such an enticement before this thoughtless fisherman. Once we finished breakfast, we headed to the shore. During the night, the Meridian had traveled several miles further. It sat three miles from the coastline, where a jagged summit rose to a height of approximately five hundred yards. I was transported by the boat along with Captain Sorel, a pair of crew members, and the equipment, comprising a barometer, a telescope, and a chronometer. During the transit, I observed many whales of the three varieties native to these southern waters: the whale, or “right whale” of the English, lacking a dorsal fin; the “humpback,” possessing a pleated chest and expansive, pale fins that, despite their designation, do not resemble wings; and the fin-back, a yellowish-brown creature and the most energetic of all cetaceans. This robust animal can be detected from a great distance when it ejects towering jets of vapor and air, appearing like spiraling smoke. These varied mammals were playing in groups within the calm sea; and I realized that this Antarctic basin acts as a sanctuary for cetaceans pursued too aggressively by whalers. I also observed massive medusæ drifting amidst the seaweed.

We touched down at nine; the heavens were lightening, the vapors drifted southward, and the mist appeared to be lifting from the frigid water’s face. Captain Sorel headed for the summit, clearly intending to utilize it as his vantage point. The climb was arduous, traversing jagged lava and pumice under air frequently heavy with the sulfurous scent of steaming fissures. Despite being unused to terrestrial travel, the Captain scaled the precipitous inclines with a nimbleness I had never witnessed before, one that any woodsman might covet. It took us two hours to reach the peak’s crest, composed of equal parts porphyry and basalt. From that height, we gazed out at an expansive ocean that marked its clear limit against the northern sky. Below us stretched plains of blinding white. Above, a faint blue sky remained clear of haze. To the north, the sun’s orb appeared as a fiery sphere, already notched by the horizon’s edge. Hundreds of liquid columns erupted from the depths of the sea. Far off, the Meridian rested like a slumbering whale upon the waves. To our rear, in the south and east, stretched a vast territory and a jumbled mass of stone and ice, its boundaries lost to sight. Upon reaching the top, Captain Sorel meticulously recorded the barometer’s average reading, as it was necessary for his calculations. At eleven forty-five, the sun, visible only through refraction, resembled a golden plate casting its final light over this lonely land and waters never before traversed by human beings. Captain Sorel, equipped with a lenticular glass that utilized a mirror to adjust for refraction, observed the sun gradually descending beneath the horizon along an elongated diagonal. I gripped the chronometer. My pulse raced. Should the sun’s semi-disc vanish exactly as the chronometer struck twelve, we would be standing at the pole itself.
“Twelve!” I shouted.
“The South Pole!” Captain Sorel answered, his tone solemn, as he passed the lens to me, revealing the sphere divided precisely into two identical halves by the skyline.
I observed the final light illuminating the summit, while the darkness gradually climbed the mountainside. Just then, Captain Sorel, who was leaning with a hand upon my shoulder, said:

“On this 21st day of March, 1868, I, Captain Sorel, have arrived at the South Pole at the ninetieth degree; and I claim this portion of the world, which is equivalent to one-sixth of the continents currently known,” said I.
“By whose authority, Captain?”
“Inside my personal one, sir!”

With those words, Captain Sorel spread out a dark flag, which displayed a gold “N” divided into four sections upon its fabric. After that, pivoting to face the sun, the final beams of which were washing over the ocean’s edge, he cried out:
“Farewell, solar light! Vanish, you brilliant sphere! sink below this vast ocean, and allow a six-month night to cast its darkness across my fresh territories!”

On the 22nd of March, the day following, at six o’clock, we started getting ready to leave. Night was absorbing the final rays of dusk. The chill was intense, and the stars sparkled with remarkable brilliance. High above, the Southern Cross—the Antarctic equivalent of the polar bear—was shining. The temperature was 12 degrees below zero, and the wind felt especially sharp as it picked up. Ice fragments were growing more frequent in the exposed water. The ocean appeared uniform in every direction. Dark spots were scattered across the water, indicating that new ice was forming. It was clear that the southern basin, having been iced over for the six months of winter, was completely blocked. Where did the whales go during that period? Surely they traveled under the icebergs to find more navigable waters. The seals and morses, being used to harsh weather, stayed on those frozen coasts. These animals possess the natural ability to create openings in the ice fields and maintain them. They surface at these spots to breathe; once the birds have flown north to escape the freezing temperatures, these marine mammals are the only inhabitants left on the polar landmass. However, the tanks were taking on water, and the Meridian began to sink gradually. It halted at a depth of 1,000 feet; its propeller churned the water, and it moved directly northward at fifteen miles per hour. By nightfall, it was already drifting beneath the massive bulk of the iceberg. At three in the morning, a powerful jolt woke me. I rose in my bed to listen in the dark, only to be tossed into the center of the cabin. The Meridian had hit something and recoiled with great force. I felt my way along the wall and toward the stairs leading to the saloon, which was illuminated by the glowing ceiling. The contents of the room were overturned. Luckily, the windows were secured tightly and had not broken. The paintings on the starboard side were pressed flat against the wall instead of hanging straight, while those on the port side were dangling at least a foot away from the bulkhead. The Meridian was resting on its starboard side, completely still. I could hear people walking and voices in a jumble; however, Captain Sorel was nowhere to be seen. As I exited the saloon, Tom Harlan and Baptiste walked in.
“Is something wrong?” I asked immediately.
“I am here to inquire of you, sir,” answered Baptiste.
“Darn it!” the Canadian cried, “I am perfectly aware! The Meridian has hit something; and, based on her current position, I doubt she will recover as she managed previously in Torres Straits.”
“However,” I inquired, “has she managed to reach the ocean’s surface?”
“We are unaware,” said Baptiste.
“The choice is simple,” I replied. I checked the manometer. I was astonished to find that it indicated a depth exceeding 180 fathoms. “What is the significance of this?” I cried out.
“We have to consult Captain Sorel,” stated Baptiste.
“However, in what location are we to discover him?” asked Tom Harlan.
“Come with me,” I told my associates.

Exiting the saloon, we found the library deserted. Near the central stairs, adjacent to the quarters of the ship’s crew, nobody was present. I surmised that Captain Sorel was likely occupied in the pilot’s cage. Waiting appeared the wisest course. We collectively went back to the saloon. For a duration of twenty minutes we stayed in that state, attempting to detect any faint sound that could be produced upon the Meridian, until Captain Sorel walked in. He appeared oblivious to our presence; his expression, usually quite stoic, displayed indications of anxiety. He observed the compass in silence, followed by the manometer; then, approaching the planisphere, he pressed his finger against a location signifying the southern seas. I chose not to disturb him; however, after a few minutes had passed, as he faced me, I spoke, employing one of his personal phrases from the Torres Straits:
“A disturbance, Captain?”
“Not at all, sir; it was an accident on this occasion.”
“In earnest?”
“Maybe.”
“Does the peril loom right now?”
“No.”
“Has the Meridian become stranded?”
“Indeed.”
“And how has this come to pass?”

“Due to a whim of the natural world, rather than human incompetence. No error occurred during the process. Yet, we are powerless to stop the consequences of equilibrium. We possess the ability to defy the laws of mankind, but we are unable to withstand those of nature,” I said.
It was an odd time for Captain Sorel to voice such a philosophical observation. His reply provided me with almost no assistance whatsoever.
“Might I inquire, sir, as to the reason for this mishap?”

“A massive chunk of frozen water, an entire mountain, has capsized,” he answered. “Whenever warmer currents or repeated impacts erode the foundation of an iceberg, its equilibrium shifts, causing the entire mass to rotate. That is precisely what occurred; one of these masses collided with the Meridian as it collapsed, then slid beneath the vessel’s frame, lifting it with unstoppable power and depositing it upon thinner layers of ice, where it now rests tilted.”
“Is it not possible to lighten the Meridian by draining its tanks, so that it might recover its balance?”

“At this very instant, that is underway. The sound of the pump is audible. Observe the manometer’s needle; it indicates the Meridian is ascending, yet the ice mass rises alongside it; and, provided no obstruction halts this upward movement, our situation remains unchanged,” I said.

The Meridian remained in its original location to the right, and surely it would level out once the obstruction ceased. Yet, at this instant, who can say if we might not be horribly flattened between those two smooth planes? I pondered every outcome of our situation. Captain Sorel kept his gaze fixed upon the manometer. Following the iceberg’s collapse, the Meridian had ascended roughly one hundred and fifty feet, though it maintained its identical tilt from the vertical. All at once, a faint shift occurred within the hull. It was clearly leveling out somewhat. Objects suspended in the saloon were noticeably shifting back to their standard orientation. The walls were approaching a vertical state. Nobody said a word. We observed and sensed the stabilization with pounding hearts. The floorboards grew level beneath us. Ten minutes went by.
“We have finally leveled out!” I cried.
“Yes,” Captain Sorel stated, as he walked toward the saloon entrance.
“Are we drifting, though?” I inquired.
“Of course,” he answered; “provided the tanks are not drained; and, once they are, the Meridian will have to ascend to the ocean’s top.”

Our vessel occupied the open ocean, yet roughly ten yards away, flanking the Meridian, stood a brilliant barrier of ice. This wall existed both overhead and below. Above, the iceberg’s underside spanned our position like a massive roof. Below, the capsized mass had gradually shifted to settle upon the side walls, which held it fixed. The Meridian was essentially trapped within a flawless icy tunnel over twenty yards wide, containing still water. Exiting was simple by moving ahead or astern, then navigating a clear path beneath the iceberg, hundreds of yards further down. Although the radiant ceiling had dimmed, the saloon remained glowing with vivid light. This resulted from the intense reflection off the glass partition, cast forcibly back toward the lantern’s panes. I am unable to convey the impact of the voltaic beams upon those strangely shaped blocks; every ridge, corner, and facet caught a unique glow dictated by the veins within the ice—a sparkling quarry of jewels, notably sapphires, whose blue glimmers intersected with emerald greens. Scattered about were opal hues of exquisite gentleness, traversing luminous points akin to fiery diamonds, which were too bright for the gaze to endure. The lantern’s intensity appeared magnified a hundred times, resembling a light shining through the lens panels of a premier lighthouse.
“So lovely! so lovely!” exclaimed Baptiste.
“Indeed,” I remarked, “the view is magnificent. Don’t you agree, Tom?”

“Yes, damn it! Yes,” replied Tom Harlan, “it is magnificent! It infuriates me to have to concede it. Nobody has witnessed such a thing before; yet this view could prove expensive for us. And, if I am to tell the whole truth, I believe we are observing phenomena here that the Almighty never meant for humanity to behold.”
Tom had spoken the truth; the sight was excessively lovely. Abruptly, a shout issued from Baptiste, causing me to pivot.
“What is it?” I inquired.
“Close your eyes, sir! Refrain from looking, sir!” With those words, Baptiste pressed his palms against his eyes.
“However, what is wrong, my lad?”
“My eyes are overwhelmed, sightless.”

I found my gaze drawn against my will to the window, yet the brilliance that appeared to consume it was more than I could bear. I grasped the situation. The Meridian had accelerated to maximum velocity. The serene glow of the glacial barriers instantly transformed into streaks of electric light. The radiance emanating from those countless diamonds was dazzling. It took a while for our agitated eyes to settle. Finally, we lowered our hands.
“I truly never ought to have trusted it,” Baptiste remarked.

The time was five o'clock in the morning when a jolt impacted the front of the Meridian. I understood that its ram had collided with an ice mass. An incorrect movement must have occurred, as this underwater passage, blocked by fragments, was difficult to navigate. I believed that Captain Sorel would alter his heading to bypass these barriers or track the curves of the corridor. Regardless, the path ahead of us could not be fully obstructed. Yet, against my anticipation, the Meridian performed a clear backward maneuver.
“Are we moving in reverse?” asked Baptiste.
“Indeed,” I answered. “There is no way out at this terminal point of the passage.”
“What followed?”
“In that case,” I remarked, “the operation is simple. We need to return, then exit through the southern aperture. That is the entire plan.”

By talking in this manner, I hoped to seem surer of myself than I truly felt. Nevertheless, the backward movement of the Meridian was growing; and, as the screw turned in the opposite direction, it propelled us forward with rapid velocity.
“This shall prove an obstacle,” said Tom.
“Provided we eventually escape, what difference do a few extra hours make?”
“Yes,” Tom Harlan reiterated, “assuming we finally manage to escape!”

I paced from the saloon to the library for a brief duration. My associates remained quiet. Before long, I collapsed onto an ottoman and picked up a volume, my gaze scanning the pages without thought. Fifteen minutes later, Baptiste drew near and asked, “Is what you are reading very interesting, sir?”
“Quite intriguing!” I answered.
“I believe that is correct, sir. You are currently perusing your own volume.”
“My book?”

Truly, I clutched the treatise concerning the Great Submarine Depths within my grasp. It was beyond my wildest imaginings. Shutting the volume, I resumed my pacing. Tom and Baptiste stood up to depart.
“Remain here, companions,” I stated, holding them back. “We should keep together until we have cleared this block.”
“Whatever you wish, sir,” Baptiste answered.

A few hours went by. Frequently, I checked the gauges suspended upon the bulkhead. The manometer indicated that the Meridian maintained a steady depth exceeding three hundred yards; the needle of the compass remained fixed toward the south; the log recorded a velocity of twenty miles per hour, a significant pace for such a confined area. Nevertheless, Captain Sorel understood that he dared not accelerate further, and that for us, minutes held the value of centuries. At eight-twenty-five, a second jolt occurred, originating this time from the rear. My face drained of color. My associates stood right beside me. I grasped the hand of Baptiste. Our gazes conveyed our emotions more effectively than speech. Just then, the Captain walked into the saloon. I approached him.
“Is our path to the south blocked?” I inquired.
“Certainly, sir. The iceberg moved, blocking all exits.”
“Are we obstructed, then?”
“Indeed.”

Consequently, surrounding the Meridian, both high and low, stood a solid barrier of frozen water. We remained captive to the iceberg. I observed the Captain. His expression had returned to its customary calmness.

“Gentlemen,” he stated with composure, “in our current situation, there exist two methods of perishing.” (This enigmatic individual possessed the demeanor of a mathematics instructor addressing his students.) “One is to be flattened; the other is to succumb to a lack of air. I make no mention of the potential to starve, as the food stores aboard the Meridian will surely outlive us. We must, therefore, determine our odds.”
“Regarding the possibility of suffocation, Captain,” I answered, “there is no cause for alarm, as our tanks are completely supplied.”

“Exactly; however, they provide enough air for a mere two days. We have remained submerged for thirty-six hours, and the Meridian’s thick air is currently in need of replacement. Our backup will be depleted in forty-eight hours.”
“Tell me, Captain, is it possible for us to reach our destination in under forty-eight hours?”
“At the very least, we shall make an effort by breaking through the barrier enclosing us,” I said.
“Which side is it on?”
“Acoustics shall provide the answer. I intend to drive the Meridian onto the bottom embankment, and my crew shall assault the iceberg at its thinnest point,” I said.

Captain Sorel departed. Before long, the sound of hissing alerted me to the fact that water was flowing into the reservoirs. The Meridian descended gradually, settling upon the ice 350 yards down, which was the level where the lower bank remained submerged.
“Our circumstances are grave,” I remarked, “yet I depend upon your vigor and bravery, my friends.”
“I am prepared to perform whatever is necessary for the collective security,” the Canadian answered, “Sir.”
“Excellent! Tom,” I remarked, extending my hand toward the Canadian.
“I shall further state,” he went on, “that since I am just as skilled using a pickaxe as a harpoon, I am at the Captain’s disposal should he require my assistance.”
“He is not going to decline your assistance. Follow me, Tom!”

I guided him toward the chamber where the Meridian’s personnel were donning their cork-jackets. I relayed Tom’s suggestion to the Captain, who agreed to it. The Canadian donned his maritime gear, becoming prepared as quickly as his peers. Once Tom was attired, I returned to the drawing-room, where the glass windows stood ajar, and, standing beside Baptiste, I surveyed the surrounding beds holding up the Meridian. Moments later, we observed twelve of the crew stepping onto the ice bank, Tom Harlan among them, identifiable by his height. Captain Sorel accompanied them. Before they began excavating the walls, he performed soundings to ensure they labored in the correct orientation. Extended sounding lines were dropped into the lateral walls, yet they were halted by the dense wall after fifteen yards. Attacking the ceiling-like surface was futile, as the iceberg reached a height exceeding 400 yards. Captain Sorel then sounded the bottom surface. Ten yards of wall there divided us from the sea, such was the ice-field’s depth. Consequently, it was required to carve out a section matching the Meridian’s waterline. Roughly 6,000 cubic yards needed removal to excavate an opening through which we might reach the ice-field. The task commenced at once and proceeded with tireless vigor. Rather than excavating around the Meridian, which would have presented more obstacles, Captain Sorel ordered a massive trench dug eight yards from the port-quarter. Then, the men applied their screws simultaneously to various points along its perimeter. Soon, the pickaxe struck this dense substance with force, and massive chunks broke away from the bulk. Through a strange result of specific gravity, these blocks, being less dense than water, rose toward the tunnel’s vault, which grew thicker at the top as it thinned at the base. Yet that was of little consequence, provided the bottom portion grew thinner. Following two hours of strenuous labor, Tom Harlan returned worn out. He and his peers were relieved by fresh laborers, whom Baptiste and I joined. The second lieutenant of the Meridian oversaw us. The water felt remarkably cold, but I warmed up quickly while wielding the pickaxe. My motions were sufficiently unhindered, despite being performed under thirty atmospheres of pressure. Upon returning after two hours of labor to consume food and rest, I noticed a distinct contrast between the clean fluid provided by the Rouquayrol engine and the air inside the Meridian, which was already saturated with carbonic acid. The air had remained stagnant for forty-eight hours, and its life-sustaining properties were notably weakened. Nevertheless, after twelve hours had passed, we had only removed an ice block one yard deep across the designated area, totaling about 600 cubic yards! Calculating that this progress required twelve hours, the entire undertaking would necessitate five nights and four days to reach a successful end. Five nights and four days! And our reservoirs only contained enough air for two days! “Without taking into account,” said Tom, “that, even if we get out of this infernal prison, we shall also be imprisoned under the iceberg, shut out from all possible communication with the atmosphere.” Quite right! Who could then predict the minimum duration required for our rescue? Might we be asphyxiated before the Meridian could reach the ocean’s surface? Was it fated to die within this icy grave, along with all those inside? The circumstances were dire. Yet every person had confronted the peril, and each was resolved to fulfill their duty until the end.

Just as I had anticipated, a fresh block measuring a yard square drifted off overnight, causing the vast cavity to deepen even more. However, upon donning my cork-jacket and crossing the mushy expanse the next morning in temperatures of six or seven degrees below zero, I noticed the lateral walls drawing inward little by little. Those pools of water most distant from the channel, unaffected by the heat of our labor, displayed signs of freezing. Faced with this immediate and growing threat, what remained of our prospects for survival, and by what means could we prevent the hardening of this fluid environment, which threatened to shatter the Meridian’s bulkheads as if they were made of glass?

I kept the fresh peril a secret from my associates. Why should I diminish the vigor they showed during the arduous task of fleeing? However, upon returning to the vessel, I informed Captain Sorel regarding this serious development.

“I am aware of it,” he remarked, employing that steady voice capable of neutralizing the gravest fears. “It represents an additional peril; yet I perceive no method to avoid it; our sole prospect for survival lies in traveling faster than the freezing process. We are required to outpace it, that is the entire situation.”

For a number of hours today, I swung my pickaxe with great energy. This labor kept me awake. Furthermore, working meant leaving the Meridian to inhale the clean air pulled from the tanks and provided by our equipment, rather than remaining in the depleted and tainted atmosphere. By dusk, the excavation had reached a depth of one additional yard.
