Upon my return to the ship, the carbonic acid saturating the air nearly choked me—oh! if only we possessed the chemical resources to expel this harmful gas. We had an abundance of oxygen; the surrounding water held a significant amount, and by decomposing it with our high-powered batteries, we could have replenished the life-giving gas. I had considered this thoroughly; yet it was useless, as the carbonic acid generated by our own breathing had permeated every section of the craft. To neutralize it, one would need to fill containers with caustic potash and agitate them constantly. Unfortunately, we lacked this material on board, and there was no substitute. That evening, Captain Sorel needed to turn the valves of his reservoirs to admit fresh air into the cabin of the Meridian; failing this measure, we could not escape the feeling of strangulation. The following day, March 26th, I went back to my mining tasks to start the fifth yard. The lateral walls and the base of the iceberg were growing thicker by the moment. It was clear they would collide before the Meridian could break free. For a moment, I was overcome by hopelessness; my pickaxe almost slipped from my grip. What was the point of excavating if I were destined to be choked and crushed by water transforming into rock?—a torment that even the cruelty of savages would not have devised! At that moment, Captain Sorel walked by. I reached out to touch his hand and pointed toward the sides of our enclosure. The port-side wall had crept to within four yards of the Meridian’s hull. The Captain grasped my meaning and gestured for me to accompany him. We boarded the vessel. I removed my cork-jacket and followed him into the drawing-room.
“We have to try some extreme measures, M. Delorme, otherwise we will be trapped in this frozen water just like we were in concrete.”
“Indeed; however, what action must be taken?”
“Oh! if only my Meridian possessed the fortitude to endure this force without collapsing!”
“So?” I inquired, failing to grasp the Captain’s concept.

“Are you unable to grasp,” he answered, “that this freezing of water shall assist us? Can you not see that through its hardening, it would shatter this expanse of ice holding us captive, just as it cracks the toughest rocks when it turns to ice? Do you not realize that it would function as a means of salvation rather than ruin?”

“Indeed, Captain, it is possible. However, regardless of the Meridian’s inherent ability to withstand compression, it would be unable to endure such immense force and would be crushed as flat as a sheet of metal,” I said.

“I am aware of that, sir. For that reason, we cannot count on nature’s assistance, but rather on our individual efforts. We are required to halt this freezing process. The lateral walls will not merely be crushed inward; furthermore, there is less than ten feet of water remaining in front of or behind the Meridian. The ice is encroaching upon us from every direction,” said I.
“For what duration shall the oxygen within the reservoirs remain sufficient for our respiration aboard?”
The Captain gazed at me. “After to-morrow they will be empty!”

I broke into a chilly perspiration. Still, should I have been surprised by the reply? On March 22, the Meridian occupied the unobstructed polar waters. We sat at 26°. For five days, we had subsisted on the ship’s emergency supplies. Furthermore, the remaining breathable air had to be preserved for the laborers. Even at this moment, as I record these events, the memory remains so intense that a spontaneous panic grips me and my chest feels deprived of oxygen. In the interim, Captain Sorel pondered in silence, and clearly a thought had occurred to him; yet he appeared to dismiss it. Finally, these words escaped his lips:
“Scalding liquid!” he whispered.
“Is the water boiling?” I shouted.

“Indeed, sir. We find ourselves within a rather restricted area. Might the continuous introduction of scalding water through the pumps elevate the heat in this section and prevent the freezing?” asked I.
“We should attempt it,” I stated firmly.
“We should attempt this, Professor.”

At that time, the temperature outside was 7°. Captain Sorel led me toward the galleys, the location of the immense distillation apparatuses that provided potable water via evaporation. These were supplied with water, and the entirety of the electric warmth generated by the piles was channeled through the worms submerged in the fluid. Within moments, the water hit 100°. It was then routed to the pumps, as new water took its place accordingly. The intensity of the heat produced by the troughs meant that seawater, pulled in and passed through the machinery, arrived at the pump body at a boil. The injection process commenced, and three hours later, the exterior thermometer read 6° below zero. A single degree had been acquired. Two hours afterward, the thermometer indicated only 4°.
“We shall succeed,” I remarked to the Captain, once I had observed the outcome of the procedure with great apprehension.
“I believe,” he replied, “that we will avoid being flattened. There is no further risk of us suffocating.”

The water’s temperature climbed to 1° below zero throughout the night. It was impossible for the injections to elevate it any further. However, since the freezing of sea-water generates a minimum of 2°, I felt secure regarding the perils of turning into ice.

On the following day, March 27th, a half-dozen yards of ice had been removed, leaving but twelve feet left to clear. Forty-eight hours of labor still lay ahead. Inside the Meridian, the atmosphere could no longer be replenished. Furthermore, this day promised to exacerbate the situation. A crushing burden weighed upon me. By three o’clock in the afternoon, this sensation intensified to a severe level. My jaws were pulled out of place by yawns. My lungs labored as they drew in this scorching fluid, which grew increasingly thin. A mental lethargy gripped me. I felt incapacitated, nearly devoid of awareness. My courageous Baptiste, despite showing identical signs and enduring the same agony, remained by my side. He grasped my hand and offered me heart, and I caught his whisper, “Oh! if I could only not breathe, so as to leave more air for my master!”

My eyes welled up as he talked in that manner. If our circumstances were unbearable for everyone inside, how quickly and joyfully we would don our cork-jackets to take our shifts! The ice-beds rang with the sound of pickaxes. Our limbs grew sore, and the flesh was ripped from our palms. Yet, what significance did such exhaustion or those injuries hold? Essential air reached our lungs! We inhaled! we inhaled!

Throughout this period, nobody extended their self-imposed duty past the allotted duration. Once finished, every individual passed the life-sustaining equipment to their gasping peers. Captain Sorel led the way, complying initially with this harsh regimen. Upon the arrival of his moment, he surrendered his device to a colleague and went back into the tainted atmosphere inside, composed, steady, and silent.

That day, the routine tasks were completed with exceptional energy. A mere two yards of distance stayed between us and the surface. Only two yards divided our position from the free ocean. However, the air reservoirs were almost drained. The small amount left needed to be reserved for the laborers; not a single bit for the Meridian. Upon returning to the vessel, I felt nearly choked. What a night! I am unable to put it into words. The following day, my respiration was labored. Vertigo joined the ache in my skull, leaving me feeling as though I were intoxicated. My associates displayed identical signs. A few of the crew members suffered from a rattling sound in their windpipes.

During the sixth day of our confinement, Captain Sorel, determining that the pickaxes were progressing with insufficient speed, decided to shatter the layer of ice that remained between our position and the open water. The composure and vigor of this individual never wavered. He overcame his bodily suffering through the power of his will.

Following his instructions, the ship was made lighter, meaning it was lifted off its icy foundation through an adjustment of its specific gravity. Once the craft was buoyant, they pulled it into position directly over the vast chasm carved at the waterline. Afterward, he filled his water tanks, submerged, and enclosed himself within the opening.

At that moment, the entire crew boarded, and the twin communication doors were closed. Resting upon the ice bed, which measured less than a yard in depth and had been pierced in countless spots by the sounding leads, the Meridian sat still. Once the reservoir valves were turned, one hundred cubic yards of water flowed inside, bringing the total mass of the Meridian to 1,800 tons. We remained in anticipation, ears alert, our miseries eclipsed by expectation. This final opportunity held our survival in its balance. Despite the ringing in my ears, I quickly detected a low drone beneath the Meridian’s frame. With a sound akin to ripping parchment, the ice fractured, and the Meridian descended.
“We’re departing!” Baptiste whispered to me.

I was unable to reply to him. Grasping his hand, I squeezed it with a convulsive grip. Suddenly, overcome by its terrifying excess of weight, the Meridian plummeted like a lead weight beneath the waves, effectively dropping as though into a vacuum. Immediately, the full electrical power was directed to the pumps, which quickly commenced discharging water from the tanks. After a few minutes, our descent ceased. Before long, the manometer showed that we were rising. The propeller, spinning at maximum velocity, caused the iron hull to vibrate to its very fastenings and propelled us in a northerly direction. Yet, if this navigation beneath the iceberg continues for another day before we attain the open ocean, I will have perished by then.

Lying partially across a library divan, I felt myself choking. My complexion turned violet, my mouth turned azure, and my senses failed. I was blind and deaf. Every concept of time had vanished from my thoughts. My limbs refused to move. I cannot say how long I remained in this state, yet I was aware of the torment growing within me. I believed my end was near. Abruptly, I revived. A few gulps of oxygen entered my chest. Had we ascended to the ocean’s top? Had we escaped the iceberg? No! Tom and Baptiste, my courageous companions, were giving their lives to rescue me. A tiny amount of air lingered in the base of a single device. Rather than consuming it, they had reserved it for my sake, and, as they suffered from lack of air, they provided me with life, bit by bit. I attempted to reject the device; they gripped my wrists, and for a short time I inhaled without difficulty. I checked the timepiece; it was 11:00 a.m. It had to be March 28th. The Meridian traveled at a terrifying speed, forty miles per hour. It ripped through the sea. Where was Captain Sorel? Had he perished? Were his associates dead alongside him? At that instant, the manometer showed we were within twenty feet of the surface. Only a thin sheet of ice stood between us and the open air. Could we shatter it? Maybe. Regardless, the Meridian would try. I sensed it tilting, dropping the rear and lifting the front. The intake of water had shifted its balance. Then, driven by its mighty propeller, it struck the ice-sheet from below like a massive ram. It fractured the ice by reversing and then charging the field, which slowly yielded; finally, slamming into it with force, it launched onto the ice-field, which shattered under its mass. The hatch was unsealed—one could say ripped away—and fresh air flooded every section of the Meridian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: I have no recollection of how I reached the platform; it is possible the Canadian transported me. Yet I was breathing, drawing in the life-giving ocean air. My pair of associates were becoming intoxicated by the crisp molecules. The remaining miserable individuals had endured such a lengthy period of starvation that they were unable to safely consume even the most basic nourishment provided to them. We, conversely, faced no limits on our intake; we were able to pull this atmosphere deeply into our chests, and it was the wind, solely the wind, that imbued us with this sharp delight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “How wonderful this oxygen is!” remarked Baptiste. “Master should have no concerns about inhaling it. There is a sufficient supply for all.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: Tom Harlan remained silent, yet he parted his mouth to a degree that would have terrified a shark. Our vigor quickly came back, and, upon glancing about, I noticed that we stood by ourselves on the platform. The overseas sailors aboard the Meridian were satisfied with the atmosphere flowing through the inside; not one of them had emerged to breathe the air outside.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: My initial utterances were expressions of appreciation and thanks directed toward my pair of associates. Tom and Baptiste had extended my existence throughout the final moments of this protracted torment. No amount of thankfulness on my part could ever compensate for such loyalty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “I am beholden to you beyond measure, and we are linked to each other eternally,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “I intend to make use of that,” the Canadian declared.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “What are you implying?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “It is my intention to bring you along once I depart from this wretched Meridian,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “Are we heading in the correct direction after everything that has occurred?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “Indeed,” I answered, “since our path follows the sun, and in this location, the sun sits in the north.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “Undoubtedly,” Tom Harlan remarked; “yet it is still uncertain if he intends to steer the vessel toward the Pacific or the Atlantic Ocean, meaning, into busy or empty waters.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: I was unable to reply to that inquiry, and I worried that Captain Sorel might prefer to steer us toward the immense ocean that borders the shores of Asia and America simultaneously. In doing so, he would finish the circuit of the submarine world and head back to those seas where the Meridian could navigate without hindrance. We needed to resolve this significant matter before much time had passed. The Meridian traveled with great speed. The polar circle was quickly crossed, and the route was set toward Cape Horn. By seven o’clock in the evening on March 31st, we were positioned off the American headland. At that moment, our previous hardships vanished. The memory of our confinement within the ice was wiped from our thoughts. We focused solely on what was to come. Captain Sorel did not show himself again in the lounge or on the deck. The location indicated daily on the map, and noted by the lieutenant, revealed to me the precise heading of the Meridian. By that evening, it was clear, to my immense relief, that we were returning North via the Atlantic. The following day, April 1st, as the Meridian rose to the surface a few minutes prior to noon, we spotted land to the west. It was Terra del Fuego, which early explorers titled as such after observing the volume of smoke rising from the dwellings of the inhabitants. The shoreline appeared low to me, though towering mountains stood in the distance. I even believed I caught sight of Mount Sarmiento, which reaches 2,070 yards above sea level and possesses a very sharp peak, serving as an indicator of either fair or foul weather depending on whether it is obscured by mist or visible. At that instant, the summit was sharply outlined against the heavens. The Meridian, submerging once more, drew near the coast, which lay only a few miles away. Through the glass portals of the lounge, I observed lengthy seaweeds and massive fuci and varech, of which the open polar sea holds so many examples, with their pointed, smooth fibers; these reached about 300 yards in length—genuine cables, greater in thickness than a thumb; and, possessing great strength, they are frequently utilized as lines for ships. Another plant, known as velp, featuring leaves four feet in length and embedded in coral formations, trailed along the seabed. It provided a home and sustenance for countless crustaceans, mollusks, crabs, and cuttlefish. There, seals and otters enjoyed magnificent feasts, consuming fish flesh alongside sea-vegetables, in the English style. The Meridian traveled over this rich and abundant terrain with great velocity. Toward dusk, it neared the Falkland islands, whose rugged peaks I identified the next day. The ocean depth was not great. Near the coasts, our nets hauled in exquisite samples of seaweed, specifically a certain fucus whose roots were packed with the finest mussels on earth. Geese and ducks landed by the dozens upon the deck and were promptly moved to the ship’s larder.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: Once the final peaks of the Falklands vanished from view, the Meridian submerged to a depth of twenty to twenty-five yards, tracking along the American coastline. Captain Sorel remained out of sight. We stayed off the Patagonian shores until April 3rd, alternating between traveling beneath the waves and cruising at the surface. The Meridian traversed the expansive estuary of the Plata, reaching a position fifty-six miles from Uraguay on April 4th. Our course was set north, tracing the extensive curves of the South American seaboard. By that point, we had covered 1,600 miles since departing the waters of Japan. Near eleven in the morning, we traversed the Tropic of Capricorn at the thirty-seventh meridian and sailed past Cape Frio, heading into the open ocean. Much to the annoyance of Tom Harlan, Captain Sorel avoided the proximity of populated Brazilian shores, driving the vessel at a dizzying pace. Neither fish nor the fastest avian species could keep up with us, and the oceanic wonders of these regions went entirely unobserved.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: For a number of days, we maintained this pace, and on the evening of April 9th, we caught sight of Cape San Roque, the easternmost extremity of South America. Subsequently, the Meridian altered its course once more, aiming for the deepest point of an underwater canyon situated between this Cape and the African coast near Sierra Leone. This chasm splits at the latitude of the Antilles, concluding in the north with a massive 9,000-yard depression. At this location, the ocean’s geological basin creates a perpendicular cliff measuring three and a half miles in height reaching toward the Lesser Antilles, while a second, equally significant wall near the Cape Verde Islands latitude serves to contain the entirety of the submerged Atlantic continent. Scattered mountains mark the floor of this vast valley, lending a scenic quality to these depths. I base these details on the manuscript charts kept in the Meridian’s library—maps clearly drafted by Captain Sorel based on his own findings. Over the course of two days, we explored these desolate, profound waters using the inclined planes. The Meridian was equipped with extensive diagonal broadsides that allowed it to reach any depth. However, on April 11th, the vessel ascended abruptly, and land emerged at the Amazon River’s mouth, a sprawling estuary so wide that it dilutes the salinity of the ocean for several leagues.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: We passed over the equator. The Guianas, a French territory, lay twenty miles to the west, offering a potential sanctuary; however, a powerful wind persisted, and the violent swells would have prevented any small craft from braving them. Tom Harlan surely grasped this, as he remained silent on the matter. I, for my part, avoided mentioning his plans for escape, as I refused to push him toward an endeavor destined for failure. I occupied my time with engaging research. Throughout April 11th and 12th, the Meridian remained upon the ocean’s surface, and our nets yielded an extraordinary collection of fish, reptiles, and zoophytes. Certain zoophytes were retrieved via the net’s chain; these were primarily exquisite phyctallines of the actinidian family, including the phyctalis protexta, which is unique to this region of the sea, featuring a small cylindrical body decorated with vertical markings and red specks, topped by a stunning display of tentacles. The molluscs included specimens I had previously noted—turritellas, olive porphyras marked with intersecting lines and red spots that contrasted sharply with the flesh; strange pteroceras resembling fossilized scorpions; clear hyaleas, argonauts, cuttle-fish (which are delicious), and specific types of calmars that ancient scholars categorized as flying-fish and which are used mainly as cod bait. I was then able to examine various fish species found in these waters. Among the cartilaginous types were petromyzons-pricka, a species of eel measuring fifteen inches with a green head, violet fins, a blue-grey back, a brown belly that was silvered and covered in luminous spots, and eyes with pupils ringed in gold—a fascinating creature carried to the sea by the Amazon’s current, as they typically live in fresh water; tuberculated streaks featuring sharp snouts and long, trailing tails tipped with jagged stingers; small sharks measuring a yard in length with grey and white skin and multiple rows of recurved teeth, commonly referred to as pantouffles; vespertilios, which are red isosceles triangles half a yard long, possessing pectorals joined by muscular extensions that give them the appearance of bats, though their horny nasal appendages have earned them the title of sea-unicorns; and finally, various balistae, such as the curassavian with its shimmering gold spots, and the capriscus, which displays a clear violet hue and shifting colors reminiscent of a pigeon’s throat.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: I conclude this list here, which might seem a bit dull, though it is highly precise, by noting a collection of bony fish I saw as I went by, including apteronotes, which possess a snout as white as snow and a body of lovely black, distinguished by a lengthy, slack, fleshy band; odontognathes, which carry spikes; sardines measuring nine inches in length, shining with a brilliant silver glow; a type of mackerel equipped with a pair of anal fins; centronotes of a dark hue, captured using torches, which are long fish reaching two yards, possessing white, firm, fatty meat that tastes of eel when recently caught and of smoked salmon when cured; labres, partly red, which feature scales solely at the base of their dorsal and anal fins; chrysoptera, where the radiance of gold and silver mixes with the luster of ruby and topaz; golden-tailed spares, which have exceptionally tender flesh and whose ability to glow reveals them within the water; orange-hued spares possessing long tongues; maigres, which have golden caudal fins, dark thorn-tails, anableps of Surinam, and so on.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: Regardless of this “et cetera,” I am obliged to note a fish that Baptiste shall recall for a great while, and with ample cause. A single one of our nets brought up a type of extremely flat ray, which, once its tail was severed, created an ideal circle and tipped the scales at twenty ounces. Its underside was white, its top was red, featuring broad circular patches of deep blue ringed by black, with a highly lustrous hide that ended in a bilobed fin. Once placed upon the deck, it writhed, attempted to flip itself over through spasmodic motions, and exerted such force that a final rotation almost propelled it back into the ocean. However, Baptiste, unwilling to allow the creature to escape, dashed toward it, and, prior to my ability to stop him, grasped it with his two hands. Instantly he was toppled, his feet pointed skyward, and half of his frame rendered numb, shouting—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “Help me, master, master!” I cried.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: This was the initial occasion on which the destitute lad addressed me with such intimacy. The Canadian and I lifted him, massaging his tightened limbs until he regained consciousness. The hapless Baptiste had encountered a cramp-fish of the most perilous variety, the cumana. This peculiar creature, within a conductive medium such as water, delivers shocks to fish from a distance of several yards, owing to the immense strength of its electric organ, the two primary surfaces of which span no less than twenty-seven square feet. On the following day, April 12th, the Meridian drew near the Dutch coast, close to the Maroni estuary. There, various clusters of sea-cows gathered; they were manatees, which, similar to the dugong and the stellera, are members of the sirenian order. These graceful creatures, gentle and harmless, measuring eighteen to twenty-one feet long, possess a weight of at least sixteen hundredweight. I remarked to Tom Harlan and Baptiste, “provident nature had assigned an important role to these mammalia.” In truth, they, much like seals, are intended to feed upon underwater meadows, thereby clearing away the buildup of vegetation that blocks tropical rivers.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FROM CAPE HORN TO THE AMAZON
text: “And are you aware,” I continued, “of the consequence following the near-total destruction of this beneficial species by mankind? The decaying seaweed has contaminated the atmosphere, and this tainted air triggers the yellow fever that ravages these lovely regions. Vast growths proliferate beneath the tropical waters, and the affliction spreads uncontrollably from the estuary of the Rio de la Plata up to Florida. According to Toussenel, this epidemic is minor compared to the state the oceans would reach if whales and seals were removed. Once overrun by octopuses, jellyfish, and squid, the seas would turn into massive hubs of contagion, for their waters would lack ‘these vast stomachs that God had charged to infest the surface of the seas.’”

The Meridian remained at a distance from the American shoreline for a number of days. Clearly, it sought to avoid the currents found within the Gulf of Mexico and the Antilles sea. On April 16th, we observed Martinique and Guadaloupe situated approximately thirty miles away. I caught a brief glimpse of their lofty summits. The Canadian, who had intended to execute his plans within the Gulf by reaching the shore or signaling one of the many vessels traveling between the islands, felt deeply discouraged. Escaping would have been entirely feasible had Tom Harlan managed to seize the boat while the Captain was unaware. However, such an attempt was impossible while in the open ocean. The Canadian, Baptiste, and I discussed this matter at length. We had been held captive aboard the Meridian for half a year. We had covered a distance of 17,000 leagues; and, as Tom Harlan said, there was no reason why it should come to an end. We could expect no assistance from the Captain of the Meridian, relying solely upon our own efforts. Furthermore, he had grown more somber, withdrawn, and unsociable as of late. He appeared to avoid me. I encountered him infrequently. In the past, he enjoyed describing the wonders of the deep to me; now, he left me to my research and stopped visiting the saloon. What transformation had he undergone? And why? Personally, I did not want my unique and fascinating findings to be lost with me. I now possessed the ability to compose the definitive account of the ocean; and I intended for this work to be published eventually. The Bahamas archipelago was the closest landmass. Towering underwater precipices blanketed in thick vegetation emerged there. It was near eleven o’clock when Tom Harlan pointed out a sharp prickling sensation, similar to an ant bite, caused by the dense seaweeds.
“These are truly suitable grottoes for octopuses,” I remarked, “and it would not surprise me to encounter a few of those beasts.”
“What!” exclaimed Baptiste; “are these cuttlefish, actual cuttlefish belonging to the cephalopod class?”
“I refuse,” I stated, “monsters of massive proportions.”
“It is impossible for me to accept that these creatures are real,” said Tom.
“Well,” Baptiste remarked, maintaining the gravest expression imaginable, “I have a vivid recollection of witnessing a massive ship being pulled beneath the surface by the tentacle of an octopus.”
“Did you witness that?” the Canadian asked.
“Indeed, Tom.”
“By means of your very own sight?”
“By my very sight.”
“Might I ask where that is?”
“In St. Malo,” replied Baptiste.
“At the harbor?” Tom remarked, with irony.
“No; inside a house of worship,” answered Baptiste.
“Inside a house of worship!” shouted the Canadian.
“Indeed; companion Tom. Within an illustration depicting the poulp at hand.”
“Excellent!” Tom Harlan exclaimed, erupting into laughter.

“He is entirely correct,” I remarked. “I am familiar with this painting; however, the depicted subject originates from a myth, and you are aware of how much weight to give myths regarding biological science. Furthermore, whenever monsters are the topic, human fantasy tends to drift. Beyond the belief that these poulps possess the strength to pull ships underwater, a specific Olaus Magnus describes an octopus measuring a mile in length that resembles an island far more than a creature. It is also claimed that the Bishop of Nidros was constructing an altar upon a massive stone. Once the mass concluded, the stone started moving and went back into the ocean. That stone was a poulp. A different Bishop, Pontoppidan, also mentions a poulp upon which an entire cavalry regiment could perform maneuvers. Finally, the naturalists of antiquity recount monsters with mouths resembling chasms, which were of such vast size that they could not navigate the Straits of Gibraltar.”
“However, what amount of these tales is factual?” inquired Baptiste.

“Nothing, my friends; at least regarding what exceeds the boundaries of reality to reach the realm of myth or folklore. Still, the tales spun by storytellers must be rooted in some basis. It is impossible to dispute that giant varieties of octopuses and squids live, though they remain smaller than whales. Aristotle recorded the size of a squid at five cubits, which equals nine feet two inches. Our own fishermen often encounter specimens exceeding four feet in length. Certain octopus skeletons kept in the museums of Trieste and Montpelier reach two yards long. Furthermore, based on the estimates of various naturalists, a creature of this kind measuring just six feet would possess tentacles spanning twenty-seven feet. That would be enough to create a terrifying beast.”
“Are they still catching them currently?” asked Tom.

“Even if they are not caught by them, mariners occasionally spot them. A friend of mine, Captain Paul Bos of Havre, has frequently maintained that he encountered one of these massive beasts within the Indian seas. However, the most incredible occurrence, which makes it impossible to refute the reality of these enormous creatures, took place a few years back, in 1861.”
“What is the truth?” inquired Tom Harlan.

“We have arrived. Back in 1861, north-east of Teneriffe, at almost the identical latitude of our current position, the sailors aboard the despatch-boat Alector spotted a giant cuttlefish moving through the sea. Captain Bouguer steered toward the creature and engaged it using both harpoons and firearms, though with little effect, as the projectiles and iron points merely slid across its yielding hide. Following a series of unsuccessful efforts, the men attempted to secure a slip-knot about the mollusc’s torso. The loop slid down until it reached the tail fins, where it caught. They then endeavored to pull the beast onto the deck, but it was so heavy that the tension of the rope caused the tail to sever from the rest of the body, and, having lost that appendage, it sank beneath the surface.”
“Truly! is that the truth?”
“A certainty, my dear Tom. They intended to call this octopus ‘Bouguer’s cuttlefish.’”
“How long was it?” the Canadian inquired.
“Was it not approximately six yards in length?” asked Baptiste, while he stood by the window, once more scrutinizing the uneven twists of the precipice.
“Exactly,” I answered.
“Was its head,” Baptiste replied, “not adorned with eight tentacles, thrashing the waves like a cluster of vipers?”
“Exactly.”
“Was its vision, situated on the rear of its cranium, not notably evolved?”
“Indeed, Baptiste.”
“And was its maw not similar to the beak of a parrot?”
“Precisely, Baptiste.”
“All right! no disrespect to the captain,” he answered, calmly; “if this is not the cuttlefish of Bouguer, it is, at any rate, one of its siblings.”
My gaze fell upon Baptiste. Toward the window, Tom Harlan rushed.
“Such a dreadful creature!” he exclaimed.

I gazed in my turn, unable to stifle a movement of revulsion. A terrifying creature, fit for the myths of the fantastic, lay before me. It was a colossal cuttlefish, measuring eight yards in length. Moving with rapid velocity, it swam perpendicularly toward the Meridian, its vast, fixed green eyes observing us. Its eight limbs, or more accurately feet, attached to its cranium—the feature that earned these creatures the title of cephalopod—extended to double the length of its torso and writhed like the tresses of the furies. One could discern the 250 suction cups lining the interior of the appendages. The creature’s maw, a chitinous beak resembling that of a parrot, moved vertically. Its tongue, composed of a horny material and lined with multiple rows of sharp teeth, protruded trembling from this true pair of blades. What a biological anomaly, the beak of a bird upon a mollusc! Its elongated, tapering frame constituted a muscular bulk estimated at 4,000 to 5,000 lbs.; its shifting hue altered with immense speed, shifting from pale grey to brownish red based on the creature's agitation. What was provoking this mollusc? Surely the proximity of the Meridian, a force more imposing than itself, against which its suckers and mandibles were useless. Still, what extraordinary creatures these poulps are! What tenacity the Creator has bestowed upon them! What power in their motions! And they are equipped with three hearts! Fortune had placed us before this cuttlefish, and I was unwilling to squander the chance to examine this cephalopod specimen in detail. Suppressing the revulsion I felt, I reached for a pencil and commenced sketching it.
“It is possible that this is identical to what the Alector observed,” Baptiste remarked.
“No,” the Canadian answered; “because this one is intact, whereas the previous one was missing its tail.”

“That provides no justification,” I answered. “The appendages and extremities of such creatures regenerate through a process of regrowth; and it is certain that within seven years the tail of Bouguer’s cuttlefish has possessed sufficient duration to develop.”

Additional poulps emerged by the port light at this moment. I tallied seven of them. Following the Meridian in a line, they trailed behind, and the sound of their beaks grinding upon the iron hull reached me. I persisted with my task. Maintaining their positions in the sea with such exactitude, these beasts appeared fixed in place. The Meridian halted abruptly. A jolt caused every plate of the vessel to quiver.
“Did we hit something?” I inquired.
“Regardless,” the Canadian answered, “we will be at liberty, since we are drifting.”

The Meridian drifted, certainly, yet it remained stationary. Sixty seconds went by. Captain Sorel walked into the drawing-room, his lieutenant trailing behind him. It had been a while since I last laid eyes on him. He appeared listless. He ignored us completely, walking straight to the wall to observe the poulps, and murmured a remark to his lieutenant. The subordinate departed. Before long, the shutters closed. The overhead lamps flickered on. I approached the Captain.
“An odd assortment of octopuses?” I remarked.
“Certainly, Mr. Naturalist,” he answered; “and we intend to battle them, human against animal.”
My gaze rested upon him. It seemed to me that I had misheard.
“Human into animal?” I restated.

“Indeed, sir. The propeller has ceased rotation. It is my belief that the chitinous mandibles of a cuttlefish have become caught within the blades. That is the reason we are unable to advance,” I said.
“How do you intend to proceed?”
“Ascend to the top, and butcher these pests.”
“An arduous undertaking.”
“Certainly. The electric projectiles lack efficacy when striking yielding tissue, as they fail to encounter sufficient impact to detonate. Nevertheless, we will engage them using the hatchet.”
“And the harpoon, sir,” the Canadian remarked, “provided you do not decline my assistance.”
“I shall agree to it, Master Harlan.”
“We are going to trail behind you,” I stated, and, trailing after Captain Sorel, our group headed in the direction of the main stairs.

Approximately ten men stood prepared for the assault, armed with boarding-hatchets. Baptiste and I each grabbed a hatchet, while Tom Harlan snatched up a harpoon. By that time, the Meridian had ascended to the surface. A sailor stationed on the topmost rung of the ladder began removing the panel bolts. Scarcely had the screws been freed when the panel was flung upward with immense force, clearly pulled by the suckers of a giant octopus tentacle. At once, one of those limbs snaked through the aperture, followed by twenty more appearing above. Captain Sorel severed this fearsome appendage with a single strike of his axe, and it tumbled down the ladder, twisting as it fell. As we crowded together, striving to gain the platform, two additional arms whipped through the air, seized the sailor standing ahead of Captain Sorel, and hoisted him away with unstoppable strength. Captain Sorel let out a shout and dashed outside. We scrambled to follow him.
Through the aperture, one of those elongated limbs slid.

Such a spectacle! Held fast by the suckers and gripped by the tentacle, the miserable individual hung suspended, tossed about by that massive appendage. Choking and gasping, he let out a shout, “Help! help!” Hearing those French words shocked me! A compatriot was on the vessel, possibly more than one! That agonizing plea! It will haunt my memory forever. The poor soul was doomed. What force could possibly liberate him from such immense strength? Nevertheless, Captain Sorel dashed toward the poulp, severing a limb with a single strike of his axe. His lieutenant battled fiercely against additional creatures crawling along the sides of the Meridian. The sailors engaged in the fray using their axes. Baptiste, the Canadian, and I plunged our blades into the pulpy flesh; a pungent odor of musk filled the air. It was ghastly!

I briefly imagined the miserable fellow, caught in the grip of the poulp, might be wrenched free from its intense vacuum. Seven out of the eight limbs had been severed. A single arm writhed aloft, waving the captive about as if he were a quill. Yet, at the very moment Captain Sorel and his lieutenant lunged toward it, the creature released a jet of dark fluid. We were rendered sightless by it. Once the mist cleared, the cuttlefish had vanished, along with my luckless fellow countryman. A dozen or so poulps were now swarming the deck and railings of the Meridian. We tumbled headlong into the center of this viperous den, which squirmed across the platform amidst pools of ink and gore. It appeared as if those viscous appendages were sprouting like the heads of a hydra. Tom Harlan’s harpoon was driven into the unblinking eyes of the cuttle fish with every thrust. However, my courageous associate was abruptly knocked down by the arms of a beast he had failed to dodge.

Oh! how my pulse raced with terror and agitation! The terrifying maw of a cuttlefish gaped above Tom Harlan. The wretched fellow was about to be severed in half. I hurried to assist him. Yet Captain Sorel arrived ahead of me; his hatchet vanished into the space between those two massive mandibles, and, rescued by a miracle, the Canadian stood up and drove his harpoon firmly into the three-chambered heart of the octopus.
“I was entitled to this vengeance!” the Captain remarked to the Canadian.

Without offering a response, Tom inclined his head. Fifteen minutes had passed since the fighting began. Once the creatures were defeated and torn apart, they finally abandoned us, sinking beneath the surface of the water. Captain Sorel, drenched in gore and bordering on collapse, stared out at the ocean that had claimed one of his crew, while heavy tears welled up within his gaze.

None of us will ever be able to erase the memory of that horrific event on the 20th of April. My account was composed while I was gripped by intense agitation. I have since gone over the narrative; I shared it with Baptiste and the Canadian. They agreed that the facts were accurate, yet they felt the impact was lacking. To capture such imagery, one would require the quill of our greatest poet, the creator of The Toilers of the Deep.

I mentioned that Captain Sorel sobbed as he observed the swells; his sorrow was profound. It marked the second associate he had seen perish since we boarded, and such a demise! That companion, mangled, suffocated, battered by the terrifying limbs of a giant octopus, crushed by its metallic beak, would not find repose alongside his shipmates in the tranquil coral graveyard! During the fray, the hopeless scream released by the doomed soul had shattered my spirit. The unfortunate Frenchman, abandoning his customary speech, had reverted to his native language to cry out a final plea! Within the Meridian’s crew, bound to the heart and spirit of the Captain, and like him shunning all interaction with humanity, I possessed a compatriot. Was he the sole representative of France in this enigmatic group, clearly made up of people from various nations? It was one of those unanswerable riddles that constantly surfaced in my thoughts!

Captain Sorel went into his quarters, and I did not lay eyes on him for a duration. Yet, I perceived his sorrow and hesitation through the ship, for he was its spirit, and it mirrored his every mood. The Meridian failed to maintain its established path; it drifted aimlessly like a dead body at the mercy of the swells. It moved without direction. He found himself unable to depart from the location of the final conflict, from this expanse of water that had consumed one of his crew. Ten days went by in this fashion. Only on the 1st of May did the Meridian return to its northward heading, subsequent to spotting the Bahamas by the entrance of the Bahama Canal. At that time, we were tracking the flow from the greatest river into the ocean, which possesses its own shores, its own aquatic life, and its own distinct heat levels. I am referring to the Gulf Stream. It is effectively a river, moving unhindered into the heart of the Atlantic, and its liquid does not blend with the oceanic waters. It is a saline river, with a higher salt content than the sea around it. Its average depth measures 1,500 fathoms, and its average width is ten miles. In specific areas, the stream travels at a rate of two and a half miles per hour. The volume of its water is greater than that of every river on Earth combined. It was upon this oceanic river that the Meridian was then traveling.

I should mention that, throughout the night, the glowing waters of the Gulf Stream competed with the electrical intensity of our watch-light, particularly during the turbulent conditions that so often loomed over us. On May 8th, we were continuing our transit past Cape Hatteras, off the coast of North Carolina. At that location, the Gulf Stream spans seventy-five miles in width and reaches a depth of 210 yards. The Meridian continued to travel aimlessly; it appeared as though all oversight had been forsaken. I believed that, given these conditions, a departure might be achievable. In truth, the populated coastlines provided a simple sanctuary at any point. The ocean was constantly traversed by steamships traveling between New York or Boston and the Gulf of Mexico, and it was crowded both day and night by small schooners navigating the various sections of the American seaboard. We could anticipate being rescued. It was a promising chance, despite the thirty miles of distance between the Meridian and the shores of the Union. One regrettable factor hindered the Canadian’s intentions. The conditions were quite severe. We were approaching those regions where storms are common, that territory of waterspouts and cyclones actually produced by the Gulf Stream’s current. Venturing onto the ocean in a delicate vessel meant guaranteed ruin. Tom Harlan admitted this himself. He grew restless, overcome by a longing for home that only escape could remedy.

“Master,” he told me on that occasion, “this has to finish. I need to confess everything. This Sorel is departing from the land and heading toward the north. However, I announce to you that I am finished with the South Pole, and I refuse to accompany him to the North.”
“How shall we proceed, Tom, given that escaping is not feasible at this moment?”

“It is necessary that we talk to the Captain,” he stated; “you remained silent while we traveled through your home waters. Now that we have reached mine, I intend to speak. Reflecting on the fact that the Meridian shall soon pass by Nova Caledon, and that a vast bay exists near New foundland where the St. Lawrence flows—the St. Lawrence being my river, the one by Quebec, the town where I was born—considering all this makes me enraged, causing my hair to bristle. Sir, I would prefer to cast myself into the ocean! I refuse to remain in this place! I am suffocating!”

The Canadian was clearly running out of tolerance. His energetic spirit found this extended confinement unbearable. His appearance changed from day to day, and his disposition grew increasingly irritable. I understood the agony he endured, as I was gripped by my own longing for home. Almost seven months had elapsed since we last received word from the shore; the seclusion of Captain Sorel, his shifted mood—particularly following the battle with the poulps—and his silence, all caused me to perceive our circumstances through a new lens.
“Is that all, sir?” asked Tom, noting my silence.
“Tell me, Tom, would you like me to inquire about Captain Sorel’s plans for us?”
“Affirmative, sir.”
“Even though he has previously revealed them?”
“Indeed; I desire a definitive resolution. Address them on my behalf, using solely my name, should you choose.”
“However, I encounter him so infrequently. He keeps his distance from me.”
“That provides even further justification for your visit to him,” I said.

I retreated to my quarters, intending to proceed from there to the location of Captain Sorel. It was vital that I not squander this chance to encounter him. I rapped upon the entrance. Silence followed. I rapped once more, subsequently rotating the knob. The portal gave way, and I stepped inside. The Captain was present. Stooped above his desk, he remained unaware of my arrival. Determined to avoid departing until I had conversed with him, I drew near. He lifted his face abruptly, scowled, and barked, “You here! What do you want?”
“I wish to address you, Captain.”
“However, I have tasks to attend to, sir; I am occupied. You are free to seclude yourself; might I not be granted that same privilege?”
Although this welcome lacked warmth, I remained resolved to listen to and address each point.
“I must discuss a subject with you that cannot wait,” I stated with detachment, “Sir.”
“What is that, sir?” he answered, with irony. “Did you find a thing I missed, or has the ocean yielded some fresh mysteries?”

Our intentions did not align. However, prior to my response, he gestured toward an unclosed document resting upon his desk and remarked, with a graver inflection, “Here, M. Delorme, is a manuscript written in several languages. It contains the sum of my studies of the sea; and, if it please God, it shall not perish with me. This manuscript, signed with my name, complete with the history of my life, will be shut up in a little floating case. The last survivor of all of us on board the Meridian will throw this case into the sea, and it will go whither it is borne by the waves.”
The name of this individual! His own account of his life! Someday, the secret surrounding him would be uncovered.

“Captain,” I stated, “I am able to endorse the concept motivating your current actions. The findings of your research must be preserved. Yet, the methods you utilize appear rudimentary to me. Who can say where the currents might transport this container, or into whose possession it might arrive? Is there no alternative method available to you? Could you not, or perhaps one of your associates——”
“Absolutely not, sir!” he exclaimed, cutting me off with haste.
“However, my associates and I are prepared to safeguard this document; and, provided that you grant us our freedom——”
“Free?” the Captain asked, standing up.

“Indeed, sir; that is the matter I desire to inquire about. We have remained aboard for seven months, and I am asking you today, on behalf of my associates and myself, whether you mean to detain us here indefinitely?”
“M. Delorme, I shall reply to you this day just as I replied seven months prior: Anyone who steps inside the Meridian is forbidden from ever leaving it.”
“You are forcing real slavery on us!”
“Call it whatever you like.”
“However, the slave possesses the entitlement to recover his freedom in every location.”
“Is there anyone who refuses you this privilege? Did I at any point attempt to bind you with a vow?”
With his arms folded, he stared at me.

“Sir,” I remarked, “revisiting this topic will prove unpleasant for both of us; however, since we have begun, we must finish. I maintain that this involves more than just me. For me, study serves as an escape, a distraction, and a passion capable of making me lose track of all else. Much like you, I am content to exist in obscurity, clinging to the slight expectation of leaving behind, for posterity, the fruits of my work. Yet, the situation regarding Tom Harlan is different. Any individual, if he is truly a man, merits some regard. Have you considered that a desire for freedom and an abhorrence of bondage might inspire plans for vengeance in a temperament such as the Canadian’s; that he might conceive of, endeavor to carry out, and execute——”
Captain Sorel stood up, and I was rendered speechless.

“Regardless of what Tom Harlan might conceive, endeavor, or pursue, how does that concern me? I never looked for him! It is not for my own satisfaction that he remains aboard! Regarding you, M. Delorme, you belong to that group capable of grasping everything, including silence. I have no further comments for you. Ensure that this initial occasion on which you have broached this topic is the final one, as I shall not grant you a hearing a second time.”
I stepped down. The circumstances we faced were dire. I recounted the talk I had to my pair of associates.

“It is clear to us at this point,” said Tom, “that we should anticipate zero assistance from this individual. The Meridian is approaching Long Island. Regardless of the conditions, we are going to get away.”

Nevertheless, the heavens grew increasingly ominous. Signs of a hurricane became apparent. The air turned misty and white. Upon the horizon, thin lines of cirrus clouds were followed by heaps of cumulus. Other low-hanging clouds drifted by rapidly. The swollen ocean surged in massive swells. All birds vanished save for the petrels, those companions of the gale. The barometer dropped noticeably, signaling intense vapor pressure. The solution within the storm glass broke down due to the electricity filling the air. The storm broke on the 18th of May, just as the Meridian was navigating off Long Island, a few miles from the New York harbor. I can depict this elemental struggle! For, rather than diving to the ocean floor, Captain Sorel, driven by an inexplicable whim, chose to face it at the surface. Initially, the wind blew from the south-west. During the gusts, Captain Sorel took his position on the platform. He secured himself to avoid being swept into the sea by the enormous waves. I had climbed up and fastened myself as well, splitting my awe between the storm and this remarkable man who was battling it. The furious sea was lashed by massive cloud-drifts, which were thoroughly soaked with spray. The Meridian, at times listing on its side, at times standing upright like a mast, pitched and rolled violently. Near five o’clock, a downpour of rain arrived, which calmed neither the wind nor the sea. The hurricane gusted at nearly forty leagues an hour. It is under such conditions that it topples buildings, snaps iron gates, and shifts twenty-four pounders. Yet, the Meridian, amidst the gale, proved the statement of a skilled engineer, “There is no well-constructed hull that cannot defy the sea.” This was no stationary rock; it was a steel spindle, flexible and agile, lacking masts or rigging, that withstood the rage unharmed. Still, I observed these turbulent waves closely. They reached fifteen feet in height, spanned 150 to 175 yards in length, and traveled at a speed of thirty feet per second. Their volume and force grew with the water's depth. Such waves, at the Hebrides, have moved a mass weighing 8,400 lbs. They are the same ones that, during the storm of December 23rd, 1864, after ruining the city of Yeddo, in Japan, crashed that same day on the American coast. The storm’s intensity grew as night fell. The barometer, as it did in 1860 at Reunion during a cyclone, dropped seven-tenths by day’s end. I watched a large ship cross the horizon, laboring heavily. She was attempting to heave to under half steam, to stay atop the swells. It was likely one of the steamers on the route from New York to Liverpool, or Havre. It soon vanished into the darkness. At ten o’clock at night, the sky glowed. The air was slashed with brilliant lightning. I could not endure the glare; meanwhile, the captain, gazing at it, appeared to covet the spirit of the storm. A fearsome sound filled the air, a multifaceted noise, composed of the shrieks of shattered waves, the howling of the gale, and the thunder’s peals. The wind shifted abruptly to every direction of the horizon; and the cyclone, originating in the east, circled back after moving through the north, west, and south, in the reverse path taken by the circular storms of the southern hemisphere. Ah, that Gulf Stream! It earns its title as the King of Tempests. It is what triggers these formidable cyclones, due to the temperature variance between its currents and its air. A rain of fire had followed the downpour. The water droplets were transformed into piercing needles. One might have believed that Captain Sorel was seeking a death fitting for him, a death by lightning. As the Meridian, pitching horribly, lifted its steel spur toward the sky, it appeared to serve as a conductor, and I witnessed long sparks erupting from it. Exhausted and powerless, I dragged myself to the hatch, pulled it open, and went down into the saloon. The tempest was then at its peak. It was impossible to remain upright inside the Meridian. Captain Sorel descended around twelve. I listened as the reservoirs gradually filled, and the Meridian submerged slowly beneath the waves. Through the saloon’s open windows, I watched large fish, panicked, gliding like ghosts in the water. Some were hit before my eyes. The Meridian continued its descent. I imagined that at roughly eight fathoms deep we would encounter stillness. But no! The upper layers were too fiercely disturbed for that. We needed to find rest at more than twenty-five fathoms deep in the ocean's depths. But there, what serenity, what stillness, what peace! Who could have guessed that such a hurricane had been unleashed on the surface of that sea?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: Due to the tempest, we had been cast toward the east again. Every prospect of reaching the coasts of New York or St. Lawrence had vanished; and unfortunate Tom, overcome by hopelessness, had withdrawn into solitude just as Captain Sorel had done. Baptiste and I, meanwhile, remained inseparable. I remarked that the Meridian had deviated toward the east. To be more precise, I ought to have stated the north-east. For a period of days, it drifted initially upon the water, and subsequently below it, through those mists so feared by mariners. How many mishaps occur because of these dense fogs! How many impacts against these crags take place when the gale muffles the sound of crashing surf! How many crashes between ships happen, notwithstanding their signal lamps, sirens, and warning gongs! And the ocean floors resemble a war zone, where the defeated of the sea remain; some ancient and already coated in growth, others recent and casting back the glow of our lamp from their metallic straps and brass plating.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: On May 15th, our position was at the southernmost edge of the Bank of Newfoundland. This bank is composed of alluvial deposits, or massive accumulations of organic debris, transported either from the Equator via the Gulf Stream or from the North Pole by the cold counter-current that runs along the American shoreline. Furthermore, erratic boulders transported by fractured ice collect there; nearby lies a sprawling graveyard of molluscs, dying there in the millions. The ocean depth near Newfoundland is shallow—merely a few hundred fathoms—yet a 1,500-fathom basin exists to the south. At that point, the Gulf Stream expands. While it sheds a portion of its velocity and heat, it transforms into a sea.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: On the 17th of May, at a distance of approximately 500 miles from Heart’s Content and at a depth exceeding 1,400 fathoms, I observed the electric cable resting upon the seabed. Baptiste, who had received no prior word from me regarding it, initially mistook the object for a massive sea-serpent. I corrected the good man’s error, and to comfort him, I shared various details concerning the installation of this cable. The initial line was placed during 1857 and 1858; however, it ceased to function after conveying roughly 400 telegrams. In 1863, engineers built a second version, 2,000 miles long and 4,500 tons in weight, which was loaded onto the Great Eastern. This endeavor proved unsuccessful as well.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: On May 25th, the Meridian sat at a depth exceeding 1,918 fathoms, positioned exactly where the break that destroyed the project took place. Located 638 miles from the Irish shore, the crew realized at 2:30 p.m. that the link to Europe was broken. The electricians aboard decided to sever the cable prior to hauling it up, and by 11:00 p.m., the broken section was retrieved. They reached a different location, performed a splice, and lowered the line back into the water. However, it snapped again several days later and could not be retrieved from the ocean floor. The Americans remained undeterred. Cyrus Field, the project’s courageous backer, having invested his entire wealth, launched a fresh subscription that was immediately met with support, leading to the creation of a new cable built with superior methods. Each bundle of conducting wires was wrapped in gutta-percha, shielded by hemp padding, and housed inside a metal casing. The Great Eastern departed on July 13th, 1866. The process proceeded successfully. One event did occur, however. On multiple occasions during the cable’s deployment, it was noticed that nails had been driven into it, clearly with the intent to sabotage the work. Captain Mercer, along with the officers and engineers, held a meeting and issued a notice stating that any culprit caught on the ship would be cast into the sea without a trial. Following this, the malicious acts ceased.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: By the 23rd of July, the Great Eastern had traveled to within 500 miles of Newfoundland, at which point a telegram arrived from Ireland reporting the armistice signed by Prussia and Austria following Sadowa. Dense fogs surrounded the vessel on the 27th as it arrived at the harbor of Heart’s Content. The mission had reached a successful conclusion; for its inaugural message, young America sent these wise words to old Europe, which are so infrequently grasped: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill towards men.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: I had not anticipated discovering the electric cable in its original condition, just as it appeared when it departed the factory. That lengthy serpent, draped in shell fragments and covered in foraminiferae, was encased in a robust layer that acted as a shield against any boring molluscs. It rested peacefully, shielded from oceanic agitation and situated under a pressure conducive to the transit of the electric spark that travels between Europe and America in .32 of a second. Surely this cable shall endure for a significant duration, as it is observed that the gutta-percha sheath is enhanced by immersion in sea-water. Furthermore, at this well-selected depth, the cable is never submerged deeply enough to risk fracture. The Meridian tracked it to its maximum depth, exceeding 2,212 fathoms, where it rested unanchored; we then arrived at the location where the 1863 accident occurred. The seafloor at that point created a valley roughly 100 miles wide, within which Mont Blanc could be set without its peak breaking the surface. This valley is bounded to the east by a vertical cliff rising over 2,000 yards. We reached that point on the 28th of May, at which time the Meridian was situated no further than 120 miles from Ireland.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: Would Captain Sorel be touching down upon the British Isles? Certainly not. Much to my astonishment, he steered toward the south, returning yet again in the direction of European waters. As we circled the Emerald Isle, I briefly glimpsed Cape Clear, along with the beacon that directs the myriad ships departing from Liverpool or Glasgow. A significant inquiry then occurred to me. Was the Meridian bold enough to navigate the Manche? Tom Harlan, having surfaced again as we approached the land, kept asking me questions. What response could I possibly provide? Captain Sorel stayed out of sight. Having offered the Canadian a view of the American coastline, was he now intending to reveal the shores of France to me?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: However, the Meridian continued its journey toward the south. On May 30th, it sailed within view of Land’s End, positioned between the furthest tip of England and the Scilly Isles, which remained to the starboard side. Had we intended to reach the Manche, a direct eastward course was required. That was not the path taken.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: Throughout the entirety of May 31st, the Meridian traced various loops upon the sea, a maneuver that held my full attention. It appeared to be hunting for a location that proved difficult to locate. At midday, Captain Sorel arrived personally to update the ship’s log. He remained silent toward me, though he appeared more melancholy than I had previously observed. What reason could exist for such sorrow? Was it the nearness of the coasts of Europe? Did he harbor memories of the nation he had left behind? If that were not the cause, what was the nature of his emotions? Was it guilt or sorrow? This notion remained fixed in my thoughts for an extended period, and I possessed a vague intuition that fate would soon reveal the captain’s hidden matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: On the 1st of June, the following day, the Meridian persisted in its previous routine. It was clearly searching for a specific location within the sea. As he had performed the day prior, Captain Sorel measured the sun’s altitude. The sky was cloudless, and the ocean was lovely. A sizable steamship was visible on the horizon, positioned roughly eight miles to the east. I was unable to identify its country of origin, as no banner flew from its mast. Shortly before the sun reached the meridian, Captain Sorel observed with intense focus while holding his sextant. The task was significantly aided by the water’s absolute stillness. The Meridian remained stationary, experiencing neither pitching nor rolling.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: Standing upon the deck during the measurement of the elevation, I heard the Captain declare: “It is here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: He pivoted and descended. Did he notice the ship that was altering its path and appeared to be drawing closer to us? I remained uncertain. I went back to the saloon. Once the panels were shut, the sound of water rushing into the reservoirs reached my ears. The Meridian commenced its descent, dropping straight down, as its propeller provided no propulsion. A few minutes passed before it halted at a depth exceeding 420 fathoms, settling upon the seabed. The glowing ceiling dimmed, the panels slid open, and I peered through the glass to behold the ocean brightly lit by the beams of our lantern for a radius of at least half a mile.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: My gaze shifted toward the port side, where I perceived only a vast expanse of still sea. However, to starboard, a significant bulge emerged from the depths, immediately drawing my focus. It might have been mistaken for some wreckage entombed beneath a layer of white shells, which bore a striking resemblance to a shroud of snow. As I studied the object with care, I managed to identify the increasingly distinct outline of a ship stripped of its masts, which had clearly foundered. It was undoubtedly a relic of a bygone era. Given that this hull was so heavily coated in marine lime, it must have already spent a great many years resting on the seabed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: What sort of craft was this? For what reason had the Meridian journeyed to this grave? Was it possible that only a sunken wreck had pulled it beneath the waves? I remained uncertain of my own thoughts, until I heard Captain Sorel speak near me in a measured tone:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: “This vessel was once known as the Marseillais. It was a seventy-four gun ship, launched during 1762. On August 13th, 1778, under the leadership of La Poype-Vertrieux, it engaged the Preston with great courage. The 4th of July, 1779, saw it present at the capture of Grenada alongside the fleet of Admiral Estaing. On September 5th, 1781, it participated in the engagement of Comte de Grasse within Chesapeake Bay. The French Republic altered its title in 1794. That same year, on April 16th, it became part of the fleet of Villaret Joyeuse at Brest, tasked with protecting a shipment of corn arriving from America, led by Admiral Van Stebel. During the 11th and 12th Prairal of the second year, this fleet encountered an English ship. Sir, today is the 13th Prairal, the first of June, 1868. Exactly seventy-four years have passed, at this precise location, in latitude 47° 24′, longitude 17° 28′, since this ship, following a heroic battle, having lost its three masts, with water filling its hold, and one-third of its men incapacitated, chose to sink with its 356 sailors rather than strike its colours; and, having fastened its flag to the poop, it vanished beneath the sea to the shout of ‘Long live the Republic!’”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: “The Avenger!” I cried out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX FROM LATITUDE 47° 24′ TO LONGITUDE 17° 28′
text: “Indeed, sir, the Avenger! An excellent title!” Captain Sorel murmured, folding his arms across his chest.

The manner in which this unexpected spectacle was depicted, the chronicle of the patriot vessel, initially recounted with such detachment, and the intensity with which this peculiar individual uttered the final syllables—the name of the Avenger, the import of which was impossible for me to miss—all left a profound mark upon my consciousness. I kept my gaze fixed upon the Captain, who, arm extended toward the ocean, observed the magnificent ruin with a burning stare. It is possible I would never discover his identity, his origins, or his destination, yet I perceived the man in motion, distinct from the scholar. It was not mere misanthropy that had confined Captain Sorel and his associates aboard the Meridian, but a loathing, whether grotesque or noble, that the passage of years could not diminish. Was this animosity still pursuing retribution? The days to come would shortly reveal the answer. However, the Meridian was ascending gradually toward the surface, and the silhouette of the Avenger faded incrementally from my view. Before long, a gentle swaying signaled that we had reached the open atmosphere. At that instant, a muffled report echoed. I turned to the Captain. He remained motionless.
“Captain?” I asked.
He remained silent. Moving away from him, I stepped onto the platform, where Baptiste and the Canadian had already arrived.
“From what direction did that noise originate?” I asked.
“A firearm was discharged,” Tom Harlan answered.
I gazed toward the craft I had previously spotted. As it approached the Meridian, it became evident that it was increasing its steam power. The distance between us had closed to within six miles.
“Tell me, Tom, what vessel is that?”

“Judging by the rigging and the elevation of the lower masts,” the Canadian remarked, “I would wager that vessel is a ship-of-war. Let it approach us; and, should the situation demand it, let it send this wretched Meridian to the bottom.”
“Friend Tom,” answered Baptiste, “what damage might it cause the Meridian? Is it capable of striking it under the water? Might its artillery fire upon us while we rest on the ocean floor?”
“I ask you, Tom,” said I, “are you able to identify the nation of her origin?”
The Canadian furrowed his brow, lowered his lids, and crinkled the edges of his eyes, while for an instant he leveled a sharp gaze at the ship.
“No, sir,” he answered; “I am unable to identify her nationality, as she displays no flags. However, I can confirm that she is a warship, since a lengthy pennant waves from her main mast.”

We observed the vessel heading in our direction for fifteen minutes. It was impossible for me to accept, though, that the Meridian was visible to her from so far away, or that she could possibly identify this submarine engine. Before long, the Canadian told me that she was a massive, two-decked, armoured ram. Dense clouds of dark smoke billowed out of her pair of funnels. Her sails were tightly gathered and secured to the yards. No flag was raised at her mizzen-peak. Because of the space between us, we could not make out the hues of her pennant, which drifted like a slender strip of fabric. She moved forward with speed. Should Captain Sorel permit her to draw near, we might have a possibility of being saved.
“If that ship sails closer than a mile to us, I intend to leap into the ocean, and I suggest you follow suit,” said Tom Harlan, “Sir.”

I remained silent regarding the Canadian’s proposal, keeping my gaze fixed upon the vessel. Regardless of whether she was Russian, American, French, or English, I was certain she would rescue us provided we managed to arrive at her side. Moments later, a plume of white smoke erupted from the ship’s bow; a few seconds passed before a heavy object plummeted into the sea, sending a spray of water against the stern of the Meridian, followed immediately by the sharp crack of a detonation.
“What! our attackers are shooting!” I cried out.
“If it pleases you, sir,” Tom stated, “the unicorn has been identified by them, and they are shooting in our direction.”
“However,” I cried out, “they must certainly perceive that there are men inside the container?”
“It might be for that reason,” Tom Harlan answered, gazing at me.

A sudden illumination flooded my thoughts. Surely they understood at last the credibility of the reports regarding the alleged monster. Without question, aboard the Evangeline, when the Canadian pierced it with his harpoon, Commander Hallett had identified the purported narwhal as an underwater craft, far more perilous than any mythical whale. Indeed, it had to be; and across every ocean, they were currently hunting this instrument of ruin. Truly frightening! if, as we surmised, Captain Sorel utilized the Meridian for acts of retribution. During the night we were confined in that chamber, deep in the Indian Ocean, had he not assaulted a ship? The individual interred in the coral graveyard, had he not perished from the impact inflicted by the Meridian? Yes, I reiterate, it must be so. A segment of the enigmatic life of Captain Sorel had been revealed; and, even if his true identity remained unknown, at the very least, the countries allied against him were no longer pursuing a phantom beast, but a human who had sworn a lethal vendetta against them. The entire terrifying history surfaced in my mind. Rather than encountering allies on the incoming vessel, we could anticipate only ruthless foes. Yet the gunfire clattered around us. Several projectiles hit the water and skipped, vanishing into the distance. However, none struck the Meridian. The ship was situated no more than three miles away. Despite the intense bombardment, Captain Sorel remained absent from the deck; yet, had one of the pointed shells impacted the hull of the Meridian, the result would have been catastrophic. The Canadian then said, “Sir, we must do all we can to get out of this dilemma. Let us signal them. They will then, perhaps, understand that we are honest folks.”
Tom Harlan reached for his handkerchief to signal with, yet no sooner had he shown it than an iron hand hit him, forcing him to collapse onto the deck regardless of his immense power.
“Idiot!” the Captain cried, “are you hoping to be impaled by the Meridian’s spike prior to it being launched at our ship?”

It was dreadful to listen to Captain Sorel; it was even more frightening to behold him. A deathly pallor covered his features, and a convulsion gripped his heart. It surely stopped pulsing for a moment. His pupils had shrunk in terror. He did not talk, he bellowed, while leaning his torso ahead and shaking the Canadian’s shoulders. Afterward, abandoning him and facing the warship, which continued to shower him with cannon fire, he shouted in a mighty tone, “Ah, ship of an accursed nation, you know who I am! I do not want your colours to know you by! Look! and I will show you mine!”

At the front of the platform, Captain Sorel spread out a dark banner, matching the one he had previously set at the South Pole. Just then, a projectile hit the exterior of the Meridian at an angle, failing to penetrate the hull; after bouncing off close to the Captain, it vanished into the ocean. He gave a shrug, and turning to me, stated curtly, “Go down, you and your companions, go down!”
“Are you intending to assault this ship?” I shouted, “Sir.”
“I intend to send it to the bottom, sir.”
“Are you not going to do that?”

“I will perform the task,” he answered with detachment. “And I suggest you refrain from judging me, sir. Destiny has revealed to you that which should have remained hidden. The assault is underway; descend.”
“What kind of ship is this?”
“Are you unaware? Fine! That is even preferable! Its origin, for your purposes, shall remain concealed. Descend!”

There was no choice but to comply. Roughly fifteen crewmen gathered around the Captain, their gazes fixed upon the approaching ship with relentless animosity. It was palpable that a shared craving for retribution stirred within every heart. I descended below decks just as a further shell impacted the Meridian, and I caught the Captain shouting:

“Attack, insane craft! Rain down your futile fire! Even then, you shall not evade the ram of the Meridian. Yet this is not the location where you will meet your end! I refuse to let your wreckage commingle with the remains of the Avenger!”

I arrived at my quarters. The Captain and his second officer stayed upon the deck. The propeller began to turn, and the Meridian, traveling rapidly, quickly escaped the range of the vessel’s cannons. Nevertheless, the chase persisted, and Captain Sorel was satisfied to maintain the gap between us.

At approximately four o'clock, unable to suppress my restlessness any longer, I made my way toward the main stairs. Finding the panel slid back, I stepped out onto the deck. The Captain continued to pace back and forth in a state of visible distress. His gaze was fixed upon the vessel, positioned five or six miles downwind.

Circling it in the manner of a savage animal, he pulled it toward the east, permitting them to follow. Yet he refrained from striking. Could it be that he remained uncertain? I desired to intervene again. However, I had barely uttered a word before Captain Sorel commanded me to be quiet, saying:

“I represent the law, just as I represent the judge! I am the one who suffers, and there stands the one who causes that suffering! Because of him, everything I held dear, treasured, and held in high regard has been taken from me—my homeland, my spouse, my offspring, my sire, and my dam. I watched every one of them die! Everything I despise is located there! Do not speak another word!”
After taking one final glance at the man-of-war as it began to build up steam, I returned to where Tom and Baptiste were waiting.
“We are going to fly!” I shouted.
“Excellent!” Tom remarked. “What name does this ship go by?”

“I am uncertain; yet, regardless of its nature, it shall be sent to the bottom prior to nightfall. Regardless, it is preferable to go down alongside it than to become partners in a vengeance whose righteousness remains beyond our ability to determine,” said I.
“I share that view,” Tom Harlan remarked with composure. “We shall hold off until dark.”

Darkness fell. A profound quiet governed the ship. According to the compass, the Meridian remained on its original heading. It drifted upon the water, swaying gently.
